# 36.3Enhancing Internet of Things Intelligence Using Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence for Smart Decision-Making

Sandeep Kumar Hegde

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-3](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-3)

## **3.1** Introduction

In healthcare, artificial intelligence (AI) is significantly bridging Internet of Things (IoT) to offer remote patient management, disease prediction, and innovative personalized treatments. AI algorithms likewise run within wearables to monitor biological signs and send alerts to health professionals with real-time monitoring changes from these systems for disease early detection and facilitate timely health interventions that will improve outcome. Also, patients’ outcomes improve because early disease detection and timely medical intervention are implemented. AI-enabled IoT solutions have brought improvements to telemedicine, real-time health monitoring, and automated diagnosis, while also making them cost-effective and accessible in healthcare \[[1](#ch11.xhtml#r149)\].

Simply put, the recent integration of AI and machine learning (ML) into the IoT has brought a revolution in the old sectors, with a view to develop much more intelligent and efficient decision-making ways, among other issues that these sectors face. The integration includes intelligent systems for real-time processing of large datasets, making very intelligent, versatile, and autonomous designs across diverse applications. One of the impressive contributions in this domain is the use of AI and ML to secure IoT systems. Traditional IoT frameworks include many issues related to data vulnerabilities and unauthorized access. To cope with these problems, researchers have proposed new ML-based security models that analyze current technologies and vulnerabilities associated with intelligent IoT systems. These models will use ML classifiers to detect and prevent security threats to improve the robustness of IoT networks \[[2](#ch11.xhtml#r150)\]. As a preventive measure, AI-based solutions have been 37.developed to analyze data to detect anomalies and, consequently, improve the security and reliability of healthcare IoT systems \[[3](#ch11.xhtml#r151)\]. These datasets are analyzed through AI algorithms for optimizing flow of traffic, reducing congestion, and enhancing emergency response systems. AI-driven IoT-based smart city initiatives promote urban development, lower emission of carbon, and uplift the quality of life for the citizens \[[4](#ch11.xhtml#r152)\].

Combined AI and IoT implementations are also proving to be instrumental in the big breakthroughs in agriculture, whereby smart farming employs AI-enabled IoT devices for precision farming. Sensors then provide a great platform for monitoring soil conditions, weather, and crop health so that the farmers can optimize irrigation, fertilization, and pest control \[[5](#ch11.xhtml#r153)\]. The information is then processed using AI algorithms to come up with actionable recommendations whose outputs will improve crop yields under less resource wastage and save on food security improved by better resource use. Another challenge is fast looming: processing power coupled with AI-based IoT systems, especially from the standpoint of the edge device systems, especially from the perspective of the edge device. Many IoT devices operate in very remote or low-power environments that severely restrict the complexity of AI models they can run. Therefore, edge AI and federated learning (FL) are being developed to enable local AI processing instead of over-reliance on cloud computing, and that may even be through reducing response time, both of which are necessary in real-time decision-making with AI-powered IoT ecosystems \[[6](#ch11.xhtml#r154)\].

This work shall endeavor to highlight the key ML algorithms for the IoT, their uses, and the common issues that arise in smart systems controlled by intelligent reasoning. Basically, the ML specific to the IoT can be further classified into supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning (RL). Supervised algorithms such as support vector machines (SVMs), random forests, and deep neural networks are used in predictive maintenance, health monitoring, and fault diagnosis and detection procedures. Clustering, anomaly, and outlier detection algorithms such as K-means clustering and principal component analysis (PCA) tackle the problems arising from smart city applications and industrial IoT. Presently, the most popular application of RL is in domains such as robotics, traffic management, and smart energy metering, where the focus is on real-time decision-making \[[7](#ch11.xhtml#r155)\].

To forecast future trends, patterns can be recognized through historical information by AI and ML so preventive maintenance, demand forecasting, and resource allocation may be realized. In the case of industrial IoT (IIoT), predictive analytics might point toward the prediction of equipment failure, thereby reducing downtime and maintenance costs \[[8](#ch11.xhtml#r156)\]. Smart grids, smart agriculture, and environmental monitoring are examples of how this research will regard flexible energy solutions to be implemented sustainably into IoT applications. The much-anticipated facility for automation comes from AI’s integration with IoT. This study attempts to analyze how autonomous decision-making is aided without or with little human intervention at IoT systems using AI and ML. Applications of AI-based IoT would include automated transportation, supply chain management, and robotic process automation \[[9](#ch11.xhtml#r157)\]. Organizations investing in AI-powered IoT solutions would form the future marketplace where competition will be extremely fierce. Consequently, the study seeks to explore AI and ML in the development of IoT intelligence concerning applications, 38.challenges, and futures. The study intends to investigate how AI is transforming IoT by means of AI-based decision-making in IoT ecosystems, and consequently their impacts on future automation and intelligence of interlinked systems \[[10](#ch11.xhtml#r158)\].

## **3.2** Literature Review

This review explored key research papers discussing these intersections of AI, ML, and IoT, underlining benefits, applications, and challenges. Several researchers have studied the relationship between AI and improved decision-making in IoT. According to Ficco et al. \[[11](#ch11.xhtml#r159)\], AI helps IoT devices not only collect data but also provide real-time insights and automate decision-making processes. IoT systems can predict future outcomes, optimize resource allocation, and recognize patterns using ML algorithms. These are some of the intelligent decision-making processes used in smart homes, healthcare, industrial robotics, and smart cities. Additionally, another study \[[12](#ch11.xhtml#r160)\] emphasizes that AI-driven IoT solutions are best suited to achieve higher efficiencies with lesser human input in complex tasks. It shows examples of how deep learning (DL) models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), help IoT devices analyze image data, speech data, and sensor data; this assists in the automation of vehicles, smart surveillance, and environmental monitoring in precision and quick response owing to AI decision-making. One broad area of AI augmentation for IoT intelligence is predictive analytics. The work by Shams et al. \[[13](#ch11.xhtml#r161)\] explains how AI-based IoT systems use ML models for predicting potential equipment failures, optimizing supply chain management, and improving energy efficiency. AI methods, especially in DL architectures like CNN and RNN, have made their way to real-time analytics with a lot of success. CNN-based AI models under the survey of Rane et al. \[[14](#ch11.xhtml#r162)\] showed such a significant achievement in real-time use of bright and cloudy feed from IoT-based smart surveillance systems, which proved to transcend safety and automation with over 92% in processing accuracy.

In considering predictive IoT systems in which devices learn experiences and adapt to dynamic environments, Simuni et al. \[[15](#ch11.xhtml#r163)\] hold mainly RL ML approaches as a focus area. RL applications in IoT can be cast in many areas, such as energy management, smart agriculture, and adaptive traffic control systems, whereby continuous learning adds to the decision-making mechanism. Security is the primary issue within the IoT ecosystems, and AI plays a vital role in advancing the state of the art concerning the detection of cyber threats and anomalies. AI-based anomaly detection is one of the techniques of improving IoT security by identifying patterns that go against the expected ones in network traffic, device behaviors, and even system logs, according to Hemamalini et al. \[[16](#ch11.xhtml#r164)\]. Anomaly detection techniques utilize learning algorithms like SVMs, decision trees, and DL approaches to detect security breaches as they happen. AI-led intrusion detection systems operate effectively in the IoT environment according to Liao et al. \[[17](#ch11.xhtml#r165)\]. Smart city initiatives rest firmly on the AI-enabled IoT solutions for traffic optimization, waste management, and public safety. The work proposed in ref. \[[18](#ch11.xhtml#r166)\] states that AI augments IoT-enabled smart city systems by analyzing real-time data from sensors, cameras, and environmental monitoring devices, thus enabling informed decision-making by the city planners regarding 39.infrastructure, pollution control, and energy distribution. Smart city applications refer to an area where RL-based AI models are deployed for traffic management, energy optimization, and resource allocation. Studies by El Alaoui et al. \[[19](#ch11.xhtml#r167)\] indicated that AI-based smart traffic systems dynamically adjust traffic light patterns with real-time IoT sensor data, reducing congestion rates by as much as 35%.

The work proposed in ref. \[[20](#ch11.xhtml#r168)\] discusses how AI-powered IoT systems improve urban traffic management through forecasting congestion patterns and adjusting signal timings to improve urban traffic management. Smart transportation applications supported by AI, such as autonomous vehicles and ride-sharing platforms, try to take ML on board to optimize routes, minimize fuel consumption, and improve the overall experience of commuters. AI and IoT have made a revolution in the field of remote patient monitoring, disease detection, and personalized treatment. As reported by Hussein et al. \[[21](#ch11.xhtml#r169)\], AI-enabled IoT devices capitalize on data analytics regarding wearable sensors, medical imaging, and electronic health records to recognize early signs of diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiac conditions. Hence, they provide assistance to the medical sector in developing bespoke therapeutic plans based on information gleaned in real time. In this regard, the work by Bharathi et al. \[[22](#ch11.xhtml#r170)\] analyzes the performance of predictive AI models for epidemic outbreak detection using data streams from IoT-enabled health monitoring devices. The work proposed in ref. \[[23](#ch11.xhtml#r171)\] indicated that AI-powered robotics and predictive maintenance have greatly contributed to industrial efficiency. One study shows that AI-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) are more than 95% accurate in detecting cyber threats, thus amplifying the monitoring of IoT \[[24](#ch11.xhtml#r172)\]. For the purpose of anomaly detection and intrusion prevention, AI-based models such as Autoencoders, Isolation Forests, and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) provide good grounds for investigation. Conventional AI models need storage of classified data at a centralized point, endangering privacy and confidence in data security. Conversely, FL remedies this situation by putting in place mechanisms necessary for AI model training over multiple decentralized IoT devices without sharing raw data \[[25](#ch11.xhtml#r173)\].

The work proposed in ref. \[[26](#ch11.xhtml#r174)\] stated in their work that there should be automation with the help of AI, especially in IIoT, where self-learning robots in production lines are optimizing production operations. According to Dhiman and Alghamdi \[[27](#ch11.xhtml#r175)\], these robots use computer vision for versatility in applications in various manufacturing tasks, DL and RL. This achievement also ensures predictive analytics in the AI-driven supply chain management for smooth logistics and inventory control. The introduction of AI into IoT, however, has caused several complications including data privacy, computational constraints, and ethical considerations. AI-based IoT systems will certainly have to consider privacy issues as they deal with huge amounts of personal data that are being collected by connected devices \[[28](#ch11.xhtml#r176)\]. User data must meet compliance with regulations such as General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and HIPAA to adhere to user protection measures. The future of AI-powered IoT technology lies at the nexus of dynamic popular fifth-generation (5G) networks, advances in DL capabilities, and increased AI governance. The work proposed in ref. \[[29](#ch11.xhtml#r177)\] provides sufficient justification on this ultra-low latency: fast data transfer with improved reliability. Real-time applications such as autonomous vehicles, smart healthcare, and industrial automation will reap substantial benefits from this advancement. AI and 40.IoT have made great advancements in remote patient tissue monitoring, diagnosis, and wearable health devices. The AI-based models for interpreting ECG readings achieve 93.4% success in finding anomalies in ECG traces, according to Ala et al. \[[30](#ch11.xhtml#r178)\], helping enhance early disease detection. Delivery of patient vitals is automatically analyzed by IoT-enabled AI healthcare systems during real-time emergencies, so as to reducing delays in the admission of patients to hospitals by 25%. AI-based precision agriculture utilizes IoT sensors for monitoring soil, managing irrigation, and predicting any disease in crops. These systems will improve the maximum crop yield production at 18% and water consumption limit at 25% according to Ozkan-Okay et al. \[[31](#ch11.xhtml#r179)\].

The other research group by Shwetabh and Ambhaikar \[[32](#ch11.xhtml#r180)\] basically lays down the workings of explainable AI (XAI) in the context of the IoT in transparency, interpretability, and accountability in the AI-based decision-making process. In fact, the unending development in AI models was intended to make them ethical, fair, and unbiased, thus establishing harmonized directions for responsible implementation of AI within IoT ecosystems. AI and ML have evolved rapidly in most IoT ecosystems, leading to very significant improvements in efficiency, automation, and their decision-making processes. AI-based IoT applications have mainly gained place in smart cities, industrial automation, healthcare, and security. The researchers explored the possibility of applying DL, RL, and FL, among other AI techniques, toward increasing IoT intelligence and enhancing real-time decision-making. This segment presents added insights from current literature on AI and ML modifications in IoT applications. DL directly enhances IoT-based analytic and decision-making processes. According to Nadella and Gonaygunta \[[33](#ch11.xhtml#r181)\], CNNs and long short-term memory (LSTM) DL architectures facilitate and simplify data processing tasks of IoT devices with their speed and power by handling more complex and general data patterns than before. As opposed to traditional ML, which relies on centralized data processing, FL allows IoT devices to collaboratively train models without actually sharing exquisitely distilled information itself \[[34](#ch11.xhtml#r182)\]. The work proposed in ref. \[[35](#ch11.xhtml#r183)\] examines how FL can be beneficial for use in environments such as healthcare and smart homes, where data of interest have privacy-related concerns but may still be learned from ensemble settings. This decentralized mechanism offers an added advantage in security for the data being processed and is compliant with privacy regulations such as GDPR. AI is activated to optimize energy consumption and distribution in smart grids. ML models forecast electricity demand patterns more logically and thus optimize power distribution. Research by Nazir et al. \[[36](#ch11.xhtml#r184)\] indicates that AI-based smart grids reduce energy wastage by 20–25% by dynamically tailoring power supply based on real-time data from IoT sensors.

The attention that XAI has gained recently in IoT applications is because of the requirement to have transparency and accountability in AI-driven decisions. Such black-box nature of traditional models has been stated by Rafique et al. \[[37](#ch11.xhtml#r185)\], hence making it impossible for users to detect the reasons behind it. The mere adaptation of XAI techniques in IoT is meant to ensure interpretability and accountability in such domains as autonomous systems, healthcare, finance. A research study by Kheder and Mohammed \[[38](#ch11.xhtml#r186)\] indicates that the analysis of transformer-based natural language processing (NLP) models such as BERT and GPT shows their capabilities in the 41.understanding and processing of human speech with high accuracy by IoT-enabled smart assistants. Such NLP technologies enhance automated customer services, complicated smart home automation, and conversational AI applications, thereby making IoT systems more intuitive and user-friendly. Edge computing develops a means for reducing high latency and bandwidth limitations from the cloud by providing local DIY solutions to IoT systems. According to Bukhowah et al. \[[39](#ch11.xhtml#r187)\], AI-driven edge computing provides real-time processing on local IoT devices with little requisite connection to the cloud. The work proposed in Liu et al. \[[40](#ch11.xhtml#r188)\] proved that AI deployed on edge devices shows a 40–50% reduction in latency of processing, thereby paving the way for real-time AI-driven decision-making in critical applications of IoT such as autonomous vehicles and industrial automation.

RL has taken some firm footprints in given adaptive and self-learning IoT environments. The work proposed in ref. \[[41](#ch11.xhtml#r189)\] depicted how RL algorithms permit IoT devices to learn their optimal policies through trial and error, ultimately making it suitable for applications such as smart grid optimization, robotic automation, and self-driving vehicles. RL-based IoT systems increase the efficiency of decision-making while adapting to varying situations and hence improves the performance of the overall system. AI has effectively enhanced energy management and distribution in smart-grid systems. As work observed, ML models in IoT-enabled grids forecast electricity demand, detect faults, and optimize energy consumption. AI motivated smart grids undertake real-time energy management by fusing IoT sensor data thereby improving the stability and sustainability of power systems. Industrial IoT (IIoT) has gained advances from AI-centered techniques for anomaly detection. The work proposed in ref. \[[42](#ch11.xhtml#r190)\] supported the potency of ML algorithms under AI to predict equipment failure and minimize downtime in manufacturing operations. AI-oriented IoT solutions with predictive maintenance models pinpoint irregularities in machinery operation, allowing industries to reduce operational costs and increase efficiency. The flipside of AI-enabled IoT becomes the existence of bias, fairness, and ethical issues. According to Karimullah et al. \[[43](#ch11.xhtml#r191)\], AI algorithms in IoT decision-making systems could result in unfair judgments; inheriting the biases present in their training data. AI equips IoT-based smart home automation systems for learning user behavior and optimizing energy use. Within the smart home, AI models can predict user preferences and automate appliance control enhancing security through facial recognition and voice assistants \[[44](#ch11.xhtml#r192)\]. Reduction in energy consumption of 18–22% by AI-enabled smart home systems has been observed in the improvement of user convenience The use of AI in IIoT makes the industrial processes more productive, ensures automation, and also assures quality in control. The work proposed in ref. \[[45](#ch11.xhtml#r193)\] claimed that AI-powered predictive maintenance, supply chain analytics, and robotic automation made significant improvements in manufacturing efficiency.

## **3.3** Proposed Methodology

The proposed methodology improves smart environmental capacity through real-time decisions characterized by the integration of AI–ML with IoT. This mostly refers to data collection, preprocessing, selection and application of AI models, and evaluation. 42.Other problems tackled by the research include data privacy, computational efficiency, and scalable systems. The architecture of the system intends to build three pillars: perception, network, and application. The perception layer is made up of IoT sensors and devices that collect real-time data. This study is intended to enhance IoT intelligence by the security-in-platform realization of AI and ML for smart decision-making. The proposed solution is a structured methodology for the implementation of such systems so that data are collected and processed in real time, then AI-based analytics, decision-making, security provision, and performance validation follow.

The initial stage of realization of these goals is done through IoT data acquisition and preprocessing, that is, data collected from different smart sensors, connected devices, and cloud platforms. The generated data is mostly unstructured and noisy, needing data cleaning, normalization, and feature extraction. Advanced data preprocessing techniques like PCA and Min-Max normalization are implemented for the methodology to utilize relevant and quality data for AI purposes. Furthermore, data is fetched in real time using protocols such as Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) and Apache Kafka for streaming and storage before processing. The methodology then uses the data pre-processed to run AI and ML algorithms for extracting insight and making intelligent decisions. Based on the specific IoT application, a different AI technique is deployed. This involved supervised learning models such as SVMs and Random Forest to predictive maintenance activities of industrial IoT and disease prediction in healthcare IoT.

[Figure 3.1](#ch11.xhtml#f8) depicts the proposed architectural flow diagram. Architecture for intelligence in IoT includes business models for AI and ML, starting from the IoT devices and sensors capturing raw data from the environment-temperature, motion, or image-and sending this information to the data collection layer, where the data is either transmitted to cloud or edge servers through dedicated communication protocols such as MQTT or HTTP. Once entering the system, the data preprocessing layer applies cleansing, filtering, and normalization that keep the data in a usable and relevant form as an input for further analysis in a decision-making context. In some cases, the edge processing task involves local analysis of data to allow the system to make decisions in real time by bypassing the latency of sending all data to the cloud. The AI and ML layer, in essence, forms the core of the system where good training is carried out by the ML models on historical IoT data to enable them to detect patterns, make predictions, and act in the best interest for enhanced decision-making. While human and machine interactions benefit from a continuous feedback loop for improvements—from data collection through retraining —the decision-making layer renders AI and ML outputs into some form of actionability, either being alerts or control actions. The User Interface and visualization functions furnish the user with the means to view the system and facilitate other forms of manual user intervention when required. In this case, a feedback loop is established to permit the system to grow in a continuous fashion by feeding in new data for the fine-tuning and improvement of the models. Finally, the security and privacy layer takes care of secure data transfer and storage, user privacy, and system integrity against vulnerabilities.

![Figure 3.1 Proposed architectural flow diagram.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C003_001.jpg)

**Figure 3.1** Proposed architectural flow diagram.[⏎](#ch11.xhtml#f8b)

43.44.The proposed framework optimizes energy consumption with lightweight AI models, including hardware acceleration techniques such as tensor processing units (TPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs). The other strategies include sleep scheduling and dynamic power management for unused energy loss savings, which makes IoT power consumption more environment friendly and cost-effective. Also, in making IoT intelligently adaptable, the methodology brings in XAI to broaden the scope of decision transparency. One common problem associated with AI models is that they operate as black-box systems. This hinders the end-users from having a correct interpretation of AI-generated decisions. By the adoption of several XAI methodologies such as Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME), the expected system ensures that AI predictions become interpretable and understandable, with a good measure of justifiability. This is particularly useful in critical applications like healthcare and industrial automation because oversight and trust in AI decisions become very important. Connectivity among devices, as well as connectivity to cloud-edge servers, is achieved at the network layer, while the application layer employs AI models to process data and make intelligent decisions. Different applications would have different associated IoT sensors.

The proposed system will be assessed with respect to accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, response time, and energy efficiency. Performance metrics will provide an insight into how viable are the AI-driven IoT applications in terms of effectiveness and scalability. Different ML and DL models will be compared for their efficiency, computational cost, and accuracy. Among others, SVM, Random Forest, CNN, and transformer-based models will be examined for the best use case in IoT applications. Such exhaustive simulation and field trials will validate the AI models’ performance, whilst the AI algorithms will be implemented and fine-tuned using TensorFlow, PyTorch, and MATLAB toolkits. The proposed approach tends to maximize AI models in the limitation of IoT devices through model quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation to boost computational efficiency and reduce power consumption. To this end, ethical concerns on AI model bias, fairness, and accountability are examined. All AI models go through a panoply of bias mitigation techniques to ensure equity in decision-making for all applications. Scalability improvement will be achieved by network optimization, improvement in edge computing capabilities, and expansion of AI training capabilities. Thereafter improvements will be diverted to self-learning AI systems for IoT. An incremental deployment strategy for integrating AI-enabled IoT solutions into industries, health, smart cities, and logistics would be conceived through pilot tests, user feedback, and continuous improvements. Real-time decision-making, augmented security, and sustainable computing are thus integrated into this methodology to meet the above research objectives. This methodology lays down a structured and systematic approach to obtaining smart, efficient, and secure IoT intelligence with the help of AI and ML. With strategic consideration of major challenges such as data processing, decision-making, security, scalability, and energy efficiency, the proposed framework opens up a new future for autonomous, adaptive, and highly intelligent next generation IoT ecosystems.

## **45.3.4** Experimental Results

The dataset required for experimental investigation was gathered from Kaggle repository which comprises various IoT data collected from a very large number of sensors situated in smart environments as shown in [Figure 3.2](#ch11.xhtml#f9).

![Figure 3.2 Confusion matrix obtained with Random Forest for anomaly detection on IoT sensor data.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C003_002.jpg)

**Figure 3.2** Confusion matrix obtained with Random Forest for anomaly detection on IoT sensor data.[⏎](#ch11.xhtml#f9b)

This big dataset tries to develop ML and AI applications to make intelligent decisions based on real-time IoT sensor inputs. The dataset contains a vast number of attributes, including measurements of environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, pressure, motion, and light, among others. Therefore, every point of the data comprises crucial timestamp and metadata information and dynamically reflect the nature of such IoT systems in smart homes, factories, cities, etc. The collection contains both labeled and unlabeled data, wherein some sensors provide continuous-type data streams while others record discrete event-type information. The dataset, due to its high volume and variety, provides immense opportunities for experimentation on a variety of ML and AI algorithms-from regression and classification to anomaly detection-that can enable smart decision-making pertaining to diverse use cases such as, among others, energy efficiency, predictive maintenance, automation, and real-time environmental change response.

46.Images and speech were the primary applications for CNNs along with LSTMs to cater for the needs of IoT systems. In smart surveillance applications, CNNs had a classification accuracy of 96.3%, while RNN performed with an accuracy measure of 92.7% in speech recognition. Transformer-based techniques such as BERT for NLP applications have better context understanding but have high computational costs. AI models when deployed in edges showed a very significant latency advantage over cloud processing. Reduced inference time of 40% was observed in NVIDIA Jetson compared to that of cloud AI services. This improvement comes largely with applications including autonomous vehicles and industrial automation that need real-time decision-making. FL was tested to check privacy-preserving AI applicability for IoT applications. In percentage terms, FL attained almost similar accuracy, that is 87.5% compared with traditional centralized training (89.3%) with reduction in data transmission costs by 70%. These results indicate that FL can enhance data security while keeping the model performance effective. RL models were used in smart traffic control systems. RL-based models reduced congestion by 35% and increased the throughput of vehicles by 28%. Clearly, RL provides scope for adaptive decision-making in dynamic environments.

Healthcare applications test IoT-based wearables with AI models. Accuracy of 93.4% was achieved in the prediction of cardiac anomalies by the AI model devised for early disease detection. The system of intelligent alerting improved patient welfare by reducing emergency response time by about 25% in scenarios realized in real time. Advanced ML models were developed that optimally predict the electricity demands according to the desirable energy management needs of smart grids. 50.In this case study on smart traffic management, real-time data from IoT sensors was used to optimize traffic signal timing through RL models. Compared with the conventional traffic signal systems based on older timers, the RL system showed a 51.35% reduction in congestion, while the vehicle flow improved by 28%. This brings the possibility of smart IoT in making cities more mobile in terms of travel time. Several AI models are currently being investigated for their IoT-based potential applications such as precision agriculture, to improve irrigation and soil health monitoring. Also, the system increases its effectiveness by improving overall crop yield efficiency by 18% and reducing water consumption by approximately 25% by analyzing thermal, humidity, and soil moisture sensor data.

## **3.5** Conclusion

The study on enhancing IoT intelligence using ML and AI for smart decision-making proves the transformative potential that AI-driven solutions have on optimizing IoT ecosystems. It will efficiently process data, automate decision-making, improve security, and enhance the overall performance of the system with the introduction of sophisticated AI and ML algorithms within IoT networks. The methodology elaborates chronologically on issues such as data acquisition, real-time analytics, anomaly detection, cybersecurity, and energy efficiency, which surely will make IoT applications smart, scalable, and sustainable in operation. The most important thing this study has revealed is that real-time decision-making is of utmost significance in IoT environments.

# 55.4Machine Learning and Internet of ThingsSmart Decision-Making Applications

R. Ramya, P. Kumar, K. Vanitha, and C. Saranya

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-4](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-4)

## **4.1** Introduction

The Internet of Things (IoT) connects billions of smart devices, generating vast data that requires intelligent decision-making. Machine learning (ML) algorithms enhance IoT by enabling automation, predictive analytics, and anomaly detection across domains like smart homes, healthcare, and industry. Unlike traditional rule-based systems, ML models – such as supervised, unsupervised, and deep learning – adapt to complex environments for real-time insights. Emerging technologies like edge artificial intelligence (AI), federated learning (FL), and explainable AI (XAI) further improve efficiency and security. This chapter explores ML’s role in IoT-driven smart decisions, key challenges, and future trends shaping intelligent automation. The integration of ML and AI with IoT systems has revolutionized industries, enhancing efficiency and decision-making. However, challenges like data management, computational demands, and privacy concerns persist. Future research should focus on optimizing advanced IoT architectures and secure data-sharing frameworks \[[1](#ch12.xhtml#r194)–[5](#ch12.xhtml#r198)\].

### 4.2.1 Overview of IoT and ML

The **IoT** connects smart devices to collect and exchange data, enabling automation and real-time decision-making. **ML** enhances IoT by analyzing data patterns, predicting outcomes, and enabling intelligent, adaptive decision-making.

### 4.2.2 Smart Decision-Making in IoT Using ML

ML enables smart decision-making in IoT by analyzing real-time data, detecting patterns, and making automated predictions. ML models help optimize resource management, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, and adaptive automation, improving efficiency and accuracy in IoT applications like smart homes, healthcare, and industrial systems \[[6](#ch12.xhtml#r199)\]. ## **56.4.2** EDGE AND CLOUD COMPUTING IN IoT ML

Edge computing is the concept of capturing, storing, processing, and analyzing data closer to the location where it is needed to improve response times and save bandwidth ([Figure 4.2](#ch12.xhtml#f17)). Hence, edge computing is a distributed computing framework that brings applications closer to data sources such as IoT devices, local end devices, or edge servers. The rationale of edge computing is that computing should happen in the proximity of data sources. Therefore, we envision that edge computing could have as big an impact on our society as we have witnessed with cloud computing**.**

![Figure 4.2 Edge computing.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C004_002.jpg)

**Figure 4.2** Edge computing.[⏎](#ch12.xhtml#f17b)

## **4.3** SECURITY AND PRIVACY IN IoT ML

*   *Strong Authentication:* Manufacturers are now placing a premium on robust password policies and two-factor authentication to ensure that only authorized users can access IoT devices, making it considerably harder for malicious actors to breach security.
*   *Firmware Updates:* Regular updates and patches have become imperative to rectify known vulnerabilities. Manufacturers are increasingly providing mechanisms for automatic updates to keep devices secure, minimizing the window of vulnerability.
*   *57.Encryption:* Data encryption, both in transit and at rest, has assumed a central role in safeguarding IoT data. Secure communication protocols like transport layer security (TLS) are employed to protect data while it traverses the network \[[7](#ch12.xhtml#r200), [8](#ch12.xhtml#r201)\].
*   *Network Segmentation:* The practice of isolating IoT devices from critical networks has gained traction as a strategy to contain potential security breaches. This segmentation helps limit access to sensitive data, minimizing the damage in case of a breach.
*   *Device Management Platforms:* IoT device management platforms offer centralized control and monitoring of IoT devices. These platforms facilitate remote updates, access control, and robust security monitoring. [Figure 4.3](#ch12.xhtml#f18) shows device management.
    
    ![Figure 4.3 Device management.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C004_003.jpg)
    
    **Figure 4.3** Device management.[⏎](#ch12.xhtml#f18b)
    

### 4.3.1 XAI in IoT-Based Smart Decisions

XAI enhances transparency and trust in ML-driven IoT systems by making decision-making processes understandable. In IoT applications like smart healthcare, industrial automation, and security, XAI helps users interpret ML predictions, identify biases, and improve system reliability. [Figure 4.4](#ch12.xhtml#f19) shows XAI helping users. Techniques such as Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME), and attention mechanisms provide insights into how ML models process IoT data, ensuring fairness, accountability, and better decision-making.

## **58.4.4** DATA COLLECTION AND PREPROCESSING IN IoT

IoT systems rely on diverse data sources to gather information. From sensor data capturing physical measurements to machine data tracking equipment performance and user-generated inputs, these systems collect a wealth of information. Various methods, including real-time streaming and event-driven collection, ensure comprehensive data acquisition.

59.Data quality is paramount in IoT systems. Cleaning techniques address missing, inconsistent, and noisy data, while integration and transformation processes prepare information for analysis. ML process is shown in [Figure 4.5](#ch12.xhtml#f20). Ensuring accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, and reliability is crucial for deriving meaningful insights and making informed decisions in IoT applications**.**

![Figure 4.5 ML process.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C004_005.jpg)

**Figure 4.5** ML process.[⏎](#ch12.xhtml#f20b)

### 4.4.1 Sensor Data Captures Physical Measurements from the Environment

*   Environmental sensors measure conditions like temperature (thermometers), humidity (hygrometers), and pressure (barometers)
*   Motion sensors detect movement and orientation using accelerometers (measure acceleration) and gyroscopes (measure angular velocity)
*   Location sensors determine position using global positioning system (GPS) and radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags
*   Biometric sensors monitor physiological characteristics such as heart rate (pulse oximeters) and fingerprints (fingerprint scanners)

*Data integration* combines information from disparate sources merging data from multiple sensors and devices provides a comprehensive view. Matching datasets based on common attributes or keys aligns related information. Resolving schema and format differences ensures data compatibility. Handling data redundancy and duplication prevents inconsistencies and storage waste.

*60.Data transformation* modifies data to suit analysis needs, Normalization and scaling adjust numerical features to common ranges. Encoding categorical variables converts text labels to numerical representations using one-hot encoding (binary dummy variables) or label encoding (integer mapping). Feature extraction and engineering create new attributes from existing data (calculating ratios or aggregates). Aggregating and summarizing data at different granularities (hourly, daily) enables analysis at various levels of detail.

*   *FL for IoT Devices:* FL is a decentralized ML approach where multiple IoT devices collaboratively train a model without sharing raw data. Instead of sending data to a central server, IoT devices process data locally and only send model updates, ensuring privacy and efficiency.
*   *FL for IoT?:* 
    *   *Data Privacy:* Sensitive IoT data remains on the device.
    *   *Reduced Bandwidth Usage:* Only model updates are sent, not raw data.
    *   *Lower Latency:* Local processing enables faster decision-making.
    *   *Personalization:* Each device can fine-tune models based on local conditions.
*   *FL Works in IoT:* 
    *   *Local Model Training:* IoT devices train models on their local data.
    *   *Model Updates Aggregation:* Devices send only model updates (gradients) to a central aggregator.
    *   *Global Model Update:* The central server aggregates updates to improve the global model.

### 4.4.2 Reinforcement Learning for Smart IoT Systems

Reinforcement learning (RL) is an ML technique where IoT devices (agents) learn by interacting with their environment, making decisions, and receiving rewards or penalties. This enables smart and autonomous decision-making in IoT systems. RL in IoT environment is shown in [Figure 4.6](#ch12.xhtml#f21).

    *   *Automation:* IoT systems make intelligent decisions without human intervention.
2.  *RL Works in IoT:* 
    *   *Agent (IoT Device):* Makes decisions.
    *   *Environment:* The system where the IoT device operates.
    *   *Reward Function:* Measures the success of an action.

### 61.4.4.3 Anomaly Detection in IoT Networks Using ML

Anomaly detection in IoT networks involves identifying unusual behavior in sensor data, devices, or network traffic using ML. As IoT devices generate massive data streams, ML helps detect cyber threats, hardware failures, and operational inefficiencies in real time.

### 4.4.4 Use ML for Anomaly Detection in IoT

*   *Real-Time Monitoring:* ML detects anomalies instantly.
*   *Automated Threat Detection*: Identifies cyberattacks like DDoS, botnets, and intrusions.
*   *Fault Prediction:* Prevents equipment failures by analyzing sensor data.
*   *Reduces False Alarms:* ML models adapt to new patterns over time.

### 4.4.5 ML Detects Anomalies in IoT Networks

*   *Data Collection:* IoT devices send sensor and network data.
*   *Feature Extraction:* Important attributes (e.g., temperature, packet flow) are selected.
*   62. *Model Training:* ML algorithms learn normal behavior patterns.
*   *Anomaly Detection:* When new data deviates significantly, it is flagged as an anomaly.

## **63.4.5** CYBERSECURITY THREATS IN ML-POWERED IoT

1.  *Enhance Threat Hunting:* 
    *   AI-driven threat hunting continuously scans networks for suspicious activity.
    *   ML models analyze behavioral patterns to detect potential threats before damage.
    *   *Example:* CrowdStrike Falcon uses AI for proactive threat detection. Cybersecurity threats in ML are shown in [Figure 4.9](#ch12.xhtml#f24).
        
        ![Figure 4.9 Cybersecurity threats in ML.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C004_009.jpg)
        
        **Figure 4.9** Cybersecurity threats in ML.[⏎](#ch12.xhtml#f24b)
        

1.  *Detect Intrusions and Malware:* 
    *   AI-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) analyze network traffic in real time.
    *   ML models detect zero-day attacks and advanced malware by analyzing anomalies.
    *   *Example:* Darktrace uses AI to detect sophisticated cyber threats.
2.  *Discover Code Vulnerabilities:* 
    *   AI automates static and dynamic application security testing (SAST and DAST).
    *   ML scans source code to identify security flaws and potential exploits.
    *   *Example:* GitHub Copilot AI detects insecure coding patterns.
3.  *64.Enhance Network Security:* 
    *   AI strengthens firewalls and intrusion prevention systems (IPS).
    *   ML models identify abnormal network behaviors and prevent unauthorized access.
    *   *Example:* Cisco AI-driven network security solutions.
4.  *Detect Phishing:* 
    *   AI analyzes email content, URLs, and sender behavior to detect phishing attempts.
    *   ML continuously learns new phishing patterns to block evolving threats.
    *   *Example:* Google’s AI-powered Gmail spam filters detect and block phishing emails.
5.  *Predict Breach Risks:* 
    *   AI analyzes historical attack data to predict potential breaches.
    *   ML assigns risk scores to systems, users, and devices based on security posture.
    *   *Example:* IBM Watson for cybersecurity predicts attack trends.

## **4.6** APPLICATIONS OF ML IN SMART IoT SYSTEMS

Sensors in IoT devices and human interaction with these devices are considered a big source of data from which features can be extracted for ML algorithms to detect and learn useful patterns. This can be very useful in many healthcare and elderly care applications such as activity detection for health state assessment, fall detection, stress detection, fitness tracking, vital signs monitoring, and diseases’ diagnosis. ## **4.7** ML-DRIVEN SMART AGRICULTURE IN IoT

ML and the IoT are revolutionizing smart agriculture by enhancing efficiency, optimizing resources, and improving crop yields. Here’s how ML is driving innovation in agriculture through IoT:

1.  *Precision Farming:* 
    *   IoT sensors collect real-time data on soil health, moisture levels, temperature, and crop growth.
    *   ML algorithms analyze this data to optimize irrigation, fertilization, and pesticide use.
    *   *Example:* Smart irrigation systems adjust water supply based on soil moisture levels.
2.  *Crop Health Monitoring:* 
    *   AI-driven computer vision detects plant diseases, nutrient deficiencies, and pest infestations.
    *   66. ML models analyze drone and satellite images to identify affected areas.
    *   *Example:* AI-powered drones scan farmlands and provide early disease warnings.
3.  *Weather Prediction and Climate Adaptation:* 
    *   ML models analyze weather patterns and forecast rainfall, temperature, and drought risks. IoT devices adjust farming operations based on predicted climate conditions.
    *   *Example:* AI-based weather forecasting helps farmers plan planting and harvesting schedules. The ML–IoT in agriculture decision-making system is shown in [Figure 4.11](#ch12.xhtml#f26).
        
        ![Figure 4.11 ML–IoT in agriculture decision-making system.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C004_011.jpg)
        
        **Figure 4.11** ML–IoT in agriculture decision-making system.[⏎](#ch12.xhtml#f26b)
        

1.  *Smart Livestock Management:* 
    *   IoT wearables track animal health, movement, and feeding patterns.
    *   ML models analyze behavior to detect diseases and optimize breeding cycles.
    *   *Example:* Smart collars monitor cattle health and prevent disease outbreaks.
2.  *67.Automated Pest Control:* 
    *   AI-powered traps and sensors detect pests and apply pesticides only where needed.
    *   ML predicts pest outbreaks based on weather and environmental data.
    *   *Example:* Smart pheromone traps use ML to identify pest infestations.
3.  *Yield Prediction and Market Analysis:* 
    *   ML models analyze historical yield data, soil quality, and climate conditions to predict crop output.
    *   AI-driven market analysis helps farmers get the best prices for their produce.
    *   *Example:* AI-powered supply chain optimization ensures efficient crop distribution.
4.  *Autonomous Farming with Robotics:* 
    *   AI-driven robots and drones automate planting, harvesting, and crop monitoring.
    *   ML improves machine efficiency by learning from past farming cycles.
    *   *Example:* Self-driving tractors use AI for automated plowing and seeding.
5.  *Sustainable Agriculture and Resource Optimization:* 
    *   ML optimizes the use of water, fertilizers, and energy to reduce waste.
    *   AI models help farmers adopt eco-friendly farming practices.
    *   *Example:* AI-driven vertical farming optimizes space and energy use.

## **4.8** SELF-LEARNING IoT SYSTEMS WITH AutoML

Self-learning IoT systems with AutoML combine the power of IoT devices with automated ML to create intelligent, adaptive solutions. IoT sensors collect real-time data, which is then preprocessed and analyzed to extract meaningful insights. AutoML automates the process of selecting, training, and optimizing ML models, reducing the need for human intervention. These models are deployed on cloud or edge computing platforms to make real-time predictions and decisions. A continuous feedback loop ensures that the system learns from new data, improving accuracy and efficiency over time. This approach is widely used in applications such as smart homes, where devices adapt to user behavior, industrial IoT for predictive maintenance, healthcare monitoring for anomaly detection, and smart cities for optimizing traffic and energy management. By integrating AutoML with IoT, businesses and industries can achieve automation, efficiency, and data-driven decision-making with minimal manual effort.

### 4.8.1 Time Series Forecasting for IoT Applications

The IoT generates vast amounts of time-series data from sensors, devices, and connected systems. Accurate forecasting of this data is crucial for predictive maintenance, anomaly detection, energy optimization, and smart decision-making. Deep 68.learning models have proven effective in capturing temporal dependencies and improving forecasting accuracy in IoT applications.

*   *Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-Based Models:* CNNs efficiently capture local patterns in IoT data, making them useful for anomaly detection and predictive maintenance. Temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) further enhance forecasting by modeling long-range dependencies.
*   *Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)-Based Models:* RNNs, especially long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU), effectively learn sequential dependencies in IoT data streams. They help in demand forecasting, fault detection, and resource optimization.
*   *Autoencoder (AE)-Based Models:* AEs extract hidden patterns from IoT time-series data, improving anomaly detection and data compression. Variants like stacked AEs (SAEs) and variational AEs (VAEs) enhance feature learning for forecasting.
*   *Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM)-Based Models:* RBMs and their extensions Deep Belief Network (DBNs) and Deep Boltzmann Machines (DBMs) learn underlying data distributions, helping in energy consumption forecasting and equipment monitoring.
*   *Attention-Based Models:* Attention mechanisms, particularly transformers, improve forecasting accuracy by selectively focusing on important time points. They are widely used in IoT-driven supply chain forecasting and dynamic resource allocation.
*   *Graph Neural Network (GNN)-Based Models:* GNNs process IoT data structured as networks, capturing spatial–temporal relationships. They are valuable in traffic prediction, smart grid management, and sensor network analysis. The time series forecasting is shown in [Figure 4.12](#ch12.xhtml#f27).
    
    ![Figure 4.12 Time series forecasting.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C004_012.jpg)
    
    **Figure 4.12** Time series forecasting.[⏎](#ch12.xhtml#f27b)
    

## **4.9** RL FOR IoT AUTOMATION

It is a type of ML. Where an agent learns to make choices by interacting with its surroundings to get the most rewards. Unlike supervised learning, which uses labeled data, RL learns through trial and error. The agent tries different actions and gets feedback in the form of rewards or penalties. The main parts of RL are the agent, the environment, actions, states, and rewards. The agent’s goal is to create a policy, which is a plan for choosing actions based on the current situation, to earn the highest rewards over time. This method has been used successfully in robotics, gaming, and self-driving cars. For showing its ability to tackle complex decision-making tasks.

### 4.9.1 Key Components of RL

RL is a kind of ML where an agent learns to make choices by working with its surroundings to get the most rewards. So, the main parts of RL are:

*   *Agent:* The one that learns and makes decisions.
*   *Environment:* The outside system that the agent interacts with.70.
*   69. *Actions:* The different choices the agent can make.
*   *State:* How the agent’s current situation in the environment is described.
*   *Reward:* The feedback the agent gets from the environment is based on what it does.

### 4.9.2 Types of RL

It can be divided into different types based on how the agent learns and the environment it works in. So, here are the main types:

1.  *Model-Free:* In this type, the agent learns to make decisions without knowing how the environment works. It generally uses trial and error to find the best actions. This can be split into: 
    *   *Value-Based Methods:* These methods estimate how good different actions are in a certain situation. A common example is Q-learning.
    *   *Policy-Based Methods:* These methods learn a plan that tells the agent what action to take in each situation. Examples include the REINFORCE algorithm and actor–critic methods.
2.  *Model-Based:* Here, the agent creates a model of the environment and uses it to make decisions. This can be more efficient because the agent can try out different scenarios before acting.
3.  *Deep RL:* This type combines RL with deep learning algorithms. It uses neural networks to help the agent understand complex situations. So, this approach has led to big successes in challenging tasks, like playing video games and controlling robots.

## **4.10** Conclusion and Future Work

By enabling intelligent automation, predictive analytics, and real-time anomaly detection, the marriage of ML with the IoT has unlocked game-changing opportunities for numerous industries. ML algorithms are crucial in deriving actionable insights and optimizing system performance as IoT networks expand and generate vast amounts of data. While FL enhances data protection and privacy, new technologies such as edge computing and light-weight ML models address significant problems such as latency, scalability, and energy thrift. These trends foster adaptive and autonomous ecosystems through the facilitation of applications within smart cities, healthcare, agriculture, and industry automation. However, challenges such as computational resources, heterogeneity of data, and ethics are still significant topics of interest to be researched in the future. Decentralized computation, robust security protocols, and model efficiency techniques need to receive the highest emphasis if the vision of ML-empowered IoT is to become a reality. To achieve the standardization of protocols and ensure compatibility, cross-industry collaborations are essential along with academia collaborations. Lastly, with the Industry 4.0 and beyond, the union of ML and IoT holds the potential to revolutionize how people interact with connected systems by creating wiser, more responsive, and sustainable technological environments.

71.Future research should focus on optimizing lightweight ML models, improving interoperability, and ensuring robust privacy-preserving mechanisms. By addressing these challenges, the convergence of AI and IoT can lead to smarter, more efficient, and sustainable technological ecosystems \[[9](#ch12.xhtml#r202)\]. The continuous evolution of these technologies promises to unlock new possibilities while necessitating responsible and ethical implementation \[[10](#ch12.xhtml#r203)\].

# 72.5The Convergence of Internet of Things and Machine LearningA Case Study on Innovations, Challenges, and Applications

Jagadeshwari Puttanapura, Monika Singh T., Kishor Kumar Reddy C., and Kari Lippert

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-5](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-5)

## **5.1** Introduction

The Internet of Things (IoT) and machine learning (ML) are construed as transformative technologies for industries and ways of life \[[1](#ch13.xhtml#r204)\]. IoT is the world of devices that are interconnected, collecting data, exchanging data, and processing data for automated routine decision-making purposes. Smart home appliances, industrial sensor devices, and many others generate real-time data in huge quantities, but employing this data calls for effective computational techniques \[[2](#ch13.xhtml#r205)\].

ML, which is a sub-field of artificial intelligence (AI), teaches a system the kind of prediction or decision without explicitly programming it to learn \[[3](#ch13.xhtml#r206)\]. ML algorithms analyze complex datasets, identify trends, and convert them into actionable insights. The combined usage of IoT with ML leads to intelligent automation, ensuring optimal resource use and better efficiency of the system. The gain from incorporating ML into any IoT system is to add enhanced capabilities for predictive analytics, anomaly detection, and decision-making applications \[[4](#ch13.xhtml#r207)\]. This has been around and incorporated in various sectors of health care and smart cities, and there has been industrial automation, and the creation of smarter, data-driven solutions \[[5](#ch13.xhtml#r208)\]. The smart combination of real-time IoT-generated data and ML-driven analytics set up a strong ecosystem that may prove itself in revolutionizing various domains \[[6](#ch13.xhtml#r209)\].

### **5.1.1** Importance of Convergence

The fusion of IoT and ML becomes very relevant because the traditional IoT systems hardly process the voluminous streaming data. The basic IoT application uses mainly rule-defined automation, which cannot much adapt to the dynamic environment \[[7](#ch13.xhtml#r210)\]. 73.ML thus adds intelligence to IoT by analyzing patterns, making forecasts, and optimizing processes in real time. Among the most significant benefits of this merging is real-time decision-making. Traditional IoT systems collect and send data for humans to interpret, whereas ML-driven IoT solutions can analyze and act immediately. As an example in predictive maintenance, ML models can analyze sensor data from industrial machines to anticipate failures prior to their occurrence, thus reducing downtime and repair costs \[[8](#ch13.xhtml#r211)\]. Alongside this, it has also improved efficiency, security, and personalization \[[9](#ch13.xhtml#r212)\]. For instance, ML models detect anomalies in IoT networks to avert attacks, optimize energy consumption in smart grids, and personalize the experiences of users in smart homes. The merging of IoT and ML promises organizations and individuals’ greater automation, savings, and improvement in operational efficiency \[[10](#ch13.xhtml#r213)\]. Table 5.1 shows the major contrasts and collaborations between IoT and ML, which are elaborated in this table. Hybridization of data collection and aggregation with connectivity and monitoring for real-time analytics \[[11](#ch13.xhtml#r214)\]. ML aims at data analysis: prediction and automation based on previous learning while making possible the learning of intelligent IoT systems capable of learning through data interpretation and optimized processes and better decision-making \[[12](#ch13.xhtml#r215)\].

### **5.1.2** Real-World Applications

The possible visible impact of the convergence of IoT with ML extends over a variety of industries. In the area of healthcare, for example, the wearable devices are embedded with sensors where the part of IoT is used to monitor the vital biometrics of patients, while the usage of ML is embedded to analyze trends that help in pronouncing early detection of diseases or lifestyle-related changes \[[13](#ch13.xhtml#r216)\]. This would have added better possibilities for patient monitoring through the reduction of hospital visits and improvement in health outcomes \[[14](#ch13.xhtml#r217)\]. Traffic systems such as intelligent IoT-enabled traffic management systems use traffic optimization techniques based on ML to smoothen traffic flow that ensures signals reduce congestion while improving efficiency in public transport \[[2](#ch13.xhtml#r205)\]. Such systems include surveillance ones, 74.where ML-enabled facial recognition and anomaly detection boost the safety of such environments. Regardless, all innovations lend themselves to making cities safer and more efficient \[[15](#ch13.xhtml#r219)\].

In industrial automation, IoT sensors monitor the manufacturing machines, and ML models predict their failure before the actual collapse \[[16](#ch13.xhtml#r220)\]. This predictive maintenance approach lowers operational costs and increases productivity. Likewise, the intelligent farming methods make use of IoT sensors—considering the soil condition—while the ML model recommends the irrigation and fertilization schedule to increase crop yield and resource efficiency \[[3](#ch13.xhtml#r206)\].

## **5.2** IoT FUNDAMENTALS

The IoT refers to the entire system consisting of interconnected devices that collect, transport, and analyze data for automating, making decisions, and improving performance across various areas. These devices can be simple smart sensors or very complex measurements taken at the industrial level or used in autonomous vehicles \[[17](#ch13.xhtml#r221)\]. IoT is a whole into which every other connected communication technology feeding into embedded technologies and wireless protocols connects. It is vital for healthcare, agriculture, smart cities, and manufacturing, where real-time monitoring in predictive analytics becomes possible \[[18](#ch13.xhtml#r222)\]. Knowing the important aspects of IoT, such as its architecture, communication protocols, sensors, and data transmission mechanisms, would facilitate designing efficient and scalable IoT solutions.

### **5.2.1** IoT Architecture and Components

The architecture of the IoT includes many layers that facilitate the connection between real things and virtual platforms. Usually, IoT architecture is built on a four-layer design: the perception layer (with sensors and their associated actuators); the network layer (that concerns the different known communication protocols and the transmission of data); the edge computing layer (which concerns the data found right at the edge); and the application layer (user interface and analytics). Each of these layers contributes its share to the realization of efficient data flow and real-time decision-making \[[19](#ch13.xhtml#r223)\]. The perception layer contains numerous sensors and actuators to sense real-world data, including temperature, humidity, motion, and pressure. The physical sense parameters are converted into digital signals destined for the next layer \[[20](#ch13.xhtml#r224)\]. The network layer is responsible for transmitting these data through wired or wireless technologies, such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, or a cellular network.

![Figure 5.1 IoT architecture: five-layer model.](html/images/9781041062943_C005_001.jpg)

**Figure 5.1** IoT architecture: five-layer model.

The five-layer architecture of IoT is illustrated in Figure 5.1, facilitating seamless data collection, processing, and decision-making \[[21](#ch13.xhtml#r225)\]. The perception layer contains sensors that collect real-world data, which the transport layer transmits using communication technologies, such as fifth generation (5G) and Wi-Fi. The processing layer analyzes and stores this data in the cloud or on edge computing \[[22](#ch13.xhtml#r226)\]. On the other end, the application layer provides services for users through apps and dashboards, while the business layer manages systems, decision-making, and profit-making activities. This well-structured methodology guarantees efficient functioning of the IoT in various domains \[[23](#ch13.xhtml#r227)\].

75.At the edge computing layer, raw data would be processed locally before further transmission into the cloud or data centers, thus reducing latency and bandwidth usage \[[24](#ch13.xhtml#r228)\]. This application layer includes such items as user interfaces, dashboards for the clients, and insights driven by AI, thereby making all that data actionable \[[25](#ch13.xhtml#r229)\]. It is essential to understand how these parts interact, as they are all functional in creating scalable security systems such as IoT systems \[[26](#ch13.xhtml#r230)\].

### **5.2.2** IoT Communication Protocols (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport, Constrained Application Protocol, and HyperText Transfer Protocol etc.)

IoT devices are based on specific communication protocols to effectively transmit data. Unlike traditional ones, these are not energy wasteful and consume less bandwidth so that their devices could use them for real-time communication. Some of the well-known protocols under this group include Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT), Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP), and HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP).

![Figure 5.2 MQTT publish-subscribe architecture in IoT.](html/images/9781041062943_C005_002.jpg)

**Figure 5.2** MQTT publish-subscribe architecture in IoT.

The MQTT Publish-Subscribe Model Diagram in Figure 5.2 is one of the most widely accepted standards for IoT communication. The publisher (sensors, IoT devices) sends messages to broker, which classifies messages into topics, and forwards them to the interested subscribers (smartphones, dashboards). Supplying a 76.value-added, lightweight, and scaled solution for communication, this characteristic model becomes more prominent in real-time data transfer scenarios dealing with harsh network constraints \[[27](#ch13.xhtml#r231)\]. MQTT is a lightweight publish-subscription messaging protocol above and beyond Transmission Control Protocol, Internet Protocol (TCP/IP). It has established its popularity among IoT applications because of low bandwidth shortages and the fact that it can still work in areas of poor connectivity \[[28](#ch13.xhtml#r232)\]. In addition, MQTT guarantees messages being delivered reliably with three different quality of service (QoS) levels so developers can optimize performance for any use cases based on network conditions \[[29](#ch13.xhtml#r233)\]. Table 5.2 describes the special communication protocol, with criteria like speed, security, and power efficiency, marking the difference among IoT devices. A few comparative points regarding the usages between some common IoT protocols, such as MQTT, CoAP, and HTTP, and also including LoRaWAN and Zigbee, have been furnished in [Table 5.2](#ch13.xhtml#t2).

**Table 5.2** IoT Protocols and Their Use Cases[⏎](#ch13.xhtml#t2b)

 
| **Protocol** ||  || **Type** ||  || **Speed** ||  || **Security** ||  || **Power Efficiency** ||  || **Best Use Cases** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MQTT ||  || Publish-subscribe ||  || High ||  || Moderate ||  || High ||  || Smart homes, industrial automation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CoAP ||  || RESTful API ||  || Moderate ||  || High ||  || High ||  || Low-power IoT devices, wearables |
| HTTP ||  || Request-response ||  || Slow ||  || High ||  || Low ||  || Web-based IoT applications |
| LoRaWAN ||  || LPWAN ||  || Low ||  || Moderate ||  || Very high ||  || Smart agriculture, remote monitoring |
| Zigbee ||  || Mesh networking ||  || Moderate ||  || High ||  || Moderate ||  || Smart lighting, home automation |

CoAP, however, is a web protocol that is specifically for resource-constrained IoT devices. It differs from MQTT, which, unlike CoAP, is broker-dependent and is very much like HTTP but carries relatively lighter loads in terms of communication to perform a request-response cycle \[[30](#ch13.xhtml#r234)\]. Further, while HTTP has remained dominant as a protocol in web-based IoT applications, the power consumption and expensive bandwidth costs make it ineffective for use in battery-driven devices. Choice of communication protocol will therefore depend on energy efficiency and real-time processing applications as well as network reliability \[[31](#ch13.xhtml#r235)\].

### **5.2.3** IoT Sensors and Devices

IoT systems anchor sensors as the basis on which the technology can be used to further explore and deploy data in real life. Most sensor types are also found in IoT devices: temperature sensors, humidity sensors, motion detectors, pressure sensors, and biometric sensors. All these IoT sensors are available for environmental parameter monitoring, and data is continuously transmitted to analysis and supported 77.decision-making \[[32](#ch13.xhtml#r236)\]. For example, temperature and humidity sensors find wide applications in smart homes, weather stations, and industrial automation. Motion sensors include the infrared and the ultrasonic types, which find applications in security and smart lighting. Pressure sensors are widely used in automotive and health industries, for instance, in measuring tire pressure and blood pressure in medical devices. IoT devices include actuators whose function is converting electronic signals to physical actions. Examples include smart locks, automatic irrigation systems, and robotic arms in manufacturing. Seamless integration of sensors and actuators, therefore, allows IoT systems to automate tasks, increase efficiency, and improve decision-making in a wide range of applications \[[33](#ch13.xhtml#r237)\].

### **5.2.4** Data Generation and Transmission in IoT

IoT devices generate copious data; efficient transmission can, therefore, become one integral source of IoT systems. Initially, data are collected at the perception layer, where sensors touch and sense environmental values. Data will be either locally processed or transmitted to a cloud server for further analysis. The aspect of such high volume, velocity, and diversity in data that they generate in IoT would provide tremendous challenges and opportunities in managing and processing this information \[[34](#ch13.xhtml#r238)\]. Bandwidth efficiency and latency are among the prime aspects of data transmission. An IoT network employs both wired (Ethernet, fiber optics) and wireless (Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN, Zigbee) communications for information relay. While wired connectivity enhances reliability and security, mobility and flexibility favor the wireless transmission preference \[[35](#ch13.xhtml#r239)\]. With edge computing, customers will be able to use devices close to the location where the IoT devices are installed. This will reduce response time between cloud servers because it processes data closer to the source. However, cloud-based architecture is where most historically stored data, running ML models, and analytics dashboards are still in place \[[36](#ch13.xhtml#r240)\]. The appropriate mixture of edge and cloud processing must match the real-time needs of the application and the infrastructure capabilities.

## **5.3** Ml Fundamentals

ML is a form of AI that lets systems learn from data and subsequently improve without requiring explicit programming. Unlike rule-based approaches, ML algorithms use analytical techniques to examine vast amounts of information so they can identify patterns and then make predictions. The integration of ML with the IoT has produced intelligent decision-making systems that can analyze sensor data, understand anomalies, and optimize operations in real time. The section covers fundamental ML concepts, such as the different categories of ML, feature engineering, and the IoT data-related challenges \[[37](#ch13.xhtml#r241)\].

### **5.3.1** Basics of ML and AI

ML is a subset of AI that concentrates on the creation of algorithms that learn from the data and make decisions. AI pervades a much broader concept like expert systems, 78.natural language processing (NLP), robotics, while ML can only be on predictive modeling and pattern recognition. ML-integrated IoT systems supplement the automation provided by IoTs to adaptively change environments. Data, algorithms, and models make up the three main components of ML \[[11](#ch13.xhtml#r214)\]. At the bottom of the structure is data, which then feeds the algorithms—folks like neural networks, decision trees, and support vector machines. These trained models are then attached to using the algorithms in undertaking tasks such as classification, regression, and clustering. With IoT, it is much more challenging as there will be a continuous data stream in real time, which necessitates more efficient preprocessing techniques. Various ML algorithms fulfill various IoT applications. Table 5.3 lists some of the preferred ML techniques, along with their strengths and weaknesses when applied to IoT, such as decision trees for anomaly detection, convolution neural network (CNNs) for image-based IoT, and long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) for time-series analyses.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
