### 11.5.2 Devices: Wearables, Sensors, and Remote Monitoring Tools

In the center of IoT healthcare systems there are multiple devices which aim at gathering this or that data related to patient. These devices include:

*   *Wearable Devices:* These wearable products include smartwatches, fitness trackers and other similar devices monitor data such as heart rate, blood pressure, glucose levels, and activity level. These are safe, easy to use, and preferred for real-time monitoring of health at home.
*   *Sensors:* Health parameters that are captured in real time while using IoT are linked devices, ECG sensors, temperature sensors along with oxygen 200.saturation sensors. Whenever these sensors may be incorporated into wearable reactors, implantable devices, or fixed medical facilities.
*   *Remote Monitoring Tools:* Smart inhalers, glucometers, and smart pill dispensers allow patients with chronic diseases to be remotely monitored ([Badiger et al., 2025](#ch19.xhtml#r376)). They make it possible to continuously send data to the providers for analysis and subsequent action.

These devices form the front-end layer of IoT systems, collecting raw data from patients and the environment for further processing.

*   *LoRa (Long Range):* LoRa is essentially a method of operation for wireless connectivity meant for IoT that are distance-n FH, power-conserving; therefore, it is ideal in rural or remote healthcare. This makes it capable of data transmission, several kilometers away depending on the prevailing environmental condition for widespread monitoring. The concerned protocol also results in low power consumption which reduces the frequent replacement of batteries in the devices. Furthermore, LoRa is easily scalable for the patient monitoring tasks, and multiple patients can be monitored at once. LoRa is applied in healthcare to monitor patients in far-reaching areas in relation to health, to gather epidemiological data using cyber-physical healthcare support system (CHSSs) and also for environmental factors such as water quality, or climatic conditions for health relevant information.
*   *Wi-Fi:* Wi-Fi is a global standard of communication that is widely adopted in cities’ health-care facilities, which are identified by high data throughput capability and a capacity to transfer huge amounts of data. Because it provides a high data transfer rate, it is suitable for the transfer of large amounts of data, for instance, someone’s X-ray or video stream for telemedicine. A majority of healthcare organizations have already established strong and reliable Wi-Fi systems, with organizations being prepared to integrate IoT technology. Wi-Fi also promotes compatibility; devices are enabled to enter existing networks and interface with utilities such as electronic health record (EHRs). In healthcare, Wi-Fi is used for transmitting data between wearable devices and hospital servers, high-definition video in telemedicine, medical equipment, asset tracking, and more.
*   *Cellular Networks (e.g., fourth-generation (4G), 5G):* When healthcare management is concerned, definite bandwidth-intensive applications like telemedicine cannot work without cellular networks ([Ansarian & Baharlouei, 2023](#ch19.xhtml#r372)). They advocate for the constant connectivity needed in mobility healthcare solutions and in the unfortunate incidences of emergencies. Also, cellular systems offer highly efficient transfer of data with high speed, especially in 5G networks, which have ultra-low latency and high bandwidth, which is suitable for vital healthcare. Their broad scope provides operational guarantees in most urban and suburban networks; mobility allows devices to remain linked even while moving, like during a telemetry emergency transportation vehicle. In healthcare, cellular networks enable tele-diagnosis and real-time tele-consultation, high-resolution 201.diagnostic images or videos for referred opinions, and mobile health clinics with IoT for outreach programs and emergencies—ambulances transmitting patients’ details to the receiving hospital.
*   *Data Processing:* After they are consumed, the raw data are cleaned, normalized, and transformed to facilitate precision. This is a process of cleaning the data by removing any duplicate data, any wrong data, and formatting the data that is suitable for analysis. Filtering is another important activity of pre-processing, which involves reducing voluminous and noisy data and information so as to improve the quality of the data ([Badiger & Mathew, 2023a](#ch19.xhtml#r374), [2023b](#ch19.xhtml#r375)). In healthcare, this could entail making structures in which data is measured, for example, to be consistent or ensure each data source uses the same time stamp when temporal analysis is needed.
*   *Analytics:* Subsequent to data pre-processing, information undergoes data analytics for processing to arrive at usable results that enhance healthcare. Both AI and ML are applied to paint roles by implementing predictive diagnostics, identifying patterns within the patient’s information, predicting numerous health-related issues, and recommending preventive actions. With historical and real-time data, big data predictive analytics uses modeling methods to discover and understand trends, which will support early interventions in chronic diseases and epidemiological investigations. In addition, transform tools such as dashboards and graphical interfaces make it easy for users to engage with data that may be difficult to translate ([Karimullah et al., 2024](#ch19.xhtml#r383)). These tools enable the healthcare providers to take informed decisions at the earliest, for example, tracking patient’s vitals/trends constantly.
*   *Storage:* The retrieved data is then elaborated and stored in large, effective, and secure databases, according to the IoT system's needs for healthcare. SQL databases are more suitable for the structured data stream, which has well-defined relations, for instance, records of patients, making it reliable as well as consistent. Massively scalable, distributed database systems, and some of them, such as NoSQL databases, are suitable for un- or semi-structured data like sensor logs, multimedia files from diagnostic tools, etc. IoT sensors yield sequenced data, and time-series databases like InfluxDB have been developed to handle time-stamped data and allow trend searches through time or time intervals ([Shaik et al., 2024](#ch19.xhtml#r391)). These storage solutions allow the frequent access and fast extraction of data needed for analysis and are highly available and strongly consistent to enable real-time decision-making, and are also highly durable over the long term.

The data management and analytics layer is a revolutionary change agent in healthcare because it addresses data management and analytics holistically while bridging demand–supply gaps and facilitating breakthroughs across multiple domains ([Batko & Ślęzak, 2022](#ch19.xhtml#r377)). One is that it promotes the provision of individualized treatment as treatments are informed by patients’ data, therefore increasing the accuracy of the healthcare delivery ([Shetty & Badiger, 2024](#ch19.xhtml#r392)).

### 202.11.5.3 Security and Privacy

The security and compliance layer is the fundamental prerequisite of the IoT healthcare system because it addresses the protection of patients’ information and guarantees the reliability of the connected healthcare solutions. This layer addresses key aspects of security and regulatory adherence through the following components:

*   *Authentication and Authorization:* Subordinate security measures help to confirm the identity of users and devices, which guarantees access to the necessary systems only to the authorized clients. Two-factor authentication, visa biometrics, digital certificates, and tokens validate people and things, while access control models such as role-based access control (RBAC) and attribute-based access control (ABAC) are based on role and attributes, respectively. For instance, there may be a situation where doctors may monitor/diagnose patients by using sophisticated patient history, whereas technicians can only view reports on the maintenance of various equipment.
*   *Encryption:* Transparency and security mean that data remains amended and locked when it is being transmitted or stored, and is most immune to interception. TLS provides protection of data transmitted by IoT devices, servers, and applications, and AES protects data when stored and makes it difficult for anyone to read the data without decryption keys.
*   *Anomaly Detection:* Real-time systems have their own applications and primarily guard data and device activity so that it can be detected if there is a threat or breach being carried out. Based on AI and ML, behavioral analysis recognizes that something is wrong or different from normal behavior; the alerting system informs administrators about something wrong or out of the norm, for instance, multiple failed log-ins or a sudden surge in traffic load. For instance, it is possible to have such systems alert to compromised devices whose main intention is to leak data.
*   *Compliance:* Regulatory compliance makes sure that healthcare IoT systems work appropriately and in legal and moral terms. Data protection and privacy are controlled by regulatory measures such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), HIPAA, and California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). Policies, audit trails, and data protection processes comply with these standards, therefore providing subject accessibility, accountability, and safeguards for the patient’s data.

The important part of facilitating the IoT healthcare risks and trust is accomplished by the security and compliance layer ([Parihar et al., 2024](#ch19.xhtml#r389)). Cyber threats and breaches are well protected for the free flow of sensitive patient data to protect their confidentiality and integrity. The combination of these measures ensures that providers can concentrate solely on providing high-quality patient care, all while ensuring the security of their data.

### 11.5.4 User Interaction and Feedback Layer

The user interaction and feedback layer can be viewed as the overlay that connects users with the IoT healthcare systems, delivering messages and facilitating straightforward 203.ways to provide reactions and control the processes. This layer aims at developing interfaces that are interactive, comprehensible, and responsive, providing decision-making information and effectively adjusting to the user's requirements without delay. Its primary components include:

*   *Interfaces:* Consequently, interfaces can be diverse and simple for users to interact with IoT systems. Mobile applications give physicians immediate data access, health and wellness figures, and system interfaces on their smartphones or tablets. Web-based dashboards provide rich analyses of information relevant to healthcare practitioners, healthcare managers, or researchers. Smart speakers also include voice control, making them preferable for people with disabilities or in dynamic situations in healthcare zones. Furthermore, training and monitoring applications are developed as possible augmented reality/virtual reality (AR/VR) platforms, like virtual anatomy classes or AR patient care.
*   *Feedback Mechanisms:* Real-time feedback is useful in ensuring that users are informed and respond to sudden changes. Other forms of awareness include notifications and alerts, the former of which can range from warning of abnormal vitals to a reminder that it is time to take the medicine. IoT systems are capable of adjusting operation more or less automatically in response to user usage patterns or environmental characteristics, such as a smart thermostat that qualifies temperature around a patient. Hypnotic recommendations, such as modifying exercises every now and then for those with chronic illnesses or changing eating habits based on analytics of data compiled from patients plans.
*   *User Experience (UX):* The findings conclude that overemphasizing accessibility and simplification of such systems are essential to the achievement of the envisaged benefits of IoT healthcare systems. Intuitive design provides recognition. Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication for interfaces, where different users have different levels of tech-savviness for complex interfaces. The measures, such as tools for visually impaired users that allow user interaction and comfortable use of the application, support of languages, and high-contrast modes, contribute to the application’s inclusiveness. End-user feedback that results from constant testing helps to fine-tune the experience throughout use, minimizing inconsistencies and increasing general user satisfaction, which in turn leads to greater interaction with the system.

### 11.5.5 Benefits of IoT in Healthcare

Advantages of IoT in the health sector: In this context, IoT presents a great range of opportunities in the healthcare industry, bringing numerous positive changes for patients and healthcare organizations as a whole ([Frimpong et al., 2023](#ch19.xhtml#r381)). IoT thus meets several issues in conventional healthcare by providing real-time collection of data, its analysis, and reporting, and presents new options. Below are some key benefits of IoT in healthcare:

#### 204.11.5.5.1 Real-Time Monitoring

Staying connected is one of the biggest benefits IoT has to offer for the healthcare industry, and this is because a patient’s vital signs and health can be monitored all the time.

*   *Immediate Alerts:* Other existing smart devices, like wearable sensors connected to a patient health record, can identify deviations in the patient health metrics, like abnormal heart rate or a drop in blood oxygen level, and notify the healthcare practitioner. This makes it easy to make proper referrals to the doctors and may even save people when they are in really bad shape.
*   *Remote Health Management:* This can also be done from the comfort of their homes, and their doctors can then make decisions without having to consult them in person. It is more effective in managing chronic illnesses such as diabetes or hypertension, which is one of the ways in which it is especially helpful.
*   *Post-Surgery Recovery:* IoT devices can help monitor recovery from surgery and other serious conditions and would allow doctors and nurses to see the status of the wound, as well as mobility improvement and overall health, without having to readmit the patient to the hospital again and again.

### 11.5.6 Enhanced Patient Outcomes

IoT healthcare systems enhance patients’ outcomes by facilitating diagnosis, treatment, and care planning and coordination.

*   *Data-Driven Insights:* The steady stream of data from IoT devices allows healthcare providers to be well-informed, thus making fewer diagnostic mistakes and increasing accuracy in treatment.
*   *Personalized Treatment Plans:* Algorithms derived from patient-collected data can be used to understand and plan a treatment program uniquely for each patient based on the variations in their condition, such as a change in dosage of prescribed medications or alteration to lifestyle. Improved Chronic Disease Management: In chronic diseases, IoT devices offer steady checking, which assists the healthcare team in early actions to prevent adverse effects on a patient’s condition.

### 11.5.7 Cost-Effective Solutions

IoT technologies present efficiency-saving solutions in patients and hospitals treatment and resource utilization that will go a long way in saving costs for both parties.

*   *Reduced Hospital Visits:* IoT through remote monitoring and telemedicine eliminates the regular visitation of the doctors, and extended hospital stays lower the costs to patients and hospitals.
*   *Optimized Resource Utilization:* IoT also makes it possible to manage many of the resources required in a hospital setting in an efficient manner, as it includes 205.information on inventory, usage of equipment, and requirements, among others, that any hospital faces on an ongoing basis. For instance, smart devices can track the occupancy of the beds in hospitals and the assignment of staff.
*   *Preventive Healthcare:* Self-diagnosis through IoT devices occurs before the onset of symptoms, thus limiting the expenses incurred for extensive treatments of diagnosed conditions and extending the philosophy of we prevent rather than cure.

The combination of IoT and the healthcare system results in informing the appropriate action when necessary, increasing patient’s life quality, and decreasing costs. As seen through notifications, health monitoring, and tailor-made solutions, IoT redefines healthcare from a reactive process you see in ordinary healthcare systems to a proactive smart system. Due to its relatively low cost, it brings increased availability of quality services that are of benefit to both customers and care organizations.

## **11.6** DATA AGGREGATION TECHNIQUES IN IoT

Data acquisition/accumulation in IoT networks presupposes the gathering, analysis, and synergistic integration of data from various sensors and appliances before forwarding the outcome to a central point, such as a hub or a cloud, for further processing ([Kuchuk & Malokhvii, 2024](#ch19.xhtml#r385)). This technique is critical in minimizing bandwidth utilization, minimizing communication expenditures, and enhancing system performance within IoT healthcare applications. The following section provides an elaborate analysis of the data aggregation process in IoT networks.

### 11.6.1 Concept of Data Aggregation in IoT Networks

Data acquisition in IoT means the accumulation and integration of data received from several IoT devices (sensors, wearables, smart devices, etc.) before transferring them to the data processing center in the cloud or further for analysis. This is essential in the management of data, particularly for healthcare devices, where a lot of data is produced in real time. Some of the prime objectives of data aggregation include the reduction of the amount of data transmitted, improvement of data quality, and finally, reduction of the latency period. Key components of data aggregation in IoT networks are listed below.

#### 11.6.1.1 Data Collection

*   *Sources of Data:* Wearable health monitors, biometric sensors, and remote monitoring devices are used in IoT to provide constant data support to operations and patient care in the healthcare sector. These devices acquire instantaneous data about the health status by monitoring pulse rate, blood pressure, blood glucose level, SpO[2], and temperature, and provide patient-specific and timely actions ([Boikanyo et al., 2023](#ch19.xhtml#r379)). It also tracks environmental status such as chamber temperature, humidity, and noise to set appropriate conditions in healthcare, thus amenities in healthcare institutions. Furthermore, IoT devices monitor and report on their working inclination, performance analysis, energy 206.competency, and connectivity to solve the reliability problem for prompt and unbroken healthcare service delivery.
*   *Types of Data:* The different forms of records collected by IoT devices in healthcare reflect the different categories that it involves; each plays a unique role in improving the quality of care that is being offered. Measurements like pulse rate, temperature, blood pressure, ability levels, and sleep duration help us to give an overall assessment of a patient’s health and plan for treatments as the problems are discovered on time. It is evident that behavioral information is important in chronic disease control and in promoting enhanced and healthier lifestyles through medication-taking behavior, number of steps walked, and eating and drinking habits. Furthermore, geolocation data helps to navigate patient mobility by identifying their locations and helps in convenient usage of needed medical equipment, its availability, and minimization of time consumption.
*   *Challenges:* The sheer volume of data produced by IoT devices in the context of healthcare delivers several key issues in terms of management. Data size is a major concern, which is due to the nature of the generated data being extremely large and can put a strain on storage and network infrastructures. To overcome this issue, it is necessary to develop solutions that are, to a certain extent, scalable. Real-time responsiveness is another challenge because business-critical applications must process a large amount of data while remaining responsive to real-time responses to important measures such as notifications, emergency messages, and decision-making procedures. Furthermore, data integration is crucial as anything from smart pills to implantable gadgets consistently contributes a wide array of data in dissimilar formats. This data must be normalized because in its current unstructured format, it cannot easily be passed and harmoniously used across systems and platforms, and even in structured formats, the insights that are derived from this data need to be usable or actionable.

#### 11.6.1.2 Data Processing

*   *Aggregation Techniques:* In the case of big data generated by IoT healthcare, aggregation techniques are very helpful in the initial pre-processing steps of IoT healthcare data as they help to cope with the excessive volumes of raw data. Reduced data size optimizes storage and transfer of data without compromising on the important details; hence, it reduces the size of the data sent while maintaining the size of the contracted data. In the case of sampling, data points are sometimes chosen at fixed intervals, with the advantages of being more resource-friendly while keeping the data received relatively accurate. The filtering process discards unwanted and unnecessary information, which could otherwise distract from the value of new information. In sum, these techniques facilitate the management of data, optimize data processing, and enable real-time decision-making in applications that constitute the healthcare field.
*   *Feature Extraction:* Feature Extraction helps drastically in analyzing the IoT healthcare data as it allows producing meaningful mean values, temporal tendencies, or rates immediately from the primary data. This intervention helps to improve the efficiency of information computation with consideration to the necessary parameters for decision-making. For example, while sending every 207.recorded temperature as part of the data stream, minute-by-minute fluctuations should be summarized into variations that can be worked with effectively.
*   *Data Fusion:* Data fusion on a patient involves the integration of inputs from two or more sensors or devices for efficiency in diagnosing the patient. When it comes to aggregation of different data types like glucose levels and data related to physical activity, it becomes quite easy to find meaningful patterns. For example, linking blood sugar patterns with exercise records can improve patient care on glucose control, thereby increasing the effectiveness of healthcare treatment.

### 11.6.2 Benefits of Data Aggregation in IoT Healthcare Systems

*   *Optimized Bandwidth Usage:* Through the condensation of data in their datasets, it is able to cut down on unnecessary data that is transferred over networks, hence decreasing the costs of transmission and increasing the efficiency of the systems. Less data transmission with the help of aggregation makes it possible to refrain from transmitting a large amount of data over the network, which is crucial for limited bandwidth environments. It also means that data that would master civic essential data rates, well-being measurements, or crisis alarms can go through without flooding the systems, making the framework more efficient. Another measure of competitive advantage that results from the decrease of data transmission is cost efficiency. This is because when sending less data for record-keeping, archiving, or collaborating with other healthcare centers, especially using costly cellular and satellite communication, the costs of using up more bandwidth are prevented. This makes healthcare systems in IoT more responsive to affordable and sustainable connectivity in low-connectivity zones. As traffic generates one or the other problem in a network, reducing traffic leads to better performance of the network. When fewer users are connected to a communication network, there is a lesser chance of traffic congestion, leading to better performance; this is important for real-time applications such as patient monitoring or response to an emergency. This guarantees that important healthcare services should not be affected due to some network confinements.
*   *Improved System Efficiency:* Improved System Efficiency: Less server overload is obtained when data are preprocessed and processed or even processed right on the edge node or on the IoT device. This approach minimizes the need to use central cloud servers for extensive computation to improve system performance and guarantee that the healthcare infrastructure can support more devices at a time. The method of aggregating data before transmission enhances the speed of response through achieving prioritization to systems. First, early exclusion of unimportant data also helps the system rapidly analyze the input data and make decisions in real time, for example, to inform healthcare providers of a patient’s condition. Resource optimization is achieved in a scenario where a small amount of data has to be analyzed and transmitted. As engorging data requirements are one of the core factors that hinder potential healthcare systems, the reduced data volume effectively enables comprehensive distribution of available computation resources for potentially supporting a greater number of related devices and users from a performance point of view. This is especially true in settings that 208.demand flexibility in their infrastructure, for example, large hospitals or mobile clinics.
*   *Enhanced Data Quality:* Data from different providers and facilities that are aggregated creates a more accurate portrayal of the patient’s condition, which is a very positive effect in achieving a diagnosis and effective treatment. Consequently, from a single view perspective, holistic health insights are obtained from various sources that include heart rate monitors, glucose trackers, and other types of activity trackers integrated into a single picture. For example, in a patient with a very healthy and physically active lifestyle, it is possible to assess health levels in terms of various complications simultaneously with some form of integration into the assessment of health status. The integration of information in the same database enhances the possibility of precise diagnostics and treatment.
*   *Real-Time Monitoring:* Similarly, timely alerts and interventions are earned from the real-time data aggregation, where healthcare systems can immediately locate health differences such as abnormal heart rate or a sudden change in blood pressure level. This makes it possible to alert healthcare providers at the earliest instance, and this perhaps helps to save lives through early handling of complications before they occur. Real-time data collection adds to prognostics and health management (PHM), especially in those who have chronic diseases. It enables regular changes of treatment regimes, diets, or dosages of drugs given to patients, making it easier for the systems to adapt to the current situation and conditions of the patient, hence promoting improvement in the overall health of the patient. In all forms of health emergencies, there is every need to have the effective and immediate aggregation of what can be termed “real-time” data in emergency healthcare emergent situations, including vital signs and oxygen levels. This ensures that the healthcare professional attending to the patient quickly gets to know the state of the patient and therefore takes quick decisions and appropriate necessary action towards the stabilization of the patient.

### 11.6.3 Types of Data Aggregation Techniques

Many IoT networks aim to make use of IoT data aggregation through these approaches, which each have their unique features ([Aga et al., 2024](#ch19.xhtml#r369)). These techniques are mainly used to access, manipulate, format, and transmit data with minimal bandwidth consumption, channel loading, and enhanced system performance. Below are the three main types of data aggregation techniques used in IoT.

### 11.6.4 Hierarchical Aggregation

Hierarchical aggregation is another approach to the practical management of a large number of IoT devices by implementing data aggregation on multiple levels of a hierarchy. This is especially useful with extensive IoT systems where the IoT architecture may be implemented in a large number of healthcare facilities or across geographically diverse regions.

*   *209.How It Works:* First, collected and aggregated data from individual sensors and devices are stored locally at the sensor scope. However, these local data values are then summed up in the intermediate nodes, which might be the gateway, regional center, or any hospital center, and are then sent to the central server or cloud. This data hierarchy assists in the simplification of the sequence of aggregation so that it can effectively and efficiently flow across the network domain.
*   *Benefits:* Another major benefit resulting from hierarchical aggregation is the minimization of data transmittal within the system, in that data is aggregated locally at different levels before being transmitted to the central system. This reduces communication waste and eases the traffic within the networks. It also gives better scalability so that the system can accommodate more devices in the future from different manufacturers. In addition, data is processed locally at intermediate levels, which, as shown above, helps to minimize latency as only the subset of filtered data is transmitted upstream.
*   *Healthcare Application:* In a large hospital setup, for example, sensor data collected from sensors originating from departments like ICU, telemetry, and ambulatory are summed locally in each of the departments. The data collected in this aggregated manner is then transferred to hospital hubs for analysis and computing before being tabulated to the centralized server. This helps to offload the main communication network and only pass relevant and important data, hence enhancing the efficiency of the system and the overall decision-making process.

### 11.6.5 Cluster-Based Aggregation

Cluster-based aggregation hierarchical aggregation is a mechanism by which IoT devices are grouped into clusters, and for each group, there exists a device called the aggregator. In the case of the cluster, individual devices in each cluster transmit their information to the cluster head, which in turn will also combine the information from the other devices and forward the integrated data to a master server. This method saves time on data transfer and improves its flow, especially in massive IoT network systems.

*   *How It Works:* Devices are divided depending on the closeness and relation they possess and the functions they perform. For instance, in a healthcare facility, devices measuring certain aspects, such as blood pressure, temperature, pulse rate, etc., can form clusters according to the zone in the health facility or type of data being captured. The cluster leader is responsible for gathering all the collected data from devices within the group, and after possibly filtering, summarizing, or compressing the data, the result is sent to the central server.
*   *Benefits:* A significant advantage observed in the use of cluster-based aggregation is energy saving as the number of broadcasts is minimized. This is particularly important for battery-operated IoT devices as it enhances their longevity. The method can also reduce the amount of information being transferred over the network, hence avoiding excessive use of the network by the various programs 210.or processes. Moreover, this approach is highly scalable as it is delocalized and spreads the computational load among various CLs suitable for large IoT networks.
*   *Healthcare Application:* In a wearable health monitoring system, the sensors that measure the vital signs such as the pulse rate, oxygen level, and blood pressure could be sub-categorized by patient area, for example, ward level or patient room. The cluster leader within the novel groups proposed would collect data from the sensors, reduce the data collected, and then upload the averaged dataset to a monitoring system. This helps in freeing some traffic space in the network and fast and effective monitoring of the health state of patients in real time.

### 11.6.6 Compression-Based Aggregation

Compression-based aggregation involves taking some data and compressing it before transmitting it through various techniques of data compression ([Ketshabetswe et al., 2021](#ch19.xhtml#r384)). This is especially handy in IoT use cases where devices are constantly creating data and the available network bandwidth is usually small. Through data compression during the transmission process, this technique helps conserve available resources.

*   *How It Works:* In direct compression of raw data generated by IoT devices, data reduction includes a set of techniques like run-length encoding, wavelet transformation, or statistical representation like mean or median of all the collected data. These methods aid in minimizing the amount of data while still maintaining the important features within the data set. After the data has been compressed, it is then segmented and conveyed in the network while maintaining most of the information, therefore being able to minimize the data flow, but at the same time guarantee optimization of the network resources.
*   *Benefits:* The advantages of using compression-based aggregation include reduced bandwidth consumption, increased throughput, and reduced power consumption. Reducing data size is beneficial in that channels are occupied less often and utilization of bandwidth is reduced, thus lowering transmission costs and making the aforementioned system economically feasible. This means that the delivery process is accelerated and the overall system performance improved in conversion, as well as in applications such as real-time health monitoring or emergency alerting systems. Also, as there are fewer bits to transmit, IoT devices draw less energy, which translates to longer battery life of devices that are portable or used in remote locations.
*   *Healthcare Application:* In smart home health monitoring systems, where devices such as a wearable glucose monitor often send data points, features can be compressed. For instance, instead of having glucose monitoring every minute, and sending one glucose alert for each of them, the system could send an average glucose level for each 60 minutes: 60 alerts instead of 60 × 60 = 3600 alerts. This means that the amount of data transmitted over the network is considerably minimized, thus improving the efficiency of the system while people still get important health information.

### 211.11.6.7 Challenges in Data Aggregation for IoT Healthcare Systems

There are several challenges that cut across the process of data aggregation in IoT healthcare systems, where solutions must be sought for the aggregations to be optimal in their effectiveness, dependable, and secure. These challenges can in turn affect the efficiency, effectiveness, and overall capacity of the system, including data integrity, speed of data transfer, and expandability, respectively. Below are the main challenges encountered in data aggregation for IoT healthcare systems:

*   *Scalability Issues:* As mentioned, as the number of IoT devices in a healthcare system increases, the relevance of the problem described above escalates, and managing data aggregation at that scale becomes an even more significant challenge. The communicated data can be higher in volumes and frequencies in each device and require processing and transmission that cannot congest the network and delay latency. 
    *   *Challenge:* Managing extensive amounts of information—High numbers of nodes in the IoT networks may amount to thousands and generate varying amounts of information within a short span of time; for instance, heart rate monitors may be sending data every few seconds. The method for funneling and broadcasting such data in real-time is complicated in order not to clog a system and affect response times. Scalability for collection—As the use of big data gets widespread, ways of engaging and processing distributed data need to be developed, as data is often grouped and processed locally at some point before it is sent to a central server.
    *   *Healthcare Solution:* Hierarchical aggregation could alleviate the problem of scalability if the network were divided into subsets or clusters, each of which is responsible for data aggregation within their cluster. This helps to share the load on a central server and create a more efficient way of growing the number of devices in the system.
*   *Real-Time Processing Requirements:* In several healthcare applications, especially those containing highly sensitive patient data (for instance, bringing out the real-time parameters of the patients), it is essential to collect and transmit data without delay. Failure in handling data in a timely manner means that a patient will miss an alert or get treated inadequately, or in the worst-case scenario, die. 
    *   *Challenge:* Real-time constraints—Data aggregation techniques need to work efficiently in terms of time to allow producers to generate timely alerts as well as respond to similar alerts. Thus, delays can effectively counter-benefit the idea of IoT in healthcare, especially for those applications that need real-time feedback, like an ECG or a glucose level monitor. Low latency requirements—Aggregation must be done as a way to offer low latency of data to facilitate real-time decisions with the unified data.
    *   *Healthcare Solution:* If edge computing is put in the context of data aggregation, then the latency can be minimized greatly. Peculiar or local data analysis is performed at edge nodes, thus making it possible to respond quickly to critical health data fed into the central server.
*   *212.Data Security and Privacy Concerns:* Personal data is encompassed in most IoT healthcare models, and this data may include health records, pulse rate, blood pressure, among others. The primary consideration that major organizations face is the safety of data collected and patients’ proper identification to avoid cases of unauthorized access. 
    *   *Challenge:* Data integrity and privacy issues are two major parts to be considered. 
        *   *Data Integrity:* When data is accumulated for larger sets, it becomes easy for outsiders to tamper with the data or manipulate it, especially if the aggregation is not secure. Maintaining data integrity is critical to reduce the incidence of having bogus health information and subsequent bogus alerts.
        *   *Privacy Issues:* User aggregation should be done while preserving the privacy of the patient. There have to be ways that data has to be anonymized and pseudonymized if it is needed.
    *   *Healthcare Solution:* To scale up the use of AI in data aggregation, data confidentiality during aggregation can be maintained by using encryption techniques like homomorphic encryption. It also has the capability to protect the data from unauthorized amendments through blockchain technology for recording deeds in an open ledger in a decentralized manner.

## **11.7** Energy Consumption

Currently, most IoT devices in the healthcare industry rely on batteries. Optimal collection of data due to the excessive use of a device’s battery can lead to device failure or reduced efficiency of monitoring devices.

### 11.7.1 Challenge

*   *Battery:* The continuous data transmission requirement for aggregating the on-body batteries of wearable devices may be drained, lowering their operating time.
*   *Optimal Data Transmission:* The data aggregation should occur seldom, but it should provide enough information for the assessment of the health condition.
*   *Healthcare Solution:* Some of the examples of data aggregation methods include the use of compression-based aggregation so that fewer pieces of data will be transferred, thereby consuming less energy. Hierarchical and cluster-based aggregation can also contribute breadth by cutting down the amount of data communicated.

### 11.7.2 Complexity of Integration

Combining data acquisition with the existing healthcare IoT systems can be challenging as there are many types of devices, protocols, and data structures. Interoperability of these components is, therefore, highly important to prevent a situation whereby some components cannot work with others.

#### 213.11.7.2.1 Challenge

*   *Interoperability Problem:* IoT devices have their way of communicating with each other through protocols such as Zigbee, Bluetooth, LoRa, etc. It is crucial for personal devices to receive information in a format that can be understood by the other devices present in the system.
*   *Standardization Needs:* Coordinating these frameworks to develop approaches for generating integrated and unified data from numerous potential sources can also contribute toward establishing standards for data aggregation to ease integration.
*   *Healthcare Solution:* Promoting interoperability can be accomplished with the use of joint standards and requirements for data accumulation, like IEEE 11073 for healthcare. Also, middleware solutions can also offer one interface that can be used to collect data from various devices.

However, there are hurdles that are as follows in data aggregation in IoT healthcare systems: scalability issues, real-time processing, security, energy consumption, and integration issues. To overcome these challenges, the application of complex approaches and tools such as hierarchical and cluster-based aggregation, signal and data compression methods, edge computing, cryptographic algorithms, and distributed ledger technology in the form of blockchain is inevitable. If these solutions are deployed to healthcare systems, data is accumulated effectively with low latency rates, high security levels, and low power usage, ensuring improved patients’ health and the overall system performance.

## **11.8** MALICIOUS NODE AND PACKET DETECTION IN IoT NETWORKS

Malicious node and packet detection in IoT networks specifically addresses the problem of increasing the harm of malicious nodes in IoT systems with an emphasis on healthcare ([Liyakat, 2023](#ch19.xhtml#r387)). These nodes can interfere with the data they transmit by feeding in the wrong information or by removing a genuine packet and, in the process, harm patients and diminish the reliability of the system. Mechanisms like rule-based systems, blockchain, and anomaly detection algorithms are required for constant surveillance of the behavior of the network and protection of accuracy and security of data in real-time IoT applications.

[Figure 11.3](#ch19.xhtml#f77) gives an enhanced view of the possible vulnerabilities within IoT networks, especially in healthcare settings, where malicious nodes can cause havoc to data and networks. In the diagram, the nodes are categorized into three distinct types: There are usual nodes, sensor nodes as blue circles, the sink nodes as blue rectangles, and the black Scares as evil nodes as yellow circles.

![Figure 11.3 IoT network.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C011_003.jpg)

**Figure 11.3** IoT network.[⏎](#ch19.xhtml#f77b)

Sensor nodes are specifically designated to collect data from the environment, such as from health monitoring devices or sensors ([Senouci & Mellouk, 2016](#ch19.xhtml#r390)). These nodes offer the functionality of data collection and transfer of the data to other nodes in the network. They are very essential for caregiving as they help to track the patient’s state frequently and collect data like heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, and many others.

214.Sink nodes are represented as centrally located in the network; they collect data from several sensor nodes and forward the collected data to higher-level data management, for example, a cloud server for additional data analysis and storage. These nodes have a better computing platform and are capable of processing a huge amount of information than other nodes. They also serve as communicators that guarantee the efficiency of transmitting information collected by the sensor nodes with the management system of the network, sparing no effort.

The malicious node, represented by N6 in the diagram, N6 poses a major threat to the integrity of the network. They can inject erroneous data or drop all legitimate packets they get; this results in wrong diagnosis or poor patient management and an unpredictable system. This type of activity is especially important now in the healthcare sector as the data could be fatal to patients’ lives.

## **11.9** TYPES OF MALICIOUS ACTIVITIES IN IoT HEALTHCARE

### 11.9.1 Packet Dropping

*   *Description:* Packet dropping is the process where some of the nodes will drop packets of data, particularly those with health information. This action can interfere with the normal operation of live tracking methods and may result in missed or delayed alerts in some emergency cases, such as a low heart rate or high blood pressure.
*   *Impact:* Packet dropping in most cases results in a scenario whereby some data is either compromised or incomplete being relayed through the system, hence limiting the efficacy of the system in monitoring the health status of the patients. 215.For instance, in emergency conditions where data has to be received within a particular time frame, packet dropping results in severe impacts on the end system.
*   *Detection Method:* Correcting means, like end-to-end acknowledgment, where a packet needs an acknowledgment receipt that aids in identifying packet loss. Furthermore, it is possible to use sequence numbers to give to data packets to make sure that data is not damaged. Such patterns can also be computed through ML models of packet dropping insights, specifically in regard to a more frequent loss or occasional gaps in the data.

### 11.9.2 False Data Injection

*   *Description:* False data injection means that some nodes will inject wrong data into the system with the aim of misleading the system. For instance, a device that provides a normal heart rate while in actuality the rate is rather high may help delay some critical action.
*   *Impact:* False data injection can result in wrong conclusions being drawn from fabricated data, endangering the lives of patients. This can also erode the confidence in the system due to health problems, which deserves correct information.
*   *Detection Method:* Some of the sophisticated methods of anomaly detection are beneficial for detecting false data injection. ML models can be trained on normal patterns of thought, and patterns outside of this normalcy can be detected.

### 11.9.3 Node Tampering

*   *Description:* The main attack on IoT, described as node tampering, is when an unauthorized party gains access to the IoT devices within the network and alters them. Malicious devices can therefore be used in interfering with the normal network flow or act as a means of spying on sensitive information, leading to a major threat to the patient’s right to privacy and the network security.
*   *Impact:* Malicious devices can feed the system with incorrect data, which negatively impacts performance, congests the network, or completely halts the system’s function. This can result in privacy invasion, and health information can easily be disclosed to the wrong people.
*   *Detection Method:* To identify node tampering, day-to-day observation of the behaviors of the devices is closely monitored. Analysis of hardware characteristics and behavior of communication with other devices can help distinguish the genuine device from the contaminated ones during the device fingerprinting. Automated tools like intrusion detection systems (IDS) can analyze the data flow as well as the traffic pattern to identify some form of interference that corresponds to tampered nodes.

## **11.10** Methods for Detection and Mitigation

To effectively address the types of malicious activities mentioned above, various strategies and technologies can be used:

### 216.11.10.1 Trust-Based Systems

*   *Description:* In such a model, nodes are associated with trust scores that are determined by their behavior and interactions in the system. High-trust-score nodes are used in the subsequent analyses as reliable, while nodes with low trust scores may be questioned.
*   *Implementation:* As positive or negative, trust scores could be given on the basis of parameters such as accuracy of data and information, frequency and activity of the flow of communication, and general reaction time. They include deviation from traditional traffic flow or density of a single node, where a node is suspected of dropping its packets or injecting fake data.

### 11.10.2 ML and AI Techniques

*   *Description:* It has been suggested that, by applying ML models, particularly anomaly-based methods, it is possible to teach the algorithms to identify patterns of malicious actions in data streams. AI models are capable of distinguishing between standard business data and anomalous signals that signal an attack.
*   *Implementation:* Clustering, decision trees, or neural models can be used to highly train models that deal with past experiences as well as with new patterns. These models can conclude whether data streams have anomalies, for example, increases or decreases in values, which may be due to false data injection or packet dropping.

## **11.11** Blockchain Technology

*   *Description:* Another area is data integrity through the possibility of recording all data transactions in the blockchain system, which is an open record and cannot be changed. This eliminates data manipulation as well as fosters strict control of data flow within the network.
*   *Implementation:* Every data packet is encrypted to be checked by multiple nodes, which allows for easy rejection of any attempt to falsify data in the network. Traceability is more visible as well as blockchain enables auditing of the data flow to detect and exclude the malicious nodes.

### 11.11.1 Adaptive Protocols and Algorithms

*   *Description:* Practical adaptability can adapt the aggregation techniques and communication protocols based on the network behavior and feedback. They can adapt themselves in real time to improve the transfer of data in a specific context dependent on the network.
*   *Implementation:* It is possible to alter dynamic clustering and hierarchical aggregation depending on the network traffic, device movements, and data traffic. This flexibility enables the use of the system while still being able to sustain reliable operation and security despite the evolving network conditions.

217.With such approaches to detection and mitigation, IoT healthcare systems can be guarded against such invasions more effectively. Through incorporating trust-based systems, ML, blockchain, and adaptive protocols, data aggregation and transmission in IoT healthcare networks could have improved security and reliability, thus protecting patients’ sensitive health information and improving patient safety ([Badiger & Mathew, 2022](#ch19.xhtml#r373)).

## **11.12** Strategies to Detect and Discard Malicious Packets

There is a need to detect malicious packets and to discard them, and ensure that the security of data in IoT healthcare networks is not compromised. The following strategies leverage advanced techniques to identify and mitigate the impact of malicious activities:

### 11.12.1 Rule-Based Detection

1.  *Description:* Rule-based detection involves setting up predefined rules or thresholds to identify anomalies in data streams that could indicate malicious activities, such as packet dropping or false data injection.
2.  *Implementation:* 
    1.  *Predefined Rules:* Such rules are based on patterns of legitimate data flow and may contain values that describe allowed deviation in the rate of packet, the size of the packet, and the contents of the packet. If any packet violates these preset parameters, then an alert is generated.
    2.  *Anomaly Detection:* Anomaly detection algorithms are applied to the analysis of network traffic to detect values that deviate from these rules. For example, when a packer from a specific node has consistent delays or the data content in the packet has changes beyond the acceptable limit, it can be a pointer that the node is involved in modifying the data maliciously or the node has been compromised.
3.  *Benefits:* It is relatively easy to design a rule-based method for detecting anomalous entities, and the approach is reliable for identifying gross outliers. Compared to other approaches, it is weaker in terms of computational necessity and should be applied for less powerful environments.

## **11.13** BLOCKCHAIN-INTEGRATED DATA VALIDATION

*   *Description:* Blockchain technology integrates with IoT healthcare systems to provide a secure and transparent mechanism for data validation. Every data packet is verified across the network through a consensus process before it is accepted into the system.
*   *Benefits:* Blockchain creates another layer of security so that any node that wishes to change some information will be easily identified by other nodes. It maintains the quality and delivers the transparency of the healthcare data and its trail.

218.By combining rule-based detection with blockchain-integrated data validation, IoT healthcare systems can effectively detect and discard malicious packets, ensuring that only valid, accurate data is used for patient monitoring and health analytics. These strategies not only protect patient data from malicious tampering but also enhance the overall reliability and trustworthiness of IoT healthcare systems.

## **11.14** CASE STUDY: REAL-WORLD IMPLEMENTATION OF SECURE IoT HEALTHCARE SYSTEMS

In response to the growing need for healthcare delivery that is efficient, secure, and cost-effective, Lemberg Solutions has created a number of IoT enabled healthcare devices. Five examples of inventive implementations are as follows:

*   *Remote Patient Monitoring:* At a German healthcare company, Lemberg Solutions developed an eMedical Tablet that is specific for Intensive Care specialists. This gadget frees up an immense amount of work for healthcare staff as they are able to continuously check the patient vital signs by themselves and only alert physicians when immediate action is necessary. Complemented with voice control for persons with disabilities, this system cuts down on constant, time-consuming inpatient consultations thereby minimizing health expenditure while, at the same time, even with stable patient conditions, the hospitals can keep track of their progress and escalate serious cases as may be necessary.
*   *Cough Sound Recognition:* A particular machine was created based on SBC that served as an IoT gateway device for a German telemedicine provider assisting with cough-type symptoms. The technology incorporates sophisticated sensors and AI algorithms to amass cough data, reduce background noise, and prepare the signals to be analyzed by a physician. The patient records are stored online on a cloud means where this feature is protected by laws governing data protection. This solution means early clinician evaluations, patient’s individual treatment modifications, and actions that minimize the risk of hospitalization.
*   *Activity Tracking:* To help support a more mobile impaired or rehabilitation patient, Lemberg Solutions incorporated an activity tracking mechanism that incorporated beacons, smart watches and remote servers. Radio frequency beacons placed within every room help the smartwatch to determine the location of the wearer and their movements; information is sent in real time to a server. Using the app dashboard, caregivers can track activity changes to prevent issues such as a fall and respond quickly, so that patient safety and care are improved.
*   *Rehabilitation Monitoring:* For physical therapy, Lemberg Solutions created the wearable gadgets that can monitor the progress, for instance, range of motion, and follow of therapy schedule. The information is processed and reported to the caregivers to enable modification of the management strategies for the purpose of the best rehabilitation gains to be achieved.
*   *Smart Medication Dispensers:* Lemberg Solutions created a smart medication dispenser to enhance adherence to prescribed treatments. The device 219.provides reminders, tracks dosages, and alerts caregivers about missed doses. It reduces errors, supports patient independence, and improves overall treatment effectiveness.

## **11.15** Conclusion

Many technologies under the umbrella of the IoT are evolving swiftly and are being applied in healthcare to produce several advancements in patient treatment that are real-time, customized, and cheap. However, it also comes with increased difficulties, especially in the aspects of data security, data accuracy, and power consumption. Solving these problems implies the use of state-of-the-art technologies, including ML, blockchain, and edge computing. Not only do these technologies provide security to detect all types of lawyer nodes and guarantee data integrity, but they also improve system performance by efficiently aggregating data, reducing the number of overheads, and minimizing delay time. Thus, lightweight encrysption consists of using adaptive protocols to support energy-efficient IoT devices’ sustainability in healthcare niches.

# 222.12GiwrfGini Impurity-Based Weighted RF of Intrusion Detection in Network Security and Feature Selection Using the Machine Learning Algorithms

S.V. Sugin and M. Kanchana

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-12](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-12)

## **12.1** Introduction

The interactions between countries, companies, and people are numerous and intricate in the complex world we live in. Information and communication technologies (ICT) are mostly used to carry out those relationships. The number of malicious users looking to take advantage of system vulnerabilities has surged along with the number of devices that are online. These malicious actors can use a variety of attacks to target organizations, governments, or people. Malicious activities range from straightforward threats like spam or phishing, parameter tampering, to more sophisticated dangers like advanced persistent threats (APTs), botnets, or social engineering assaults that make use of open-source intelligence techniques (OSINT) and domain generation algorithms (DGAs) \[[1](#ch20.xhtml#r394), [2](#ch20.xhtml#r395)\]. Cybersecurity experts aim to help clients secure their networks, systems, and digital assets using various tools, such as intrusion detection systems (IDSs), antivirus, or firewalls. These tools produce a huge number of details on the form of network data through a variety of normal interactions and threat ones. In addition, the appropriate combination of additional activity logs and other digital evidence assets is crucial for the successful execution of the security lifecycle \[[3](#ch20.xhtml#r396), [4](#ch20.xhtml#r397)\]. The automatic analysis and treatment of sample data is a crucial step in the implementation of adaptive and effective defensive techniques due to the establishment of quantities of security-related information \[[5](#ch20.xhtml#r398)\]. Consequently, it is exciting to use a single method that can be applied to analyze these logs to reduce tasks and support analyst’s decision-making. For such a work, our strategy involves developing parameter-free procedures \[[6](#ch20.xhtml#r399)\].

In this research, we analyze and clarify the usage of an earlier approach according to compressing data \[[7](#ch20.xhtml#r400)\] in a larger circumstance that includes several binary categorization issues in the present cybersecurity context. We train a machine learning (ML) 223.system that uses these features to categorize the data by utilizing the normalized-compression distance (NCD) \[[8](#ch20.xhtml#r401)\] to identify a group of attributes that describe the imbalanced network data related to every issue. The generalizing of our method, which shows an integrated framework for the investigation of network data in an overall cybersecurity environment, is demonstrated by our results in various situations. Despite the fact that we do not provide the best modern solutions for every problem under consideration, we still get competitive outcomes across all disciplines.

A Gini impurity-based weighted Radio Frequency (GIWRF) model was created in our suggested method to choose the critical and appropriate attributes based on the priority level. The scores for attribute relevance were determined by using the Gini impurity criterion to partition the trees and modifying the overall weight in the Random Forest (RF) algorithm for an imbalanced distribution of classes. However, for the ML-based IDS framework, datasets were used to create the Ada Boost, gradient boosting tree (GBT), decision tree (DT), gated recurrent unit (GRU), long short-term memory (LSTM), and multilayer perceptron (MLP). Before the models are tested and trained, data engineering or data preprocessing is needed. Three processes made up the data-preprocessing phase and will be covered later in this study. However, the binary classification task’s performance to conduct the analysis, the network dataset UNSW-NB15 \[[9](#ch20.xhtml#r402), [10](#ch20.xhtml#r403)\], which is a relatively new set of data containing modern attack patterns.

A binary classification task using supervised ML models was carried out in this study. When the supervised ML method is tasked with classifying a discrete value as either an attack or normal instance, binary classification takes place. The study’s dataset is rather sizable and has many feature space dimensions. It is crucial to select an attribute selection strategy for removing insignificant characteristics from a huge dataset and using only the crucial set of features in both the testing and training steps \[[11](#ch20.xhtml#r404)\]. The method of reducing the set of relevant data during the process of feature selection is used to create predictive models. Most of the time, improving the performance of prediction models is desired. Additionally, irrelevant features negatively impact the performance of the model. However, because the IDS handles so many data samples that have redundant or irrelevant attributes, it not only increases the computational cost but also lowers the accuracy of detecting scores \[[12](#ch20.xhtml#r405)\]. By locating the relevant attributes that contain the data required for the classification method, feature selection provides remedies to several frequently occurring errors in IDS \[[13](#ch20.xhtml#r406)\].

## **12.2** Methods and Materials

It is necessary to note that the greater portions of the earlier discussed strategies are problem-specific. The discipline is lacking a general technique that approaches all of these challenges from a similar angle, even if all of the problems described include some sort of network data analysis. In this part, a general method for extracting a group of numerical characteristics that defines a set of data using a compression-based analysis, such as the NCD, is discussed. Calculating the separation between a *T* text and *k* a set of extra texts (*g*[1], *g*[2], …, *g*[k]), referred to as Attribute Generator (AG), is the main goal when given a text *T*. This generates a vector of *k* numbers that indicate the text *T* in a *k* dimensional attributes space as an input for a classification 224.model \[[14](#ch20.xhtml#r407)\]. However, in this research, we have utilized ML classifiers; it is important to emphasize that our method for any other classification algorithm can be used with attribute extraction.

The specific steps are as follows for a UNSW-NB15 dataset made up of data from two different classes: The data are randomly split into two groups, *G* and *I*, each of which contains *m* and *n* data. Both groups have equal numbers of datasets for the two classes, making them both balanced. The attribute generators are constructed using the first group, *G.* To accomplish this, *k* generator files with data from only one class each are created from the data in *G*. As a result, each class has *k/2* generators. After being distinguished by the distances to the generators of attributes, the second group (*I*) includes the set of data that is utilized to instruct the classifiers. To get the vector, we measure the distance between every string *S*[*i*] in *I* and each of the *k*\-attributes generators:

*S*[*i*] = (*x*[*i* 1 ],*x*[*i* 2],……,*x*[*i* *k*]) (12.1) 

It is used to describe the data *S*[*i*]. The following equations provide the components *x*[*ij*] of *S*[*i*]:

*x*[*i**j*] = *D*(*g*[*j* ],*s*[ *i* ]) (12.2) 

where *D*(*g*[*j*],*s*[*i*]) denotes the reduced data about the normalized conditions between the string (*s*[*i*]) and the generator (*g*[*j*]):

$D\\left( {g\_{j~},~s\_{i~}} \\right) = \\frac{C\\left( s\_{i~|~~g\_{j}~} \\right)}{C\\left( {~s\_{i~~}} \\right)}~ = ~\\frac{C\\left( {~g\_{j}.~s\_{i~}} \\right) - C\\left( g\_{j~} \\right)}{C\\left( s\_{i~~} \\right)}~~~$ (12.3) 

The dot operator is used to indicate altogether, and *C*(*s*) represents the reduced size of (*s*). We make use of the gzip compressor in the tests as it performs faster than other compression methods.

Once utilize the feature vectors for the full set of data in *I* to train a classification algorithm that anticipates the class that each item of data belongs to using an radial basis function (RBF) kernel. The scikit learn Python package is used to implement the approach, and accuracy, and the area under the curve (AUC) area under the measurements of the operational feature curve of the receiver are used to determine the performance of the classifiers. The performance of the ML model is based on two hyperparameters, the kernel complexity *C* and the width *γ*, which are determined in each *k* using the traditional fivefold cross-validation approach as defined in ref. \[[14](#ch20.xhtml#r407)\]. [Figure 12.1](#ch20.xhtml#f78) shows the complete procedure, from the primary dataset to the final categorization.

## **12.4** Proposed Methodology

To provide a comparison, the outcomes of the ML methods described in the familiar ML technique (DT), deep neural network (LSTM, GRU), artificial neural network 226.(MLP), and ensemble method (AdaBoost, GBT) would be used to identify intrusions over imbalanced datasets. The main objective of the research was to use an effective feature selection strategy for an unbalanced dataset. These models were trained over the datasets described in the UNSW-NB15 network dataset chapter. The recommended approach diagram is shown in [Figure 12.2](#ch20.xhtml#f79).

### 12.4.1 Coding for Categorical Features

State, Proto, and Service are the three categorical features included in the network dataset UNSW-NB15. Response coding was utilized to convert the string attributes of the UNSW-NB15 network dataset, while use of Label Encoding to encrypt the categorical features of UNSW-NB15. Each categorical characteristic in Label Encoding is determined a distinct integer value based on alphabetical sequence. In contrast, encoding techniques shows the probability that a given category of information instances belongs to a particular class. *N* new features for (*N*) class classification that insert the (*P*) probability of an information instance for every class, depending on the 227.category of data value, are constructed for each category. One method of presenting a mathematical expression is:

*P*(*X* | *B*) = *P*(*B*∩*X*) / *P*(*B*) (12.4) 

where *B* stands in for the feature category and *X* is indicated as a class. Given that the Network UNSW-NB15 dataset has a number of categorical features, its large memory requirements prevent it from being used to modify string features.

### 12.4.2 Feature Scaling

The datasets include certain features whose magnitudes, units, and ranges are highly unpredictable. A few algorithms, like the MLP, make incorrect predictions because of the dataset’s high degree of variation. Additionally, it calls for plenty of computer power. In regard to normalizing the range of independent variables, one often used method is feature scaling. For some ML algorithms that determine the separation between data, feature scaling is required. Two frequently employed features of scaling methodologies in ML are standardization and normalization. In this experiment, data between the ranges of 1 and 0 were normalized using normalization or minimum and maximum scaling. The general normalization equation is as follows:

*h*^(− ) = \[(*h*−minimum(h))/(maximum(*h*)−minimum(*h*))\] (12.5) 

where (*h*^(*−*)) is the normalized attributes, and *h* is the original attributes. The feature’s maxi and mini values are denoted by minimum(*h*) and maximum(*h*), respectively.

### 228.12.4.3 Gini Impurity-Based Weighted RF

RF is an ensemble classification that supports different feature significance metrics and is constructed on a number of DTs. One of them is to train the classifier to determine the score of significance. The models are developed without taking into account the possibility of an imbalanced distribution of classes in the training data, as the conventional ML classification technique anticipates that all the categories in the training data will emerge with the same relevance \[[16](#ch20.xhtml#r409)\]. After the Gini impurity was measured by the classifier, *i*(*𝜏*), this attribute selection method used a weight modification method in RF to understand the compatibility of attributes with the outcomes of the asymmetric data. A split’s ability to equally entire binary class samples into two equal parts in a given node is indicated by its Gini impurity. It can be represented mathematically as follows:

*i*(*τ*) = 1 − *P*²*p* − *P*²*n*  (12.6) 

where the percentages of negative and positive samples, respectively, out of the entire amount of samples (*N*) at node *𝜏*, are denoted as *p*[*p*] and *p*[*n*], respectively. For each node *τ* in the weighted trees (*M*) in the forest, the decrease in Gini impurity because of each optimized split ∆*i*[*f*] (*τ*, *M*) is collected, separately for each feature. It can be expressed mathematically as:

$I\_{g}\\left( f \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{M}W\_{p,n}\\sum\\limits\_{\\tau}\\Delta i\_{f}\\left( {\\tau,M} \\right)$ (12.7) 

Allocating the weight (*w*[*p,n*]) characterizes an asymmetric class distribution in the ML algorithm, where *I*[*g*] is the Gini significance, which describes the frequency of a related attribute (*f*) as a chosen for the divide and the importance of the attributes all aspects value of discriminative for the binary categorization problem.

$~~\\text{Positive~class~weight,~}W\_{p} = \\frac{n\_{n}}{N}$ (12.8) $~\\text{Negative~class~weight,~}~W\_{n} = \\frac{n\_{p}}{N}$ (12.9) 

*w*[*n*] + *w*[*p*] = 1 and *w*[*p*] ≠ *w*[*n*] for data from an unbalanced class. The positive occurrences are indicated as *n*[*p*], and the number of negative cases is shown as (*n*[*n*]). The training dataset’s total instance count is *N*. [Table 12.3](#ch20.xhtml#t17) explains the pseudo code for the algorithm used to choose the features using the sklearn package. [Table 12.4](#ch20.xhtml#t19) includes a list of the selected attributes for the UNSW-NB15 dataset.

**Table 12.3** GIWRF: Gini Impurity-Based Weighted Random Forest Algorithms[⏎](#ch20.xhtml#t17b)

### 12.4.4 Evaluation Metric

229.The objective of this experiment was to increase the proportion of accurate binary classification outcomes in the test set. Several ML performance metrics, including 230.false positive rate (FPR), precision, recall, accuracy, etc., are applied to evaluate the effectiveness of IDS based on ML \[[17](#ch20.xhtml#r410)\]. However, the most frequently employed metric for assessing how well models perform in binary classification situations is the accuracy score. It is described by the equation below:

$\\text{Accuracy} = \\frac{\\left\\lbrack \\left( {~\\mathbf{TP}~ + ~\\mathbf{TN}~} \\right) \\right\\rbrack}{\\left\\lbrack \\left( {\\mathbf{TP} + \\mathbf{TN} + \\mathbf{FP} + \\mathbf{FN}} \\right) \\right\\rbrack}$ (12.10) 

where TN and TP denote the true negative and true positive. The amount of accurately identified assault events is known as the true positive rate. The instances that are appropriately identified as normal are counted by TN. False positive (FP), on the other hand, refers to the quantity of genuine traffic that is incorrectly categorized as an attack. The number of assaults is counted using false negative (FN) cases that are mistakenly regarded as typical instances. Fewer FN is often anticipated in the detection of incursion as it poses a greater risk than FP. Although for asymmetric information about classes, particularly when the goal is to accurately identify the assault, four additional rules, such as FPR, Recall, Precision, and F1 score are also taken into account in added to the original value determined.

1.  *FPR:* The ratio of the total number of negative events to the number of negative occurrences that are mistakenly labeled as positive is known as the FPR. The expression is as described below:

$\\text{FPR} = \\frac{\\mathbf{FP}}{\\left( {\\mathbf{FP} + \\mathbf{FN}} \\right)}$ (12.11) 

1.  *Precision:* When a model positively predicts an instance, precision measures how often the forecast is accurate to assess how well the model performs. It can be described mathematically using the equation below:

$\\text{Precision} = \\frac{\\mathbf{TP}}{\\left( {\\mathbf{TP} + \\mathbf{FP}} \\right)}$ (12.12) 

1.  *Detection Rate/Recall:* It measures how well the ML model detected occurrences of TPs. Recall measures the model’s precision in locating relevant data. For this reason, it is sometimes identified to be delicate or TPR. The logical equation is represented as follows:

$\\text{Detection~rate/recall} = \\frac{\\mathbf{TP}}{\\left( {\\mathbf{TP} + \\mathbf{FN}} \\right)}$ (12.13) 

1.  *F1 Score:* The tradeoff between recall and precision determines the ML method’s overall accuracy by accounting for both FP and FN. The following equation represents the F1 score:

231.$\\text{F}1\\text{~score} = \\frac{\\left( {2\*\\mathbf{Recall}\*\\mathbf{Precision}} \\right)}{\\left( {\\mathbf{Recall} + \\mathbf{Precision}} \\right)}$ (12.14)

## **12.5** Results and Experiments

This research was performed in two states and considered six ML models, including the GBT, LSTM, DT, Ada Boost, GRU, and MLP. The effectiveness of ML techniques for binary categorization was assessed in the first stage, which made use of every characteristic of the network dataset UNSW-NB15. In the second stage, the binary classification was once again carried out using six models, and only 20 attributes for the network dataset UNSW-NB15 were selected based on the suggested attributes selection technique. One consistent strategy used to train all the models was parameter adjustment, which helped this experiment increase accuracy and F1 score as well as FPR value is reduced. However, [Table 12.7](#ch20.xhtml#t21) compares the performance with the effective algorithm DT reported in this article after selecting the effective algorithm from every literature review that utilized the UNSW-NB15 network dataset. It has been confirmed that using DT with our suggested attribute selection (GIWRF), compared to other works, achieved satisfactory performance in regard of F1-score, which is an appropriate assessment criterion for inaccurate data. In addition to the Gu and Lu \[[18](#ch20.xhtml#r411)\] proposal, the accuracy value was discovered to be greater than similar works already in existence. In this instance, the suggested GIWRF-DT outperformed the NB-SVM with a slightly lower accuracy score (0.74%) but an increased Detection Rate/Recall (0.03%). That described the proposed DT's ability to identify intrusions effectively. They opted to employ a different training size employed in the proposed research.

## **232.233.12.6** Conclusion

This research aimed to develop and determine the ML algorithms: GBT, LSTM, Ada Boost, DT, GRU, and MLP for the binary classification challenge of IDS based on ML. On the premise that the imbalanced distribution of classes would have an impact on the attribute selection process, a GIWRF was proposed as the attribute selection procedure to choose an appropriate collection of attributes from the imbalanced datasets in UNSW-NB15. The UNSW-NB15 network dataset attributes were decreased using the feature selection technique to 20 (from 49), respectively. The model’s effectiveness in detecting the intrusion was analyzed using the metrics FPR, Accuracy, Recall, Precision, and F1 score. The entire feature set across datasets was initially used in the research. The research was then repeated, utilizing only the selected attributes that the attributes selection algorithm had extracted. For several datasets, the algorithm's performance was compared with full attribute field and with decreased attributes. The DT performed better in the network dataset UNSW-NB15 when using the attribute selection techniques.
