# 236.13Discrimination of Power System Disturbance and Cyber-Attacks through Machine Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence

Niharika Agrawal and Sheila Mahapatra

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-13](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-13)

## **13.1** Introduction

Machine learning (ML) plays a critical role in discriminating between power system disturbances and cyber**\-**attacks in modern smart grids (SGs). As SGs become more interconnected and reliant on digital communication, distinguishing between natural system faults and intentional cyber threats becomes increasingly challenging. ML algorithms help detect and classify events in power systems by analyzing real-time data patterns. They can differentiate between natural disturbances such as equipment failures, line faults, or load changes and cyber-attacks, including data injection, Denial of Service (DoS), and control signal manipulation. ML models analyze features like voltage and current waveforms, frequency deviations, Load patterns, and communication network data, which help distinguish between legitimate disturbances (e.g., a short circuit) and malicious manipulations. ML models can provide real-time detection of abnormal patterns using autoencoders for detecting the deviations from normal operation and recurrent neural network (RNNs) for time-series predictions and identifying temporal anomalies. By combining data from both the cyber (network logs, user activity) and physical (sensor readings, control commands) layers, ML can detect coordinated attacks that affect both the cyber and physical systems. It can identify subtle attacks like false data injection that can be difficult to detect through conventional methods. ML tools are able to forecast and predict possible failures and cyber threats prior to their occurrence, facilitating anticipatory maintenance planning and automated response systems that isolate compromised sections of the grid. The different challenges are:

*   237. *Data Quality and Availability:* Labeled data for cyber-attacks are often limited.
*   *Adversarial Attacks:* Attackers can manipulate ML systems if not properly secured.
*   *Scalability:* Managing large-scale power grids requires efficient models.

### 13.1.1 Major Techniques

*   *Supervised Learning:* (e.g., support vector machine (SVM), Decision Tree (DTs)) trained on labeled data to classify events.
*   *Unsupervised Learning:* (e.g., K-Means, density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN)) for anomaly detection when labeled data are not available.
*   *Deep Learning:* (e.g., convolutional neural network(CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTMs)) for more complex pattern recognition and time-series analysis. [Figure 13.1](#ch21.xhtml#f82) shows the types of learning.
    
    ![Figure 13.1 The types of learning.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C013_001.jpg)
    
    **Figure 13.1** The types of learning.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f82b)
    

Ref. \[[1](#ch21.xhtml#r420)\] presents a novel approach for enhancing cybersecurity in cyber-physical production systems (CPPS) through a hybrid DL-based attack graph model. The authors focus on early-stage detection of cyber-attacks, specifically those targeting Operational Technology (OT) networks, combines Operational Technology Graph Convolutiona (GC)-LSTM and CNNs for real-time anomaly detection. It achieves an accuracy of over 96%**,** outperforming existing time-series anomaly detection models. It is tested using simulations of cyber-attacks like distributed denial of service (DDoS) and network reconnaissance.

### 13.1.2 Types of Cyber-Attacks

*   TSA: Disrupts system timing using spoofed GPS signals.
*   Denial of Service (DoS)/DDoS: Blocks or overwhelms communication channels.
*   DRA: Reuses valid data packets to deceive systems.
*   FDIA: Alters data to manipulate control systems.
*   238. MITM**:** Intercepts and modifies communications stealthily. 
    *   *Physical Attacks:* They include direct interference like electromagnetic damage or RA**,** which manipulate system frequencies.
    *   *CCPA:* Combine cyber and physical methods for a more destructive, synchronized attack.

The 2019 Venezuelan SG attack used both cyber and electromagnetic disruptions. [Figure 13.2](#ch21.xhtml#f83) shows the types of cyber-attacks.

![Figure 13.2 The different types of cyber-attack.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C013_002.jpg)

**Figure 13.2** The different types of cyber-attack.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f83b)

Ref. \[[2](#ch21.xhtml#r421)\] presents an ML-based intrusion detection system (IDS) designed to enhance cybersecurity in SGs. It focuses on protecting communications using International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 61850 Generic Object-Oriented Substation Event (GOOSE) critical messages for substation automation. A novel IDS has been developed for GOOSE messages using ML to differentiate between normal operations and cyber-attacks. A realistic dataset of GOOSE messages under normal operations and simulated cyber-attacks has been created for model training and validation. The vulnerabilities in GOOSE messages are that there is no built-in encryption, message integrity, or authentication mechanisms, and the protocol is susceptible to replay**,** man-in-the-middle**,** and masquerade attacks. The IEC 62351 has certain limitations, like it provides communication-level security but lacks intrusion detection mechanisms at the operational layer. Supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) is an essential system used for monitoring, controlling, and automating industrial processes, including power systems. It facilitates real-time control and monitoring of electrical grids, enabling operators to manage infrastructure efficiently across vast geographical areas. This system plays a major role in ensuring the efficiency, reliability, and stability of SGs \[[3](#ch21.xhtml#r422)\]. Its main functions are included in [Figure 13.3](#ch21.xhtml#f84). SCADA systems are a primary target for cyber-attacks. Key vulnerabilities include legacy systems, weak authentication mechanisms, lack of encryption. With the integration of remote access and IoT devices, the attack surface has significantly expanded. Various measures related to cybersecurity for SCADA systems in SGs are:

![Figure 13.3 The SCADA functions.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C013_003.jpg)

**Figure 13.3** The SCADA functions.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f84b)

*   *Stuxnet (2010):* A malware attack targeting industrial control systems, demonstrating the potential for cyber–physical sabotage.
*   *Ukraine Power Grid Attack (2015):* A well-coordinated cyber-attack that disrupted power supply using malware designed to compromise SCADA system.

### 241.13.1.4 Cyber-Attacks in India

India’s power grid, a critical component of the nation’s infrastructure, has been the target of several notable cyber threats, particularly focusing on SCADA systems. These incidents underscore the vulnerabilities present in the SG’s control systems and the ongoing efforts to enhance cybersecurity measures \[[7](#ch21.xhtml#r426)\].

1.  *Targeted Attacks by Chinese State-Sponsored Groups:* In 2021, cybersecurity firm recorded future identified a concerted campaign by Chinese state-sponsored groups targeting India’s critical infrastructure. The campaign focused on ten Indian power sector organizations. Additionally, two Indian seaports were targeted. These attacks aimed to gather information and potentially disrupt operations within India’s power grid.
2.  *Attempts to Disrupt Power Distribution Near Ladakh:* In early 2021, the Indian government reported two attempts by Chinese hackers to target electricity power distribution centers. While these attempts were not successful, they highlighted the persistent threats to India’s power infrastructure. Power Minister R.K. Singh stated that defenses had been strengthened to counter such a cyber-attack.
3.  *Vulnerabilities in the SCADA System:* Confidential data from Computer Emergency Response Team – India (CERT-IN) show occurrence of many attacks on SCADA systems. While many of these attacks have been small-scale, there is anecdotal evidence suggesting an increase in both the frequency and scale over the years. The availability of information on breaching SCADA systems on the internet exacerbates these vulnerabilities.
4.  *Malware Attack on Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant:* This plant experienced a malware attack in September 2019 that infiltrated its administrative network. The malware, identified as Dtrack and linked to the North Korea–affiliated Lazarus Group, was designed to collect sensitive information. While the operational network remained unaffected, this incident underscored the potential risks to critical infrastructure from cyber threats.
5.  *Security Enhancements and Monitoring Initiatives:* In response to these threats, GRID-INDIA has established an SOC to monitor security events and incidents across RLDCs and the NLDC. Additionally, the IT infrastructure of the NLDC has been upgraded with advanced security features. POWERGRID, another key entity, has also set up an SOC for 24 × 7 monitoring of critical assets. These initiatives aim to bolster the cybersecurity posture of India’s power grid and protect against future attacks \[[8](#ch21.xhtml#r427)\].

These incidents highlight the ongoing challenges in securing SCADA systems within India’s power grid. [Table 13.1](#ch21.xhtml#t23) shows the description from ref. \[[9](#ch21.xhtml#r428)\].

The contributions of this work are:

1.  Implementation of various ML techniques for the discrimination of power systems disturbances and cyber-attacks in a Python environment
2.  242. Development of CM, CR, and Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROCC) for ML models.
3.  Calculation of different performance metrics, like accuracy, precision, for all the models.
4.  The implementation of XAI with SHAP and LIME methods is done for three types of classifiers.
5.  This research contributes to enhancement of reliability, safety, and efficiency of modern power systems, all of which are foundational to achieving Goal 7 of 17 SDG
6.  By leveraging ML and XAI for addressing cyber-physical threats, this research contributes to a future where energy systems are transparent, intelligent, and act as the pillars of clean and affordable energy access.

## **13.3** Methodology

In this manuscript, various ML classifiers are applied for IDS in power system. The CR, CM is developed for all the classifiers. Classifier performance is assessed based on ref. \[[10](#ch21.xhtml#r429)\]:

*   *CM:* The CM is used to show how well classifiers are performing. By combining the actual classes with the predicted outcomes, it can display the specifics of the classifier’s classification outcome.
*   *ROCC:* It was proposed as a new criterion because validation accuracy cannot accurately represent a classifier’s true performance when the sample distribution is unbalanced. As shown in [Figure 13.6](#ch21.xhtml#f86), the Y-axis of the ROCC indicates the TPR, or sensitivity, and the X-axis shows the FPR.
    
    ![Figure 13.6 The ROCC and AUC.⏎ ¶ Source: Ref. \[2\].](html/images/9781041062943_C013_006.jpg)
    
    **Figure 13.6** The ROCC and AUC.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f86b) ¶ *Source:* Ref. \[[2](#ch21.xhtml#r421)\].
    
*   *Area Under Curve (AUC):* In general, the classifier performs better the further it is from the ROCC to the Reference Line (a brown color line in [Figure 13.6](#ch21.xhtml#f86)). Even while ROCC can intuitively represent a classifier’s performance, researchers always prefer to evaluate performance using a straightforward figure. Area under this ROCC is known as AUC. Thus, a high AUC value indicates a good classifier. 246.In this study, the effectiveness of several classifiers is assessed using these criteria \[[11](#ch21.xhtml#r430)\].

## **13.6** Work on Xai: Application of Shap

*   *Model 1 XGB: The Waterfall Plot:*

The SHAP method is used for model’s predictions. The explanation of the first prediction is visualized using the command shap. plots. waterfall(shap\_values\[0\]‌). The input provided to this plot is explanation object’s one row. Waterfall plot is intended 269.to show explanations for individual predictions. The expected Value (0.351 here) of the output of XGB is shown at the plot’s bottom part. Each row illustrates how each feature’s positive (red) or negative (blue) contribution shifts the value from the expected model output over the background dataset to the model output for this prediction. By default, SHAP uses the margin outputs of XGB Classifier to explain them before the logistic link function \[[23](#ch21.xhtml#r442)\]. Thus, log-odds units are on the X-axis.

*Waterfall Plot:* This plot depicts the impact of various features on 50th instance. Every row in [Figure 13.40](#ch21.xhtml#f120) illustrates how the negative (blue) or positive (red) contribution of each feature alters the value from the anticipated output (E \[f(x)= 0.351\]) to the value predicted by the model (f (x)). Here, f(x) = E(f(x)) + SHAP value for each feature. The number next to each feature row reflects its associated observed value.

![Figure 13.40 Work flow of XAI.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C013_040.jpg)

**Figure 13.40** Work flow of XAI.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f120b)

Each feature’s value for this sample is indicated by the gray text that appears before the feature names. When the feature numbers in the model surpasses the max display parameter, the features are arranged in the waterfall plot’s bottom part according to the SHAP magnitudes. Eighty-nine least significant features have been condensed into a single term in the explanation above. The max display argument can be used to alter the default limit of 10 rows. It is kept 40 in this plot. The command shap. plots.waterfall(shap\_values = 50, max\_display = 40) displays this plot for the 50th instance of the dataset. Red features are those that raise the prediction, while Blue features are those that lower it. [Figure 13.40](#ch21.xhtml#f120) shows this plot.

### 13.6.1 The Force Plot for Instance (50) for Label “0”

270.For looking the feature’s role in influencing the model’s prediction the “label” in a SHAP force plot refers to the predicted class or target value associated with the data point, while the “instance number” refers to the index of the data point chosen, essentially which row from the dataset is being explained \[[24](#ch21.xhtml#r443)\]. The force plot illustrates how each feature affects the prediction for that particular data point. Every bar on 271.the plot denotes a feature, and the length of the bar shows how much of the prediction it contributed. The features that contributed to the “0” result are identified by looking at the first sample in the testing set. This will be accomplished by providing the SHAP, expected values and testing sample along with this force plot. The red bars typically show Positive\_ Contributions, which push the prediction toward a greater value, and Blue bars show Negative\_Contributions, which pull the prediction toward a lesser value.

[Figure 13.41](#ch21.xhtml#f121) shows the visualization of the 50th instance with a force plot using the command. This plot is created by selecting the instance number (50) and the corresponding label “0.”. The model output with index (0) is 0.95. After being converted into probability space, this “raw” value yields the final output of “0” and “1.” [Figure 13.41](#ch21.xhtml#f121) displays the base value as well as the features’ contributions to the “0” outcome. The mean of all the models’ output values during training is the base value. The contribution of Feature RP-M410: *I* = 632.6 is displayed in blue, while R2-PA5: IH = 162.4 is displayed in red. Other features’ contributions to label “0” for this instance are also displayed in [Figure 13.41](#ch21.xhtml#f121). The final output predicted by the model is “0” as the predicted value (0.95) is higher than (0).

![Figure 13.41 Force plot-1.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C013_041.jpg)

**Figure 13.41** Force plot-1.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f121b)

### 13.6.4 The Dependence Scatter Plot

The dependence scatter plot (DSP) is used for showing the effect of a single feature across the entire dataset. DSPs, as opposed to summary plots, illustrate the connection between a particular feature and the anticipated result for every data instance. Gaining more detailed information and checking the feature’s significance under study by supporting or refuting the outputs of the summary plots or other global feature importance metrics are just two of the many reasons this analysis is carried out. The X-axis shows the feature values to examine \[[25](#ch21.xhtml#r444)\]. The SHAP value, for the model’s prediction for each data point, is displayed on the Y-axis. The various plots are displayed in [Figures 13.48](#ch21.xhtml#f128) to [13.51](#ch21.xhtml#f131). The SHAP feature dependence plot shows interaction visualization. R1-PA1: VH interacts with R2-PM5: I. In values close to –150, the occurrence of an R2-PM5: I increases the value of R1-PA1: VH. [Figures 13.50](#ch21.xhtml#f130) and [13.51](#ch21.xhtml#f131) show horizontal and vertical relationships.

![Figure 13.48 DSP-1.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C013_048.jpg)

**Figure 13.50** DSP-3.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f130b)

### 13.6.5 The Scatter Plot

This plot uses the X-axis for plotting the feature’s value and its SHAP value on the Y-axis. This demonstrates how the model is reliant on the specified characteristic. The data points are used to represent the participants in this plot. This plot shows the Shap value for the variables in question placed against the underlying raw value. Different SHAP values can be produced from the same raw variable value because to interactions with other variables \[[26](#ch21.xhtml#r445)\]. ### 13.6.6 The Bee Swarm Plot

273.274.275.276.277.278.279.280.Each feature’s SHAP value for every sample is used for plotting. This is for providing a summary of the features that are most necessary for a model. [Figure 13.54](#ch21.xhtml#f134) employs SHAP values for depicting the distribution of each feature’s impact on the XGB’s 281.output. For all the samples, this graph organizes features according to the total of the magnitudes of the SHAP values. The feature’s values are represented by blue low, red high colors. The consequences of all the main characteristics are summed up in this plot. The ranking mean absolute SHAP values for all the variables in the dataset are shown on the Y-axis of the SHAP summary graph \[[27](#ch21.xhtml#r446)\]. The command utilized for summarizing the impacts of all the features is shap. plots. beeswarm (shap\_values).

## **13.7** Work on Xai: Application of the Lime Method

To implement XAI using the LIME approach in Python, the LIME package is installed using the command! pip. The classification\_report from sklearn.metrics, train test\_split are imported. The data is split into a test dataset and a train dataset \[[32](#ch21.xhtml#r451)\]. The training of the model is done using an ML model for making predictions on the testing dataset. The matplotlib.pyplot as plt is imported, and JS visualization code is loaded to the notebook as shap.initjs() . Using explainer = shap.TreeExplainer (clf) the explainer is created. It is required to import Shap, lime, lime\_tabular, explanation class, and other required packages. The dataset is loaded. The coding is used for training an RF model on this OpenCV AI Ki (OAK) dataset by the use of RF classifier class from the ensemble module of sklearn. The coding is used for creating a LIME explainer instance with the help of lime\_tabular module \[[33](#ch21.xhtml#r452)\].

The subsequent step involves storing the output produced by the LIME explanation in an HTML file called op.html. The HTML file generated as output serves as the LIME explanation for the 50th instance in the OAK dataset. For the OAK dataset, the LIME explanation illustrates the contribution of each feature (P A1: V H – P A3: VH, etc.) to the predicted class (Natural, Attack) of the 50th instance. The outcome includes three primary pieces of information arranged from left to right.

1.  The predictions from the model
2.  The contributions from features300.
3.  299. The real value for every feature

The following figures are generated using the RF classifier that displays a LIME result for the 50th instance and presents the final feature contribution in the form of table in orange and blue colors. It is observed that the 50th instance is predicted to have an attack with 100% confidence. [Figures 13.83](#ch21.xhtml#f163) to [13.91](#ch21.xhtml#t45) show the results obtained from Python.

## **301.13.8** Conclusion and Future Work

Power system attacks and disturbances are the most frequent issues that regularly arise due to events caused by humans or nature. The biggest difficulty lies in identifying the primary reason for power disruption and taking suitable actions in response to it. Human judgment alone is not effective in forecasting power disturbances. It is a challenge to the operators to observe the system’s status. The objective of this research is to deploy various ML models and algorithms for identifying disturbances and dependably categorize them as either a natural or a harmful attack. The OAK dataset is used for implementing the ML algorithms with Python programming. The SG consists of a dual-layered framework: physical systems and cyber systems. The merging of the two systems establishes the cyber–physical setting. The PMU is operating in the digital component. It is used for providing the current information for managing the physical layer through energy control. The phasor data includes details regarding voltage and phasor measurements, including location of equipment like the switches, circuit breakers, transformers, and relays.

The SHAP and LIME methods from XAI are used for assessing the three models: ETC, RF and Light GBM. The highest values of the four metrics are obtained from the ETC model. The different visualization plots are shown for three models. A force plot, which is especially helpful for debugging model behavior or identifying areas where the model might be making incorrect predictions, is shown. The bee swarm plot is based on their individual SHAP values. Each participant of the dataset is represented by a dot on the bee swarm plot. When there is a large density of SHAP values, the dots are piled vertically. Each dot’s color represents the raw variable value of that person/feature. A high raw value is indicated by red, and a low raw value is shown by blue.

302.Future studies should deal with the real-time implementation of the proposed ML in the power system, integrating adaptive learning for evolving cyber-attack patterns. Expanding the dataset, incorporating DL, and fusing multi-source data can enhance accuracy. Further development of XAI will boost operator trust and decision-making in complex, high-risk cyber–physical scenarios.

# 315.14Artificial Intelligence (AI) GestureDraw: Hand Gesture-Based Drawing Interface with AI-Assisted Output Using Computer Vision and AI

Swathi Gowroju, Shilpa Choudhary, Annoji Sri Poojith, Puvvula Haritha, Shaga Preethika, and G. Sai Kiran

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-14](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-14)

## **14.1** Introduction

In the past few decades, human–computer interaction (HCI) has changed dramatically from the traditional input devices of keyboards and mice to more natural and intuitive modalities such as touchscreens, voice commands, and hand gesture recognition. Of these, hand gesture recognition is one of the most transformative ways of allowing people to interact directly with digital systems. For instance, the initial motivation for gesture-based interfaces in the 1980s, in the “Videoplace” system developed by Myron Krueger, was fundamentally straightforward to make technology accessible and entertaining. Techniques have been advanced in computer vision and artificial intelligence, allowing very accurate and efficient recognition of gestures and bringing into reality innovative applications from gamification through to healthcare, education, and creative design. The existing works on hand gesture recognition are based on using different algorithms and technologies for the accurate interpretation of human gestures. For example, the traditional approach relies on edge detection and contour analysis as handcrafted features for the identification of gestures. Generally, all these methods were prone to failures because of variations caused by changes in lighting conditions, presence of background clutter, and inconsistent positioning or movement of hands, which adversely affected the accuracy of gesture recognition. 316.Due to deep learning, this discipline was revolutionized to let the machines learn even complex patterns from large datasets. So far, models such as convolutional neural network (CNN) and recurrent neural network (RNN) have been used in many gestures to achieve superior performance in different gesture recognition applications. Pre-trained models like MediaPipe Hands and OpenPose have continued to make hand detection and tracking in real time much easier using robust frameworks in gesture recognition applications.

Building on all the above developments, the proposed system, artificial intelligence (AI) GestureDraw, presents a novel hand gesture recognition that is combined with AI-driven output generation. While AI GestureDraw is unique in integrating real-time hand tracking coupled with advanced AI capabilities that go beyond interpretation for enhancing user-generated sketches as well as ensuring a seamless, intelligent user experience. In addition to letting users create digital sketches by tracing real-time hand gestures, this system uses AI to analyze and enhance the user’s sketches. As such, it essentially uses techniques in computer vision together with deep learning models to make sense of how hand movements will be translated to meaningful outputs. AI GestureDraw has several key elements that make up its innovative functionality:

1.  *Hand Tracking and Gesture Recognition:* (a) The system employs some state-of-the-art hand detection and tracking techniques that may identify the most important landmarks of the hand and interpret gestures with very high accuracy. (b) Algorithms such as CNNs may analyze spatial and temporal features of hand movements, and thus, the system will be able to distinguish which gesture stands for drawing, clearing the canvas, or invoking AI processing.
2.  *Dynamic Content Generation:* It has used artificial intelligence to interpret any sketch that is created, therefore providing context-related outputs. Such a process deals with interpreting a hand-drawn input and finding responses or solutions directly to that user’s intention.
3.  *Interactive Interface:* The system offers an intuitive and user-friendly platform for real-time interaction, where users can view their hand movements translated into drawings on the canvas while simultaneously receiving AI-generated feedback or solutions.

The proposed system transforms digital creativity and engagement via the use of artificial intelligence and computer vision. It dispenses with conventional input devices by deciphering natural hand motions, enabling users to create or sketch naturally. By improving forms, fixing mistakes, or offering original ideas instantly, AI improves this process. The applications are numerous and include rehabilitation, which provides accessible tools for people with motor impairments; creative arts and design, which enable complex creations; and education, which gives interactive learning experiences. Other applications include product design and prototyping, which streamlines idea generation; immersive virtual reality and augmented reality (VR/AR) experiences, which enable users to engage with three-dimensional (3D) places; gaming, which enables gesture-based interactions; and collaborative tools for 317.virtual meetings. This technology transforms by combining AI-driven improvements with simplicity. AI GestureDraw is a prime example of taking human instinct toward technological precision and its application in a methodical and integral manner. Combining gesture recognition capabilities at advanced levels with generative AI (GenAI), the system both simplifies processes in the creation and interaction with digital content but offers new scopes of innovation across domains. This paper provides insight into the technical foundation that supports AI GestureDraw, such as its development and underlying algorithms for the purpose of revolutionizing engagement in digital systems.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 14.2 includes the literature survey, and the proposed system is discussed in Section 14.3. Section 14.4 shows the result analysis and comparative analysis of the proposed system with state-of-the-art techniques. Sectiosn 14.5 concludes the proposed work.

## **14.2** Literature Survey

Hand gesture recognition is one of the developing domains in HCI with several breakthroughs designed to enhance precision, real-time execution, and usability of the applications, including touchless interfaces. A good portion of work performed in the above domain \[[1](#ch22.xhtml#r453)–[12](#ch22.xhtml#r464)\] differs in the applied techniques, such as CNNs, optical flow, and media-based hand tracking, and each technique offers a unique contribution toward accuracy and proficiency in gesture recognition. Despite that, the research regarding integrating gesture-based interaction with AI-powered feedback mechanisms remains very low, indicating more depth in this domain. [Table 14.1](#ch22.xhtml#t46) shows the survey of literature of AI-based hand gesture recognition.

Reddy et al. \[[1](#ch22.xhtml#r453)\] and Khan et al. \[[5](#ch22.xhtml#r457)\] have explored CNN-based hand gesture recognition models to significant benefits by providing 95.2% and 96.8% accuracy rates, respectively. Though the methods work fairly well with isolated gesture recognition, the actual implementation of such systems in interactive real-time systems usually appears to suffer from challenges faced in uncontrolled lighting conditions and complex environments. Other related researchers come forward and have proposed hand detection with the solution of MediaPipe and YOLO proposed by Yusuf et al. \[[2](#ch22.xhtml#r454)\] and Podder et al. \[[3](#ch22.xhtml#r455)\], respectively, which are able to solve some of the discussed issues mentioned above, particularly in dynamic settings, but for real-time tracking, there is still much room for improvement.

Recently, significant interest has developed in systems that recognize gestures and facilitate communication in creative fields, drawing, or educational tools. Few really depend on the camera positions. Researchers \[[4](#ch22.xhtml#r456), [7](#ch22.xhtml#r459)\] have explored deep learning techniques along with traditional computer vision algorithms, for example, Haar Cascade features and Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) features. However, the accuracy of those methods, while being efficient, remains suboptimal compared with much more sophisticated models, specifically CNN and long short-term memory (LSTM)-based models \[[6](#ch22.xhtml#r458)\]. Other approaches are based on machine learning and techniques of optical flow as proposed by Alonazi et al. \[[8](#ch22.xhtml#r460)\] and Rastgoo et al. \[[7](#ch22.xhtml#r459)\], which have also been found promising toward gesture recognition with potential applicability in gesture-based user interfaces, but point to difficulties in the accuracy 318.of tracking when gestures are too fast or ambiguous. Lastly, several research studies recently have actually pointed out context-aware recognition systems, especially AI-based feedback, as cited by Ansar et al. \[[10](#ch22.xhtml#r462)\]. These are actually designed to be even more adaptive in responses, depending on hand movement and combinations of gestures toward intelligent applications that are gesture-driven. Despite this, it is evident that the effort to design systems more robust and flexible with a view toward accepting a variety of hand postures and real-time situations will remain an important objective of this future research.

## **319.14.3** Proposed Work

The introduction of new ideas to increase user interaction and creativity with innovative hand gesture recognition and artificial intelligence is done in the current paper \[[13](#ch22.xhtml#r465)\]. AI GestureDraw is developed based on the strong foundation of techniques related to computer vision and deep learning. The proposed system will allow people to create an interactive way of making drawings with hand gestures, thus possibly accelerating the process of drawing and elevating it by AI-assisted output generation \[[14](#ch22.xhtml#r466)\]. At the end of completing a sketch, the system intelligently analyzes the drawing and gives task-specific responses for it to be a versatile tool for various applications\[[15](#ch22.xhtml#r467)\]. AI GestureDraw allows for smooth, engaging user experience while encouraging creativity, harnessing the power of analytics through AI, in giving meaning to sketches in real time \[[16](#ch22.xhtml#r468)\]. The methodology proposed for this application involves capturing video input live through a webcam, identifying user hand gestures as illustrated in [Figure 14.1](#ch22.xhtml#f164) to interpret their drawings, and generating meaningful outputs according to the drawings input \[[17](#ch22.xhtml#r469)\].

![Figure 14.1 Workflow of AI gesture draw.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C014_001.jpg)

**Figure 14.1** Workflow of AI gesture draw.[⏎](#ch22.xhtml#f164b)

The system architecture shown in [Figure 14.1](#ch22.xhtml#f165) describes how the proposed model works. First, the video input is given which is through the camera; it captures live video of the user. The camera first detects the user’s hand and then finds out all the sensor marks out of our hand deciding on identification of the fingers. The purpose of all these functions will be to identify face(s) in a live video input—a constant stream of data to be processed. This input is divided into frames, where each frame offers a glimpse of the video \[[18](#ch22.xhtml#r470)\]. These frames are subsequently transformed into grayscale images, discarding color data that does not contribute to recognizing the structure. The most important element to classify is the gesture. This is then followed by a pre-processing step where things like noise reduction, normalization, and contrast enhancement can be performed to make the frames ready for further analysis. This makes sure raw input data appears consistent and clean so the model can accurately detect and classify images.

![Figure 14.2 Capturing live video input through a webcam. (a–d) Images from dataset; (e) recognizing hand; (f) index finger for drawing; (g) all fingers closed for clearing; (h) four fingers raised for output generation.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C014_002.jpg)

**Figure 14.2** Capturing live video input through a webcam. (a–d) Images from dataset; (e) recognizing hand; (f) index finger for drawing; (g) all fingers closed for clearing; (h) four fingers raised for output generation.[⏎](#ch22.xhtml#f165b)

This process will consist of a series of steps:

*   *Data Collection:* The initial step would be the collection of various datasets of hand gestures and drawings. This dataset contains a variety of hand movements and sketch examples from different users, which would serve as a basis for training the gesture recognition model.
*   *Gesture Recognition:* The system will apply computer vision techniques for the live feeds from the webcam to analyze it. It implements a pre-trained model like Mediapipe to detect accurate hand gestures that represent the drawing actions with strokes, shapes, and symbols. Such recognition by gestures ensures accurate interpretation of the user’s intentions.
*   *Input Capture:* Once the user completes their drawing, user can halt the live feed of the video using some specific gesture, as shown in [Figure 14.2](#ch22.xhtml#f165). This will capture the input so drawn, and then the system will freeze the video and proceed to perform the concerned sketch for further processing.
*   *AI Output Generation:* The system captures the input as a sketch and sends it to a model of AI, which evaluates the content (using the gesture from [320.321.Figure 14.2](#ch22.xhtml#f165)f). Here, the AI uses the deep learning techniques to comprehend the drawing and produces relevant output depending on the intent of the user-to solve a problem, answer a question, or give feedback.
*   *Presenting the Output to the User:* The outcomes thus produced are presented in an easy-to-follow accessible style where the user can easily interact with the results. This could be through text, visual enhancements, or other active elements that encourage user-friendliness of the system.

The system introduces a strong mechanism of feedback which allows users to alter the illustration or input it produces based on the AI output. In this way, the process generates creativity and gives results that meet the expectations with the closest results possible. This harmonious HCI generates an overall enriched user experience where the outputs align with the user’s vision.

After pre-processing, the hand detector runs on each frame to check for the presence of a hand as shown in [Figure 14.2](#ch22.xhtml#f165). The system loops back to continue checking the video feed if no hand is detected. Upon detection of a hand, the system proceeds to gesture recognition stage which employs a deep learning model based on MobileNetV2. It is also a full CNN with 53 layers, perfect for real-time applications, building efficiency and accuracy. Using the pre-trained models under cvzonelike, MobileNetV2 analyzes the hand data to recognize specific gestures according to predefined patterns. However, data is ongoing to learn the recognized gestures by the system, so the system can know and reciprocate them accordingly.

[Figure 14.2](#ch22.xhtml#f165) shows how a computer vision-based AI interface that uses hand gestures operates. Landmark identification of the hand is demonstrated in the first phases ([Figure 14.2](#ch22.xhtml#f165)a–d), where nodes stand in for joints or fingers and connecting lines, most likely produced by pose estimate techniques, create the hand structure. Active gesture detection is demonstrated in stage ([Figure 14.2](#ch22.xhtml#f165)e), which shows the raw video stream with the user’s hand identified and tracked using a bounding box. In the last step ([Figure 14.2](#ch22.xhtml#f165)f–h), the interface is displayed where the system decodes gestures like “number 1” or a “fist,” and produces AI-assisted outputs marked “Answer.” This demonstrates the smooth transition from hand recognition to gesture interpretation, opening the door for uses such as sign language translation, virtual sketching, and gesture-based control systems.

The gesture recognition module is capable of recognizing multiple commands. For example, when detecting only the index finger, the system is able to “draw,” but recognizing all five fingers closed would delete the previous drawing. Zooming operates with gestures similar to index and thumb fingers together, and all fingers except the thumb represent a video freeze operation. Once the gesture has been processed, an AI-based output is generated depending on the detected gesture. This textual output yields an output (like drawing a space or freezing a block) or a summarization of the system response. This multi-layered structure enables the seamless integration of live gesture recognition, action execution, and feedback, and is suitable for applications such as virtual drawing boards, gesture-controlled presentations, or smart environments. All the components work together to provide a seamless and immersive user interface.

### 322.323.14.3.1 Training

The model is intended for tasks involving feature extraction and classification. It starts with two 16-filter convolutional layers (Conv2D). While the second convolutional layer shrinks the spatial dimensions to (22, 22, 16), the first convolutional layer generates an output of size (48, 48, 16).

Batch normalization comes after these layers, normalizing the feature maps to speed up and stabilize the training process. The model has two MaxPooling2D layers that downsample the feature maps to (24, 24, 16) and (11, 11, 16) correspondingly to further minimize the spatial dimensions and avoid overfitting. To enhance the model’s capacity for generalization, Dropout layers are also used following each pooling operation, randomly removing a portion of neurons during training. The graphs illustrated in [Figure 14.2](#ch22.xhtml#f165) show how well a model performs throughout training and validation across several epochs. The training and validation accuracy progression is displayed in the accuracy graph. The model is successfully learning from the training data when the training accuracy (blue line) rises gradually across epochs and approaches 1.0. In a similar vein, the validation accuracy (orange line) achieves excellent accuracy with very slight variations. The model appears to generalize effectively to unknown data without experiencing severe overfitting, as indicated by the tight alignment between training and validation accuracy.

The loss and accuracy graphs are shown in [Figure 14.3](#ch22.xhtml#f165). It shows that plots for training and validation loss are decreased over the same time periods. The model’s predictions on the training data are getting increasingly accurate as the training loss (blue line) drops off dramatically in the first few epochs and then gradually till it approaches zero. Comparable to the training loss, the validation loss (orange line) 324.shows a similar pattern, sharply decreasing and leveling out at a low number. For training and validation data, the model performs admirably overall, demonstrating high accuracy and minimal loss. Effective learning and superior generalization to unknown data are highlighted by the strong correlation between the training and validation parameters. This result shows that the dataset, model architecture, and hyperparameters are all set up for the job.

### 14.3.2 Evaluation Parameters

The proposed system uses gesture recognition accuracy (GRA), latency (L), and AI output relevance (OR) to ensure the performance of the proposed system. GRA is calculated using Equation 14.1, which helps to identify the total number of correct gestures out of total number of gestures performed.

GRA = (T\_correct/T\_total) × 100% (14.1) 

where T\_correct is the number of correctly recognized gestures, and T\_total is the total gestures tested. L is calculated using Equation 14.2, which helps to identify the approximate time to identify the gestures that are being performed.

  
$$\\text{L} = \\frac{\\left( {\\sum\_{\\text{i} = 1}^{\\text{n}}\\text{T}\\\_\\text{recognize},\\text{i}} \\right)}{}\\text{n}$$  
 (14.2) 

where T\_recognize, i is the Time taken to recognize gesture I. n is the number of gestures tested. OR is calculated using Equation 14.3, which helps to identify the number of relevant AI outputs out of the total number of outputs received.

OR = (S\_relevant / S\_total) × 100 % (14.3) 

where S\_relevant is the number of AI outputs deemed relevant by evaluators, S\_total is the total outputs evaluated.

## **14.4** RESULTS

The proposed system uses advanced gesture recognition technology, combined with GenAI, to ensure a responsive and interactive experience. Incorporating computer vision, hand tracking, and AI-powered capabilities, this system provides gesture-based interactions in real-time designed for creative, educational, and problem-solving applications. It provides an integrated platform for users to visualize concepts, execute actions, and get contextual AI-generated answers. The results of the proposed system show the operation and output of the AI-powered hand gesture detection and interactive app. Utilizing computer vision, hand tracking, and generative AI, this system examines users in real-time and enables an interactive experience driven by gestures. This application utilizes powerful libraries, including OpenCV and cvzone 325.for gesture detection, as well as Google’s GenAI for generating responses, thereby creating a real-time interface where users can visualize their imaginations and interact using gesture-based actions to get AI-generated responses. The entire system is initiated with a real-time webcam input where cvzone HandTrackingModule fetches and analyzes hand gestures. Upon the user’s index finger, the system receives this gesture, and the tracking of its movement starts. Then the user can draw freehand on the virtual canvas (as shown in [Figure 14.4](#ch22.xhtml#f167)). Drawing is fluid and responsive, simulating the experience of drawing directly against the surface while also having the accuracy to track the finger’s path.

### 14.4.1 Comparative Analysis

One of the major advantages of the proposed system is its real-time gesture-based drawing functionality. In contrast to most of the systems presently available \[[1](#ch22.xhtml#r453)\], the proposed system allows the HCI in real time by directly raising the index finger to engage in the dynamic process of direct drawing. Most of the other systems present today focus on static gesture recognition and some classify previously defined hand movements. This capability brings in a more interactive and engaging environment for the system, making it more flexible and user-friendly. In contrast, traditional systems are limited to only detecting and interpreting gestures without enabling direct manipulation of the drawing or visual output.

The inclusion of AI into the proposed system introduces an important feature that may largely be missing in most of the existing systems. However, once the user has produced his or her drawing, the system transfers the captured image to an AI model for processing the produced drawing and generating context-specific outputs. This might be solving a particular problem, giving long detailed explanations, or creating creative content based on the entered input. Currently, however, such systems as those based on CNNs or support vector machines (SVMs) only indicate that gestures can be recognized and classified and do not present any additional output or interaction. This proposed system will be full of many capabilities due to the AI nature, but these are expanded functionalities that make it capable for more rigorous applications-educational tools, creative platforms, and AI-driven design.

328.The key idea behind this proposed system is its capability to map a variety of actions onto a number of gestures. For instance, one could draw with one gesture and erase with another. This gesture control, driven by a more refined user experience compared with the current systems limited to only recognizing predefined static gestures without providing the capacity to carry out complex tasks, is another promising development. For example, one can clear the canvas using a simple thumb gesture or even initiate a new drawing using another gesture. This dynamic control over the actions executed by the system makes it very efficient for creative tasks and has a positive advantage over other existing gesture recognition systems, which do not have multi-action capabilities.

Although the proposed application has higher diversity and application than the existing systems, mainly used for the recognition of simple gestures or classification in HCI and sign language interpretation, the system’s capabilities only extend into more diverse practical applications. Combining the gesture recognition aspect with that of AI, the system becomes very suitable for use in interactive drawing tools, digital art creations, education settings, and virtual whiteboards. The capability to solve problems, such as mathematical equations or even diagrams drawn by a user, is also integrated into AI. This extension of the scope of application definitely highlights the flexibility of the proposed system while providing the end-users with a more complete tool compared to the clearer definitions, yet simpler system types derived from the literature study.

### 14.4.2 Positive Aspects

It lets users draw and touch a virtual canvas in real time using hand gestures, creating a dynamic, immersive experience compared to most static gesture recognition systems. With AI processing integrated to process the drawn input, beyond gesture recognition, the system is enabled to be more intelligent and far more versatile when users can get context-specific outputs. It gives the user an added advantage with control and flexibility through support that can be drawn, erased, or stopped to maximize the efficiency of the tool for creative and productive purposes. The very integration of gesture recognition and AI combines manifold applications, from virtual whiteboards to digital art, educational platforms, to problem-solving tools.

Within the past 10 years, many hand gesture recognition systems have been proposed ([Table 14.3](#ch22.xhtml#t48)). Most of them adopted different algorithms and techniques along with different datasets that helped overcome these problems with detecting and classifying gestures correctly. Zhang and Lu \[[19](#ch22.xhtml#r471)\] used a CNN for gesture recognition but added Kalman filtering with accuracy at 95.2%. Similar work also involves Gupta et al. \[[20](#ch22.xhtml#r472)\]. It used a CNN-based deep learning approach that exhibited high accuracy up to 96.8% on the Hand Gesture Recognition Database (HGRD). Bhiri et al. \[[21](#ch22.xhtml#r473)\] used MediaPipe for the detection of hand landmarks and K-nearest neighbors (KNNs) for gesture classification. Patel et al. \[[22](#ch22.xhtml#r474)\] adopted OpenPose for hand key point detection coupled with a Random Forest classifier, with both systems achieving remarkable accuracy: 92.7% and 91.0%, respectively.

329.Although these existing systems, as shown in [Figure 14.4](#ch22.xhtml#f167), have very high recognition accuracy, they focus mostly on gesture detection and classification, with very minimal interactivity and feedback. Approaches like those from Lee et al. \[[23](#ch22.xhtml#r475)\], which use YOLO for hand detection, and Kim et al. \[[24](#ch22.xhtml#r476)\] using Haar Cascade Classifiers, have shown high levels of performance in gesture recognition but do not offer real-time, context-aware responses based on the recognized gestures.

The proposed system offers a novel addition by presenting the integration of real-time GenAI responses together with gesture recognition. Compared to existing approaches, the system under discussion differs significantly in the respect that the approach has made its primary emphasis on the integration of the model of a GenAI so as to dynamically and in accordance with contexts produce feedback given by recognized gestures. This AI-powered interaction enables the system to accomplish tasks such as mathematical problem-solving, answering questions, or giving appropriate information based on user gestures. This interactivity layer is of significant value and makes the experience of the user much more personal and responsive in nature. Unlike existing systems, the proposed system offers a more versatile solution that can adapt to various user needs because it is not limited to gesture detection and classification. The system utilizes Streamlit for the user interface to ensure smooth and efficient real-time processing, and the GenAI model makes it intuitive and seamless for users. By combining gesture recognition with AI-powered feedback, the proposed system represents a significant advancement in the field, providing a more comprehensive solution for applications such as HCI, virtual assistants, and sign language translation, setting it apart from traditional models that focus exclusively on gesture detection or classification without offering meaningful post-gesture actions.

330.The video feed system also provides another form of benefit through hand gesture control, where specific movements in the hand, including lifting all fingers, send a signal to freeze the real-time feed with that particular content to be captured, meaning that there is a certain intuitive and accuracy attribute of control as the person controlling the drawing process does not have to stretch out to touch some form of remote control. This functionality is not possible in existing systems because they are mainly designed for classifying gestures from continuous video feeds. The pause and resume support of video feeds through gestures makes the overall system much more interactive in nature and gives the user maximum flexibility to capture content at the right moment.

## **14.5** Conclusion and Future Scope

In this proposed system, we developed an interactive hand gesture recognition application using the latest computer vision techniques and machine learning algorithms to allow real-time user interaction. The system consists of several functional modules, such as hand and finger detection algorithms (using techniques like CNNs and Haar Cascades) to precisely locate hand landmarks and follow their movements in videos or images. Using KNNs, SVM, decision tree and machine learning algorithms were used for gesture recognition, where classification is done based on the relative position of fingers and hand movements to recognize the gestures. Integrating these methodologies allows the program to interactively react to user inputs, allowing for actions in real-time such as sketching on a canvas or potentially erasing it from specific gestures. The key to detection and classification accuracy during implementation is to preprocess the input data, such as by minimizing noise in the audio and making sure that all frames are processed in the same manner. These results also proved the advantage of starting with a clean and responsive canvas to improve the user experience and provided a clear demonstration of the system’s ability to provide an accurate and reliable gesture-based method of interaction.

Although the proposed system managed to include vital features such as drawing and clearing the canvas by gestures, there are several opportunities for improvement in the future. One exciting direction includes exploiting state-of-the-art machine learning methods like deep learning models. For example, using CNNs for more efficient feature extraction or using RNNs for processed gesture data could improve the accuracy of recognition greatly. Furthermore, integrating handwriting analysis techniques, particularly optical character recognition (OCR) or CNN models for character recognition, would broaden the system’s applications in areas like digital handwriting recognition and signature verification. For further development, we can even use different kinds of algorithms like Naive Bayes Classifier or LSTM networks, as we could even do a sentiment analysis of users based on the gesture. Furthermore, extending the system to accommodate a wider selection of gestures as well as allowing greater interactivity in real time would further develop the application. In the fast-evolving field of user interface design, the proposed system could keep pace with technological advancements and changing user requirements.

# 333.15Improved Fetal Electrocardiogram Detection Using a Hybrid Wavelet-Based Denoising Method

K. Naga Sankar Reedy, Peddapullaiahgari Hariobulesu, Shaik Karimullah, Anwar Bhasha Pattan, Fahimuddin Shaik, and Mudassir Khan

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-15](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-15)

## **15.1** Introduction

There are two main ways to measure fetal electrocardiogram (fECG): aggressive and non-invasive. Non-invasive abdominal electrocardiogram (ECG) records a signal that includes both the mother’s and the baby’s heartbeats. Invasive methods, on the other hand, entail putting electrodes unswervingly on the baby’s scalp once the cervix has opened during delivery \[[1](#ch23.xhtml#r478)\]. You can start monitoring a baby’s heart rate without surgery as early as the first trimester by putting electrodes on the mother’s stomach. However, noise from power cables, skin-electrode impedance, and the mother’s muscular activity can often hamper the working of this method \[[2](#ch23.xhtml#r479)\]. It is very important to look at the fECG to check the health of the baby’s heart and find problems such as congenital cardiac abnormalities, bradycardia, tachycardia, and hypoxia \[[3](#ch23.xhtml#r480)\]. There are various ways to extract fECG data, namely linear decomposition, adaptive filtering, and nonlinear transformation \[[4](#ch23.xhtml#r481)\]. A linear method like single-value decomposition (SVD) will provide additive segregated sources in terms of both their temporal and spectral characteristics that are based on a base function that may be predetermined or data-driven \[[5](#ch23.xhtml#r482)\]. A blind source separation (BSS) method, such as independent component analysis (ICA) and its variants, assumes the signal source matrices are statistically independent. The more recent concept of periodic component analysis (πCA) has been demonstrated as a semi-blind separation method when working with or without a priori knowledge \[[6](#ch23.xhtml#r483)\]. A situation in which fECG data is contaminated with extensive noise requires non-linear methods, such as using delayed copies of the disturbed 334.signal to approximately recover its state space, and thus properly filtering the signal by still using a method like principal component analysis (PCA) or similar \[[7](#ch23.xhtml#r484)\]. These types of methods do work quite well with noticeable improvements in accuracy, but are computationally intensive and can be contingent on subjective bounds determined by expert opinion \[[8](#ch23.xhtml#r485)\]. Adaptive filtering is still used frequently today, but it typically requires an ECG signal reference from the maternal fetus and would also certainly require committed signal channels from the maternal ECG (mECG) if it is independent \[[9](#ch23.xhtml#r486)\]. In the absence of an ECG reference source, fECG can be computed using successive cancellation methods, although there will not necessarily be any satisfactory performance in eliminating all mECG activity ([Figure 15.1](#ch23.xhtml#f169)). There are also variants proposed based on wavelet transform (WT)-based methods that have been proven to perform satisfactorily too, especially when adaptive thresholding is applied to the wavelet coefficients. Extended Kalman smoothers are capable of extracting fECG from single-channel data, but they struggle when maternal and fetal signals blend. In summary, fetal ECG extraction from abdominal recordings is difficult due to overlapping signals and outside noise \[[10](#ch23.xhtml#r487)\]. Complex signal processing techniques are necessary to enhance the quality and diagnostics of signals.

![Figure 15.1 Adaptive filtering configuration.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C015_001.jpg)

**Figure 15.1** Adaptive filtering configuration.[⏎](#ch23.xhtml#f169b)

There are many approaches for fECG extraction. Kalman filter (KF) is becoming a valid solution to reduce noise in adaptive filtering. It has been recommended that an extended state KF could be used to extract fECG data after mixed abdominal signals. This method is more effective than standard Kalman filtering approaches. Recently, researchers have studied various approaches used to extract single-channel fECG, using qualitative and quantitative measures. One of these studies presents a new method of adaptive filtering to detect fetal QRS complexes in the maternal abdomen ECG signals. In addition, there is a proposed adaptive noise remover that incorporates many sub-filters to deliver a better fECG. The research is substantial, 335.and the techniques point toward a hybrid system of utilizing different techniques for estimating fetal heart rate (FHR). However, fECG signals are often concealed from the noise and artifacts of the abdominal signals and the fetal R-peak is not accurately discovered. In these moments, the stationary wavelet transform (SWT) is important because it is able to analyze non-stationary signals with frequency components that are continually changing. SWT is a useful method for extracting fECG because it may break down complicated abdominal signals. This is especially useful for monitoring and diagnosing abnormalities that happen before birth.

## 15.2 LITERATURE REVIEW

Camps et al. \[[11](#ch23.xhtml#r488)\] suggested a way to get fECG data using a finite impulse response (FIR) neural network combined with a framework for adaptive noise reduction. This method worked better than typical least mean squares (LMS) and normalized least mean squares (NLMS) algorithms because it used nonlinear dynamic characteristics. It was able to extract fECG from both simulated and actual datasets. Sameni and Clifford \[[12](#ch23.xhtml#r489)\] wrote a thorough assessment of the problems and future possibilities in fECG signal processing. They pointed out important obstacles, such as small signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), the lack of standardized benchmark databases, and the fact that we do not know much about how baby hearts work. The study also looked at how acquisition and signal dispensation techniques have improved over the past 40 years. Kanjilal et al. \[[13](#ch23.xhtml#r490)\] came up with a way to extract a single-channel fECG by means of SVD. They showed that this method works well for separating maternal and fetal signals at a reasonable computational cost. Al-Zaben and Al-Smadi \[[14](#ch23.xhtml#r491)\] built on this by creating a hybrid method that used SVD and a neuro-fuzzy reasoning system to adaptively cancel noise. Their solution combined reference signals produced from SVD and fuzzy logic to improve filtering. It worked very well on equally synthetic and real-world fECG data.

## 15.3 EXISTING METHOD

There has to be a way to correctly find fetal heartbeats so that fetal heart health can be monitored during early pregnancy. This paper suggests two hybrid algorithms for extracting fECG data using the recursive least squares (RLS) approach. Finding the fetal R-peaks accurately is very important for diagnosing and treating congenital cardiac problems. The main goal is to separate the fECG signal from the combined abdominal recording. RLS is a commonly used method in adaptive signal processing to reduce noise and separate signals \[[15](#ch23.xhtml#r492)\]. The RLS algorithm works by continuously estimating the mECG and then subtracting the mECG estimated from the abdominal signal, in a time-varying manner, and letting the fECG in the remaining error be more easily viewable. The RLS algorithm will continually adjust the filter coefficients for different time instances of the input signal to ensure that the difference between the input signal and the reference signal is as small as possible. Some of the extraction components of RLS are filter settings, residual error calculations, filter weight adjustments, and Kalman gain calculations. RLS is ideal for real-time applications as it continually optimizes the filter as the estimate is intended to be closer to the signal 336.the measurement of interest. These points make RLS a powerful method for differentiating fECG from mECG and ambient noise.

### 15.3.1 Signal Preprocessing

*   *Band-Pass Filtering:* Apply a band-pass filter to the raw abdominal ECG signal to isolate the frequency range of the ECG (e.g., 0.5–50 Hz) and remove high-frequency noise and baseline wander.
*   *Segmentation:* Break down the signal into smaller segments if needed for processing efficiency.

### 15.3.2 RLS Filter Setup

*   The RLS filter adapts to minimize the error e(k)e(k)e(k) between a reference input (mECG) and the abdominal ECG (mixed mECG and fECG).

### 15.3.3 Key Components

*   *Reference Signal:* A clean mECG obtained from chest electrodes serves as the reference signal.
*   *Primary Signal:* The abdominal ECG, which contains both mECG and fECG.
*   *Filter Coefficients:* The weights w(k), which are iteratively updated.

### **15.3.4** Filter Equations

*   *Prediction Error:*

e(k) = d(k) − W^Tx(k) (15.1) 

*   where d(k) is the desired signal, x(k) is the input vector (reference signal), and w(k) is the weight vector.
*   *Kalman Gain:*

$\\text{K}\\left( \\text{k} \\right) = \\frac{\\text{P}\\left( {\\text{k} - 1} \\right)\\text{x}\\left( \\text{k} \\right)}{\\lambda + \\text{X}^{\\text{T}}\\left( \\text{k} \\right)\\text{P}\\left( {\\text{k} - 1} \\right)\\text{x}\\left( \\text{k} \\right)}$ (15.2) 

*   where P is the inverse correlation matrix, and λ is the forgetting factor (close to 1 for slower adaptation).
*   *Filter Update:*

w(k) = w(k−1) + K(k)e(k) (15.3) 

*   *Covariance Update:*

$P\\left( k \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\lambda}\\left\\lbrack {P\\left( {k - 1} \\right) - K\\left( k \\right)X^{T}\\left( k \\right)P\\left( {k - 1} \\right)} \\right\\rbrack$ (15.4) 

### **337.15.3.5** mECG Cancellation

*   Apply the RLS filter to adaptively subtract the mECG (as modeled by the reference) from the abdominal ECG.
*   The output e(k)e(k)e(k) is primarily the fECG with residual noise.

### **15.3.6** Post-Processing

*   Apply additional filtering or noise reduction techniques to enhance the fECG signal.
*   Techniques such as wavelet denoising or ICA can further improve signal quality.

## 15.4 PROPOSED METHOD

To reliably assess fetal cardiac activity during early pregnancy, an elaborate method is required to detect fetal heartbeats. In this paper, we will provide two methods to recover fECG using a combination of the SWT and RLS algorithm. In the wavelet domain, we will use either a threshold-based denoising technique or an improved spatially selective noise filtering (ISSNF) method to enhance the fECG signal, remove noise and artifacts, and accurately find R-peaks. Accurate identification of R-peaks is relevant to early diagnosis and treatment of fetal heart abnormalities while providing doctors with valuable evolving data about the state of the fetus. A major aim is to produce an obvious articulatory fECG from a very disorganized stomach ECG. The proposed method begins with separating the abdominal signal into multiscale components using an SWT. The scale of decomposition can be adjusted according to the noise content. The RLS algorithm is used to suppress the mother’s ECG components of the fECG before utilizing either the threshold-based technique or the ISSNF filtering approach to suppress the noise. We used our method on synthetic and real datasets. We used qualitative and quantitative metrics, such as visually inspecting the data, identifying the QRS complex, and calculating the SNR, to evaluate performance. The results of the experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms traditional adaptive filtering methods, and the resulting SNR is consistent, with significantly less interference and accurate extraction of clean fECG data ([Figure 15.2](#ch23.xhtml#f170)).

![Figure 15.2 Flow of proposed method.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C015_002.jpg)

**Figure 15.2** Flow of proposed method.[⏎](#ch23.xhtml#f170b)

WT is a powerful tool for processing biological signals and has been widely used in applications such as noise removal from the ECG signal. The WT does not have any restrictions and is capable of processing non-stationary and time-varying signals, making it particularly useful for fECG data analysis. Wavelet processing allows for more flexible multiresolution analysis, which enables analysis of the low-frequency trend of the signal, as well as the higher frequency components of the signal. This is necessary for fECG extraction, as fetal heart signals can generally be lost inside the mECG signals and other noise sources. Furthermore, as WT may transition through multiple frequency bands, it provides a greater capacity for the separation of fetal heart activity also. The use of SWT is applied here, as it provides a stable time-frequency representation which is particularly helpful when seeking the dynamic features of the 338.fECG signal, specifically locating the R-peaks in the fECG signal accurately. The wavelet domain is also a potential pathway for filtering noise ultimately by capitalizing on the positive features of the fECG signal sparsity and energy concentration features. We reconstruct the extraction process using the RLS method in the wavelet domain, which provides a useful capability to remove the noise and interference contributed by the mother while retaining important fetal heart properties.

### 15.4.1 ISSNF Technique

To extract the fECG accurately, it is necessary to develop an effective denoising strategy based on wavelet analysis, and one of the derived methods, the spatially selective noise filter (SSNF), is a robust way to analyze biological signals and processes ([Figure 15.3](#ch23.xhtml#f171)). The SSNF can effectively remove noise without losing the original signal of fECG, including the signal features resulting from the waveform shape, amplitude, and frequency content. The SSNF’s approach allows for the removal of undesired components without altering the fECG signal. Importantly, the SSNF can reject multiple sources of interference, including but not limited to, baseline drift, powerline noise, and noise from electromyographic signals. The fECG signal can provide diagnostic clarity after removal of most, if not all, the noise.

![Figure 15.3 Methodology for fECG extraction.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C015_003.jpg)

**Figure 15.3** Methodology for fECG extraction.[⏎](#ch23.xhtml#f171b)

339.The ISSNF method is an improved version of the conventional SSNF used to improve SNR performance. This method is based on finding the spatial correlation, CorR(g, k), in distinct parts of the signal at each wavelet scale g. The idea behind this method is that the components of the signal are more physically linked in space whereas the components of noise are weakly correlated or not correlated. ISSNF exploits the difference to favor retention of more important structures of the signal while removing uncorrelated noise. This will help make the meaning of the signal more apparent and ensure the best possible fECG readings are obtained.

### 15.4.2 Threshold-Based Algorithm

Both hard and soft thresholding are common methods used to remove noise in the wavelet domain. While soft thresholding is generally very good at smoothly shrinking wavelet coefficients, hard thresholding has even been shown to have better results in some cases, particularly when the focus is on preserving sharp features in the signal. Research has shown that hard thresholding operates quite well with the undecimated wavelet transform (UWT) or the SWT. This is because hard thresholding is capable of preserving important signal patterns over all scales. In this case, a simple, but effective hard thresholding algorithm is described. This algorithm is a simple way of achieving signal de-noising while preserving the structure of the fECG signal.

### 15.4.3 Method for fECG Extraction

This research examines two hybrid approaches to extract fECG signals, as the abdominal ECG signals are complex and changing. The proposed methods offer two different processing pathways, which would allow an overall assessment and comparison of the outputs between the two methods. In Method 1, the RLS algorithm, the 340.SWT, and the ISSNF were employed. Method 2 is similarly arranged, but instead of ISSNF, it uses a threshold-based denoising approach.

There are four main steps in each method:

*   Using SWT for multi-resolution decomposition
*   RLS-based adaptive filtering to cancel out the mother’s ECG,
*   Using either ISSNF (Method 1) or thresholding (Method 2) to get rid of noise,
*   Measuring and analyzing fECG.

The SWT breaks down both abdominal and thoracic signals into several degrees of resolution. We have assessed the reconstruction performance of different wavelets as selected from the MATLAB Wavelet Toolbox. The performance of the reconstruction of Bior 1.5 was selected, as it had the best quality of reconstruction. A level of decomposition of five is chosen due to the nature of the signal’s frequency characteristics. Adaptive RLS filtering is then performed on the approximation and detailed coefficients in the wavelet domain. The abdomen coefficients will be considered the primary input, and the thorax coefficients will be considered the reference input. This adaptive filtering technique will effectively start to isolate and remove the mECG process while still prioritizing the fECG process above the remaining signals. There can still be artifacts or noise present in the recovered signals. Method 1 uses the ISSNF algorithm to selectively eliminate noise. This algorithm assumes that signal components are strongly correlated in space while noise components are weakly correlated. Method 2, on the other hand, uses a rigorous thresholding method to get rid of noise while keeping important parts of the fECG. For each wavelet scale, spatial correlations are calculated for both the approximation and detail coefficients to help with the denoising process. We evaluate the findings from both methods to see how well they keep the signal’s integrity and make the fECG clearer.

## 15.5 RESULTS

[Figure 15.4](#ch23.xhtml#f172) shows the steps in Method 1 for fECG extraction that require processing the signals. The top plot shows the raw abdominal signal, which is a combination of the mother’s ECG, the baby’s ECG, and other noise signals. The main peaks in this signal are mostly caused by the mother’s heart beating, which can hide the smaller parts of the fECG. The middle plot displays the thoracic signal taken from the mother’s chest. Most of it is a clean mECG. This reference signal is very important for adaptive filtering, especially the RLS algorithm, because it lets us accurately estimate and subtract the mECG from the abdominal signal. The bottom figure shows the final fECG that was retrieved after using signal processing methods such as the ISSNF algorithm, the SWT, and inverse wavelet reconstruction. The resulting waveform clearly shows fetal heart activity, with a lot of noise and maternal artifacts being removed. These results show that Method 1 works to separate fECG signals from complicated recordings of the abdomen.

![Figure 15.4 ECG signal processed in Method-1.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C015_004.jpg)

**Figure 15.4** ECG signal processed in Method-1.[⏎](#ch23.xhtml#f172b)

[Figure 15.5](#ch23.xhtml#f173) shows how to find the R-peak in the fECG signal that was taken using Method 1. The blue waveform shows the final fECG signal that was left after taking 341.out the mother’s ECG parts and noise artifacts. There are red markers on top of this signal that show where the identified R-peaks are. These are the most conspicuous and quick upward deflections in each cardiac cycle. Finding these R-peaks correctly is very important for figuring out the FHR and checking on the baby’s health during pregnancy. The successful detection of R-peaks shows that the extraction approach works and that the important morphological features of the fECG have been kept. In addition, being able to accurately identify R-peaks provides a way to check that the whole signal processing pipeline is strong and accurate. These results prove that Method 1 can reliably separate the fECG from the rest of the data while keeping the diagnostic features needed for clinical evaluation.

![Figure 15.5 R-peak detection process applied to the fECG signal.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C015_005.jpg)

**Figure 15.5** R-peak detection process applied to the fECG signal.[⏎](#ch23.xhtml#f173b)

[Figure 15.6](#ch23.xhtml#f174) shows the outcomes of Method 2’s signal processing pipeline for extracting fECG. The top figure shows the raw abdominal signal, which is a mix of background noise, mother ECG, and fECG. Like Method 1, the mother’s heart activity is the strongest part of the signal, which makes the fetal parts less visible. The middle plot depicts the thoracic signal taken from the mother’s chest. It has a clear mECG. This reference signal is very important for adaptive filtering to find and get rid of maternal signals from the abdominal recording. The last fECG taken using 342.Method 2 is shown in the bottom plot. In this scenario, the waveform has sharper and more obvious R-peaks with a larger amplitude than those obtained in Method 1. This suggests that Method 2 may use a more aggressive or improved way to separate signals. This could mean that the fetal signals are better isolated, but it could also mean that the signal reconstruction method had some amplification effects. However, the retrieved waveform clearly shows different fetal heart rhythms with less interference from the mother. The results show that Method 2 works to separate the fECG, which could be useful for later analysis like estimating the FHR and checking the health of the mother before birth.

![Figure 15.6 ECG signal processed in Method-12.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C015_006.jpg)

[Figure 15.7](#ch23.xhtml#f175) shows how the R-peak detection procedure works on the fECG data that was taken out using Method 2. The blue waveform shows the final fECG signal after the mother’s parts were taken out and the signal was made stronger. The red marks show the recognized R-peaks, which are the places with the largest amplitude in each cardiac cycle. These are important for getting an accurate FHR. The R-peaks in Method 2 are sharper, clearer, and more pronounced than those in Method 1. This 343.means that Method 2 makes a cleaner and stronger fECG signal. The peak amplitude observed was more than 200 units, which could mean that the signal became clearer or that amplification was added during processing. The accurate and clear detection of R-peaks proves that Method 2 successfully separates fetal heart activity while keeping the shape of the heart intact for clinical evaluation and ongoing fetal surveillance.

![Figure 15.7 R-peak detection process applied to the fECG signal.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C015_007.jpg)

344.Using eigenvalue analysis on 12 test cases, [Figure 15.8](#ch23.xhtml#f176) compares the SNR of Methods 1 and 2. The data show that Method 1 always gets higher SNR values, with big peaks in Cases 5 and 6, where the SNR is over 4.5 dB. This means that Method 1 is better at picking out the fECG signal while getting rid of any leftover maternal signals and noise. Method 2, on the other hand, is less reliable and works well in certain circumstances (like Case 6) but shows a big drop in SNR in others (like cases 9 345.and 10). This inconsistency suggests that Method 2 might not be as strong or useful for a wide range of subjects or signal situations.

![Figure 15.8 Comparison of SNR.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C015_008.jpg)
