# 419.20A Deep Learning and Optimization-Based Cardiac Diagnosis System for Heart Disease Classification Using Electrocardiogram Signals

C. Venkatesh, L. Sivayamini, M. Venkata Dasu, Shaik Karimullah, and T. Lakshminarayana

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-20](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-20)

## **20.1** Introduction

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) pose a significant challenge to global health, accounting for nearly one-third of deaths worldwide every year \[[1](#ch28.xhtml#r604)\]. This broad category of disorders affects the heart and vascular system, including conditions such as arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, etc. \[[2](#ch28.xhtml#r605)\]. The growing incidence of CVDs is influenced by factors like an aging population, changes in lifestyle, and increasing prevalence of hypertension and diabetes, which together place a heavy burden on healthcare systems internationally. As the leading cause of death, cardiovascular diseases demand urgent attention \[[3](#ch28.xhtml#r606)\]. Timely and accurate diagnosis of heart diseases is essential as it directly impacts patient care and outcomes. Different cardiac diseases affect the heart’s electrical function, structure, and mechanical performance, which can be observed through various clinical and physiological signs. Healthcare providers typically rely on diagnostic tools such as angiography, electrocardiograms (ECGs), and blood tests to assess cardiac health \[[4](#ch28.xhtml#r607)\]. Angiography offers detailed imaging of blood vessels to detect blockages or abnormalities, while blood tests measure markers indicating heart muscle injury or stress. The ECG remains the most widely used and accessible diagnostic tool, capturing the electrical impulses generated by pacemaker cells that regulate the heartbeat. This makes ECG an invaluable strategy for observance of conduction pathways, and other vital cardiac functions, enabling diagnosis of multiple heart conditions \[[5](#ch28.xhtml#r608)\].

420.Advancements in computational technology have revolutionized the interpretation of ECG data. Traditionally, ECG analysis depended heavily on manual review and classical signal processing, which involved extracting specific features from the signal, selecting relevant ones, and then classifying them. These methods can be labor-intensive, prone to human error, and limited by the challenge of choosing features that fully represent the complexity of cardiac signals. To overcome these limitations, deep learning has evolved into an established approach in recent times to automate and enhance ECG interpretation accuracy.

These models can detect subtle and intricate patterns within the data that conventional techniques might miss. The availability of large, well-annotated datasets, such as those from the PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge (CinC), has been crucial for training these models, resulting in high accuracy for detecting arrhythmias, coronary artery disease, and other cardiac disorders \[[6](#ch28.xhtml#r609)\].

While deep neural networks impact on improving diagnostic accuracy has been widely recognized across multiple medical fields, including neurology, dermatology, and cardiology \[[7](#ch28.xhtml#r610)\]. Overall, deep learning enhances the ability to analyze complex biomedical signals and medical images, making it an indispensable tool for advancing healthcare diagnostics and prognostics \[[8](#ch28.xhtml#r611)\].

To further refine classification accuracy, this study incorporates the osprey optimization procedure a nature-inspired metaheuristic based on the hunting techniques of osprey birds—into the model training process \[[9](#ch28.xhtml#r612)\]. This optimization approach is particularly effective in solving complex, nonlinear problems without relying on gradient information, thus improving the model’s capacity to accurately classify heart diseases from ECG data \[[10](#ch28.xhtml#r613)\]. Proven effective in various engineering and resource allocation applications, this algorithm offers a promising strategy for optimizing medical signal analysis \[[11](#ch28.xhtml#r614)\]. By combining this optimization with convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the research aims to boost diagnostic precision, support early detection of CVDs, and ultimately help reduce mortality related to heart conditions.

## **20.2** Literature Survey

Recent advancements in CVD diagnosis have increasingly focused on leveraging deep learning and optimization algorithms to enhance predictive accuracy and reliability.

In 2025, Zhang et al. \[[12](#ch28.xhtml#r615)\] introduced an integrated networks for early cardiovascular disease detection using multi-lead ECG recordings sourced from the PhysioNet database. Their approach demonstrated a significant improvement in overall diagnostic performance, achieving an accuracy of 93.5%. The integrated strategy allowed the model to capture complex cardiac signal dynamics effectively. However, the method demands extensive computational resources and relies on large, well-annotated datasets, which could limit its accessibility in clinical settings with limited infrastructure.

In 2024, Kumar et al. \[[13](#ch28.xhtml#r616)\] examined several means to choosing traits in conjunction with ensemble learning methods applied to electronic health records (EHRs) for CVD prediction. Their study found that RFE combined with Gradient Boosting classifiers 421.outperformed other configurations, reaching an accuracy level of 89%. Despite the promising results, the research was confined to a single institutional dataset, which poses challenges in validating the model’s generalizability and effectiveness across broader, more diverse patient populations.

The work of Lopez-Morales et al. \[[14](#ch28.xhtml#r617)\] in 2023 addressed not only classification accuracy but also model transparency by proposing an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework using attention-based CNNs for arrhythmia detection from ECG data. Achieving a classification accuracy of 91.2%, their model also generated attention maps that visually highlighted critical regions in the ECG signal contributing to predictions, thus fostering clinical trust. Nevertheless, the study’s relatively limited sample size and focus on specific arrhythmia categories restricted the scope of applicability and robustness of their solution.

Farhan et al. \[[15](#ch28.xhtml#r618)\], in 2022, explored the optimization of one-dimensional (1D) CNN architectures with genetic algorithms for diagnosing coronary artery disease through ECG signal analysis. Their optimized CNN model achieved 90.7% accuracy and exhibited faster convergence during training compared to baseline networks. However, the presence of imbalanced datasets and absence of validation on external data limited the reliability and wider clinical relevance of their findings.

A comprehensive review by Singh and Gupta \[[16](#ch28.xhtml#r619)\] in 2022 underscored the growing integration of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies with machine learning for continuous cardiovascular health monitoring achieving accuracy above 92% in detecting arrhythmias via wearable devices. Despite these advances, they highlighted persistent challenges, including concerns around patient data privacy, and the scarcity of large-scale publicly available datasets, which hindered broad implementation.

In 2021, Hassan et al. \[[17](#ch28.xhtml#r620)\] proposed an ensemble diagnostic model combining CNNs and Random Forest algorithms for predicting heart failure by utilizing echocardiographic images alongside clinical data. Their model achieved an accuracy of 90.1% across multiple patient cohorts, demonstrating robustness and effectiveness. Yet, dependence on echocardiographic imaging limits applicability in resource-poor environments where such imaging may not be routinely available.

Similarly, Oliveira et al. \[[18](#ch28.xhtml#r621)\] in 2021 developed a comprehensive deep learning pipeline that fused raw ECG signals with clinical metadata to classify a range of cardiac conditions simultaneously. Trained on a large, heterogeneous dataset, the model attained an accuracy of 88.6%. The primary constraint of their approach was the considerable computational effort required, alongside the need for extensive, high-quality labeled data to maintain performance.

Collectively, these studies reflect significant progress in applying deep learning and optimization methods to cardiovascular diagnostics. However, common limitations persist: models often depend on specific datasets or diagnostic modalities, suffer from class imbalances, and sometimes lack interpretability, which is crucial for clinical acceptance. Additionally, high computational demands and limited validation across diverse populations restrict real-world applicability.

The methodology proposed in this study intent to overwhelm these challenges by implementing CNNs for fully automated ECG signal classification. This is enhanced by the Osprey Optimization Algorithm (OOA), a metaheuristic approach designed to fine-tune model parameters effectively without reliance on gradient information, 422.improving classification accuracy. This strategy minimizes human error, promotes early and accurate diagnosis, and increases robustness across varied datasets and clinical environments.

## **20.3** Proposed Methodology

Constructing an efficient and precise computational diagnostic approach to the recognition and categorization of ailments associated with the heart using ECG data is the key objective of the implied approach. To offer a trustworthy diagnostic solution, the model integrates signal pre-processing, optimization, feature extraction and classification steps. [Figure 20.1](#ch28.xhtml#f202) showcases the system’s architectural flow.

![Figure 20.1 Proposed block diagram.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C020_001.jpg)

**Figure 20.1** Proposed block diagram.[⏎](#ch28.xhtml#f202b)

This research introduces a structured approach to identifying heart-related disorders using ECG signal analysis. The initial phase involves acquiring ECG data from well-established medical databases such as PhysioBank, which provides a rich collection of recordings from both healthy individuals and patients suffering from various cardiovascular conditions. These signals serve as the foundational input for the diagnostic system.

To improve the quality and reduce inconsistencies that may arise from individual sources, a data fusion process is employed. By combining multiple ECG signals from different leads or time instances, the system creates an improved and legitimate representation of the heart’s electrical activity. This pre-processing step helps suppress unwanted noise and enhances the clarity of clinically important features.

Once the data has been fused and normalized, the next step focuses on extracting diagnostic features using the Pan–Tompkins strategy. The algorithm works by filtering the signal, emphasizing rapid transitions, and applying dynamic thresholding to locate significant peaks.

After identifying these key features, an optimization step is introduced to the classification model. The OOA is used here to fine-tune the selected features by prioritizing those that offer the greatest diagnostic value.

The refined features are then passed to a CNN, a model particularly effective for pattern recognition tasks. The CNN processes these features through multiple layers 423.to relegate the ECG signals. Early identification of abnormalities through this system supports timely medical intervention, thereby improving patient survival rates and reducing the risk of critical cardiac events.

### **20.3.1** ECG Signal Acquisition

To initiate the diagnostic process, the study relies on ECG signals as the primary data source. These signals were obtained from the PhysioBank database, a widely recognized and publicly accessible repository that houses a diverse range of physiological recordings \[[19](#ch28.xhtml#r622)\]. PhysioBank offers curated datasets from both healthy individuals and patients with conditions such as cardiac arrhythmias, heart failure, epilepsy, and sleep apnea. These recordings are particularly useful in biomedical engineering and medical research due to their quality, diversity, and availability for open use \[[20](#ch28.xhtml#r623)\].

The ECG signal plays a vital role in assessing heart function by tracking the electrical activity that occurs during each heartbeat. This activity is captured through a series of electrodes placed at specific locations on the skin, typically on the chest and limbs. The signal reflects the flow of electrical impulses across the heart muscle, corresponding to its contraction and relaxation phases \[[21](#ch28.xhtml#r624)\].

An ECG waveform consists of several key components that represent different phases of the cardiac cycle. The representation of ECG is shown in [Figure 20.2](#ch28.xhtml#f203).

![Figure 20.2 Representation of ECG signal.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C020_002.jpg)

**Figure 20.2** Representation of ECG signal.[⏎](#ch28.xhtml#f203b)

The P-wave shows that the atria have depolarized, initiating the contraction that moves blood into the ventricles. When the ventricles abruptly depolarize, the muscles contract, as indicated by the QRS complex and the pumping of blood throughout the body. Following this, the T-wave appears, implying the ventricles’ repolarization as they prepare for the next cycle. Occasionally, a U-wave may be visible, which is associated with the final phase of ventricular repolarization \[[22](#ch28.xhtml#r625)\].

Once the ECG signals are acquired, they undergo a data fusion process, which combines multiple recordings or leads into a single, coherent signal. This step enhances the consistency and clarity of the signal by reducing artifacts and aligning the features across different inputs, forming a more accurate basis for further analysis in disease classification \[[23](#ch28.xhtml#r626)\].

### **424.20.3.2** Signal Fusion

ECG signals are essential in detecting CVD because they provide a real-time, non-invasive snapshot of the heart’s electrical activity \[[24](#ch28.xhtml#r627)\]. However, relying on a single ECG lead can limit diagnostic precision. This limitation arises because individual leads may be affected by noise, movement artifacts, or may not fully capture the heart’s electrical signals due to their specific anatomical placement. Different leads view the heart from various angles, and certain heart abnormalities may only appear clearly in specific leads \[[25](#ch28.xhtml#r628)\]. To address these challenges, combining data from multiple ECG leads through a process called multi-source signal fusion is used \[[26](#ch28.xhtml#r629)\].

Multi-source ECG signal fusion involves integrating several ECG signals, each representing electrical activity from different leads, into a single combined signal. This approach enhances the overall quality of the cardiac signal by reducing the impact of noise and artifacts, resulting in a more reliable basis for further analysis \[[27](#ch28.xhtml#r630)\]. The fusion process expressed as shown in Equation (20.1):

$P\\left( t \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 0}^{T}M\_{n}.E\_{n}\\left( t \\right)$ (20.1) 

In this equation, *E*[*n*](*t*) is the ECG signal from the *n*th lead at time *t*, *M*[*n*]  denotes the weight assigned to that lead, and *T* is the number of leads being fused. These weights are assigned based on the signal’s reliability or importance, which can be measured through various quality indicators such as noise levels or signal clarity \[[28](#ch28.xhtml#r631)\]. Alternatively, these weights can be optimized through learning algorithms that adjust them dynamically to prioritize cleaner and more informative signals \[[29](#ch28.xhtml#r632)\].

By combining ECG leads in this way, a fused signal  *P*(*t*)  is generated that captures the heart’s electrical behavior more completely. This enhanced signal allows for more effective feature extractio n such as identifying heartbeats, intervals, and waveforms which improves the accuracy of CVD detection and classification models \[[30](#ch28.xhtml#r633)\].

### **20.3.3** Feature Extraction

It is a fundamental step that reduces the uncertainty of raw data while preserving essential information needed for accurate analysis. This process not only decreases computational load but also improves the effectiveness of classification models by converting the original signals into a set of meaningful and compact features. In the context of CVD diagnosis, extracting precise features from ECG signals is critical for capturing the heart’s electrical behavior with minimal processing effort \[[31](#ch28.xhtml#r634)\].

The Pan–Tompkins algorithm is employed for features extraction from ECG signals, primarily focusing on detecting QRS complexes in real time. The Pan–Tompkins method efficiently locates R-peaks by combining signal pre-processing techniques and decision rules. The steps of Pan–Tompkins is shown in [Figure 20.3](#ch28.xhtml#f204).

![Figure 20.3 Steps of Pan–Tompkins.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C020_003.jpg)

**Figure 20.3** Steps of Pan–Tompkins.[⏎](#ch28.xhtml#f204b)

425.The algorithm follows these sequential steps:

1.  *Bandpass Filtering:* The raw ECG signal, denoted by *M*(*t*) contains various interferences such as baseline wander and high-frequency noise. To eliminate these unwanted components while preserving QRS characteristics, the signal is passed through a bandpass filter. The filtering process can expressed using Equation (20.2):

*B*(*t*) = *M*(*t*) \* *R* , (20.2) 

where *R* represents the filter response. This filtering enhances the signal-to-noise ratio, facilitating better feature extraction \[[32](#ch28.xhtml#r635)\].

1.  Differentiation: To emphasize the steep slopes characteristic of the QRS complex, the filtered signal is differentiated using Equation (20.3). This operation highlights rapid changes by computing a weighted difference of neighboring samples:

$S\\left( t \\right) = \\frac{1}{8}\\left\\lbrack {- X\\left( {t - 2} \\right) + X\\left( {t + 2} \\right) + 2X\\left( {t + 1} \\right) - 2X\\left( {t - 1} \\right)} \\right\\rbrack.$ (20.3) 

This step accentuates edges and helps in distinguishing the R-peaks from other wave components \[[33](#ch28.xhtml#r636)\].

1.  Squaring: The differentiated signal *S*(*t*)  is then squared using Equation (20.4) to magnify larger values associated with the QRS complex while suppressing smaller fluctuations from noise and other ECG waves

*K*(*t*) = \[*S*(*t*)\]² (20.4) 

This nonlinear operation ensures all values are positive and enhances the prominence of significant peaks.

1.  *Moving Window Integration (MWI):* To capture both the duration and shape of the QRS complex, a moving average filter integrates the squared signal over a window of *M* samples using Equation (20.5):

$W\\left( t \\right) = \\frac{1}{M}\\sum\\limits\_{n = t - M + 1}^{t}K\\left( n \\right)$ . (20.5) 

426.The choice of window size *M* is critical and depends on the ECG sampling frequency. This smoothing aids in producing a waveform that reliably reflects the QRS morphology and facilitates peak detection.

1.  *Adaptive Thresholding and Decision-Making:* Finally, adaptive thresholds are applied to the integrated signal *W*(*t*) to identify the locations of R-peaks using Equation (20.6):

*R*[*p*] = max(*w*(*t*).*T*) (20.6) 

Here, *T* is a threshold factor adjusted dynamically to separate true peaks from noise artifacts. Additional decision rules, such as peak width and amplitude checks, are employed to reduce false detections.

While the Pan–Tompkins algorithm is effective, its performance may degrade in the presence of noise or abnormal ECG morphologies, causing missed or spurious peak detections. To address this, optimization of filter parameters, threshold adaptation, and window size selection is necessary. Advanced methods, such as machine learning–based threshold tuning or filter design refinement, can be integrated to improve robustness, particularly for ambulatory or noisy recordings. Enhancing the Pan–Tompkins method through such optimizations promises improved feature extraction \[[34](#ch28.xhtml#r637)\].

### 20.3.4 OOA for Feature Selection in CVD Classification

It is a nature-inspired, population-based metaheuristic that simulates the migratory and predatory behaviors of ospreys to solve complex optimization problems \[[35](#ch28.xhtml#r638)\]. Its design makes it especially suitable for tasks such as feature selection and parameter fine-tuning in biomedical classification systems. In the present study, OOA has been adopted to optimize feature subsets extracted from ECG signals. The algorithm incorporates three key enhancements—adaptive weighting, Cauchy distribution-based variation, and Fuch chaotic mapping—to maintain solution diversity and avoid premature convergence on suboptimal solutions.

#### **20.3.4.1** Initialization Phase

The algorithm commences by setting critical parameters including population size (i.e., number of ospreys), the dimensionality of the search space (equal to the number of features), and the upper and lower search bounds. Each candidate solution, representing a potential feature subset or parameter configuration, is initialized randomly within these limits using Equation (20.7):

*Y*[*i*] = *L*[*b*] + *R*[*a*](*m*,*n*) × (*U*[*b*]−*L*[*b*]), (20.7) 

where

*   •  *Y*[*i*] is the position of the *i*th  osprey,
*     
    •  *L*[*b*]  
     and *U*[*b*]  denote the lower and upper bounds,
*   427.•  *R*[*a*](*m*,*n*) generates a random matrix of size  *m* × *n*,
*   • *m* is the total number of ospreys,
*   • *n* is the number of features in the search space.

#### **20.3.4.2** Fitness Evaluation

Once initialized, each solution’s performance is measured using a predefined fitness function. In the context of ECG-based disease classification, the fitness function is generally derived from classification accuracy, error rate, or a similar metric \[[36](#ch28.xhtml#r639)\]. The algorithm identifies the most optimal solution in each iteration using Equation (20.8):

*Y*[*b**e**s**t*] = arg min *O*(*Y*[*i*]), (20.8) 

where *O*(*Y*[*i*]) represents the fitness score of the *i*th candidate.

#### **20.3.4.3** Position Update Mechanism

To search for improved solutions and escape local optima, each osprey updates its position based on a set of mathematical transformations inspired by osprey hunting dynamics using Equation (20.9). The updated positions are clipped to ensure they remain within the defined boundaries:

*Y*[*n**e**w*] = max (min(*Y*[*n**e**w*],*U*[*b*]),*L*[*b*]). (20.9) 

This process ensures that the exploration does not exceed the search space and that all solutions remain feasible.

#### **20.3.4.4** Exploration Enhancements

OOA integrates several stochastic components to enhance search behavior:

*   *Cauchy Mutation:* This allows sporadic long-distance moves in the search space, facilitating global exploration \[[37](#ch28.xhtml#r640)\].
*   *Fuch Chaotic Mapping:* This is used to inject unpredictability into the optimization process, mitigating the risk of early stagnation.
*   *Adaptive Weighting:* This dynamically adjusts the influence of various update terms, improving convergence reliability.

After the first round of position updates, a new set of candidate positions is recalculated using a second round of random sampling of Equation (20.7). Again, updated solutions are bounded using Equation (20.9).

#### **20.3.4.5** Selection and Iteration

The newly generated solutions are evaluated, and if any offer an improvement over the current best, they replace the inferior ones. This process is repeated iteratively, and the algorithm continues updating the positions when the iterations is reached or no further improvement is observed.

#### **428.20.3.4.6** Final Output

At the end of the optimization run, the algorithm outputs the best-performing solution, which corresponds to the most effective subset of features. This optimized feature set is then passed to a CNN model, which performs the final classification of CVD conditions.

#### **20.3.4.7** Classification Using CNNs

CNNs have become highly popular due to their ability to automatically learn hierarchical representations of features, from low-level edges to high-level semantic concepts \[[38](#ch28.xhtml#r641)\]. CNNs are widely used in numerous applications including image recognition, object detection, and medical diagnosis. They have been successfully applied in biomedical signal processing tasks, such as classifying CVDs from ECG signals \[[39](#ch28.xhtml#r642)\]. The structure and key layers of CNNs is shown in [Figure 20.4](#ch28.xhtml#f205).

![Figure 20.4 Structure of CNN.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C020_004.jpg)

**Figure 20.4** Structure of CNN.[⏎](#ch28.xhtml#f205b)

A CNN typically consists of several fundamental layers

1.  *Input Layer:* For image or signal-based tasks, the input is typically multidimensional array (tensor) representing pixel intensities or transformed signal representations. The attribute of the input correspond to the height, width, and depth (number of channels) of the data \[[40](#ch28.xhtml#r643)\].
2.  *Convolutional Layer:* It is responsible for detecting local patterns within the input data. It achieves this by sliding multiple small filters, also called kernels, across the input volume. Each filter convolves with the input to produce a 2D feature map \[[41](#ch28.xhtml#r644)\]. The size of the output feature map depends on the filter size, stride, and padding used, and can be computed using Equation (20.10):

$S\_{Z} = \\frac{D - F\_{s} + 2P\_{a}}{S\_{t}} + 1,$ (20.10) 

1.  where *D* is the input dimension, *F*[*s* ] the filter size, *P*[*a*]  the padding added to the borders of the input, and *S*[*t*]  the stride, or step size of the filter movement \[[42](#ch28.xhtml#r645)\].
2.  *Batch Normalization Layer:* This layer normalizes the activations by adjusting them to have a mean close to zero and variance near one. Batch normalization helps stabilize the training process by reducing internal covariate shift and 429.accelerates convergence. It normalizes the input to subsequent layers on a per-mini-batch basis \[[43](#ch28.xhtml#r646)\].
3.  *Pooling Layer:* Average pooling, for instance, calculates the mean value within each region of the feature map, thereby summarizing local features while reducing resolution. Pooling also provides some degree of spatial invariance, making the network less sensitive to exact feature positions \[[44](#ch28.xhtml#r647)\].
4.  *Fully Connected Layer:* Positioned near the network’s output, fully connected (dense) layers act similarly to traditional neural networks. They receive flattened feature vectors from previous layers and compute weighted sums with learned weights and biases to generate the final classification output. The calculation in this layer can be represented in Equation (20.11).

*F* = *W*[*m*] × *v* + *b*[*i*], (20.11) 

1.  where *W*[*m*]  denotes the weight matrix, *v* the input vector, and *b*[*i*]  the bias term \[[45](#ch28.xhtml#r648)\].
2.  *Activation Functions: Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and Softmax:* Important non-linearity is incorporated into a system using nonlinear activation functions like the ReLU. For negative inputs, the ReLU function returns zero; for positive inputs, it returns the input value

*R*[*e*](*X*[*i*]) = max (0,*X*[*i*]) (20.12) 

1.  This simple transformation shown in Equation (20.12) helps the network model complex functions and mitigates problems like the vanishing gradient issue \[[46](#ch28.xhtml#r649)\]. At the final stage, softmax activation converts the class probabilities for multi-class classification tasks. For binary classification, sigmoid activation is often used \[[47](#ch28.xhtml#r650)\].

CNNs learn features progressively through their layered structure. The initial convolutional layers extract basic features such as lines, edges, or color gradients. Pooling layers systematically reduce spatial resolution, helping to condense information and reduce the computational burden \[[48](#ch28.xhtml#r651)\]. Batch normalization supports consistent training by standardizing activations, which stabilizes gradients and improves model robustness \[[49](#ch28.xhtml#r652)\].

In the context of biomedical applications, such as ECG signal classification, CNNs can detect subtle patterns indicative of cardiovascular abnormalities. Their ability to capture spatial and temporal dependencies in the data makes them highly effective for this purpose \[[50](#ch28.xhtml#r653)\].

#### **20.3.4.8** Statistical Attributes

To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed CVD classification model, a comprehensive performance analysis is carried out using a set of well-established statistical parameters. These include accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, etc. These metrics assess the correctness of the model’s articulation.

430.The classification results are primarily categorized into four outcomes like **T**p**o**s*, *F**p**o**s*, *T**n**e**g*, *F**n**e**g**. These serve as the foundation for the computation of each performance metric, each of which emphasizes a different dimension of classification performance.

##### ***20.3.4.8.1*** Accuracy

In medical diagnostics, accuracy serves as a basic but important measure to understand the general effectiveness of the model. It is calculated using Equation (20.13):

$A = \\frac{Tpos + Tneg}{Tpos + Fpos + Tneg + Fneg}.$ (20.13) 

A high accuracy indicates that the classifier is generally making correct decisions across both positive and negative classes. However, it should be interpreted in conjunction with other metrics, particularly when the dataset is imbalanced.

##### ***20.3.4.8.2*** Sensitivity

It is a crucial metric in healthcare applications where failing to detect a condition may have serious or life-threatening consequences. Sensitivity is computed using Equation (20.14):

$Sen = \\frac{Tpos}{Tpos + Fneg}$ (20.14) 

A higher sensitivity value indicates fewer false negatives and ensures that the system is reliable in detecting actual disease cases.

##### ***20.3.4.8.3*** Specificity

Specificity quantifies the proportion of correctly identified negative cases. In medical applications, this translates to how accurately the model identifies individuals without the disease. Minimizing false positives is essential to avoid unnecessary medical interventions or anxiety. The formula for specificity is shown in Equation (20.15):

$Spe = \\frac{Tneg}{Tneg + Fpos}.$ (20.15) 

Together with sensitivity, specificity helps provide a balanced view of model performance in terms of both classes—those with and without the disease.

##### ***20.3.4.8.4*** Mean Square Error

It is particularly useful when analyzing signal reconstruction or output images. Lower values of MSE imply higher prediction precision. It is computed using Equation (20.16):

431.*M**S**E*\= *m*(*s**i**g*)². (20.16) 

Here, the error represents the mean operation where it helps average these errors across the dataset.

##### ***20.3.4.8.5*** Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio

Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) is a ratio expressed in decibels (dB) that compares the maximum power of a signal to the power of corrupting noise. It is widely used in image quality assessments, particularly for comparing the original and processed medical images. A higher PSNR value generally implies better visual quality and less distortion. The PSNR is calculated using Equation (20.17):

$PSNR = 10.log\_{10}\\left( \\frac{MAX\_{1}^{2}}{MSE} \\right)$ (20.17) 

Here, MAX denotes 255 for eight-bit grayscale images

## **20.4** Simulation Results and Discussion

This research introduces a sophisticated deep learning framework for the identification and classification of three critical cardiovascular conditions: arrhythmia, coronary artery disease, and aortic disease. The diagnostic pipeline is initiated with the acquisition of ECG signals, retrieved from established and publicly accessible databases, particularly the PhysioBank ATM repository. As non-invasive diagnostic instruments, ECGs capture the heart’s electrical activity and play an instrumental role in the timely detection of pathological cardiac rhythms by analyzing waveform patterns such as P-waves, QRS complexes, and T-waves.

In this study, ECG data were collected from a cohort of thirty individuals, each diagnosed with one of the cardiovascular disorders. The objective was to design a comprehensive and reliable classification pipeline capable of differentiating between normal and pathological cardiac rhythms across varied disease classes. ECG signals of three different patients are illustrated in [Figure 20.5](#ch28.xhtml#f206).

![Figure 20.5 Input ECG signals. (a) PE-1, (b) PE-2, and (c) PE-3.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C020_005.jpg)

**Figure 20.5** Input ECG signals. (a) PE-1, (b) PE-2, and (c) PE-3.[⏎](#ch28.xhtml#f206b)

Following data acquisition, the raw ECG signals underwent a pre-processing phase that employed a signal fusion technique. Specifically, a multi-source fusion strategy was adopted to integrate multiple ECG segments into a cohesive signal representation. This method enhances discriminative features by consolidating temporal and morphological patterns from various timeframes, thereby improving classification robustness. The fused signals corresponding to the three representative patients are displayed in [Figure 20.6](#ch28.xhtml#f207).

![Figure 20.6 Fused ECG signals. (a) PE-1, (b) PE-2, and (c) PE-3.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C020_006.jpg)

**Figure 20.6** Fused ECG signals. (a) PE-1, (b) PE-2, and (c) PE-3.[⏎](#ch28.xhtml#f207b)

The next stage involves feature extraction from the pre-processed ECG waveforms. The Pan–Tompkins algorithm was employed for this purpose due to its proven efficacy in identifying QRS complexes in ECG signals. The algorithm sequentially applies filtering, differentiation, squaring, and integration to isolate the QRS complex, 432.facilitating the extraction of key physiological features such as RR intervals, waveform amplitude variations, and heart rate variability.

[Table 20.1](#ch28.xhtml#t55) summarizes the clinical features typically associated with each cardiac condition under study. For instance, arrhythmia is generally linked to irregular pulse patterns and dizziness, while coronary artery disease manifests as chest discomfort and difficulty breathing. Aortic disease often results in acute pain in the chest or back, occasionally accompanied by pulsation near the abdominal region.

**Table 20.1** Signal-Based Features for Different Diseases[⏎](#ch28.xhtml#t55b)

 
| **CardiovascularType** || **Features** |
| --- | --- |
| Aortic disease || Widened QRS complex |
| --- | --- |
| Arrhythmia || Irregular RR intervals, missing/extra P-waves |
| Coronary artery disease || ST-segment elevation or depression |

Following feature extraction, an optimization phase was executed. This step is critical for reducing feature space redundancy, enhancing classification precision, and minimizing computational complexity. The OOA was utilized, known for its superior global convergence capabilities and balanced exploration–exploitation dynamics. Its integration into the feature selection process contributed significantly to boosting the classification model’s efficiency and precision.

For the classification stage, a CNN architecture was adopted due to its exceptional ability to capture spatial and temporal dependencies within biomedical signals. The CNN not only serves as a robust feature learner but also functions as the primary classifier, segmenting input signals into either normal or abnormal categories based 433.on learned discriminative features. The dataset consisted of 30 labeled ECG signals, each annotated according to the presence or absence of a pathological condition.

The CNN-generated output categorizes signals into two major classes:

*   *Normal:* ECG traces displaying regular rhythmic patterns and waveform morphology within clinically accepted norms.
*   *Abnormal:* Signals reflecting deviations such as altered QRS morphology, distorted T-waves, or rhythm irregularities indicative of underlying cardiac dysfunction.

Detection of QRS complexes plays a pivotal role in this classification process, forming the basis for accurate heartbeat identification and rhythm assessment.

To quantitatively assess the model’s performance, several standard evaluation metrics were employed: accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PSNR, and mean squared error (MSE). These metrics provide a comprehensive view of both the diagnostic 434.accuracy and the signal quality achieved post-classification. The performance outcomes for the three selected cases are provided in Table 20.3.

Each model shows excellent accuracy, with values close to 99%, indicating strong overall performance. Specificity scores, which indicate how well the models identify healthy individuals, range from about 95.8% to 96.2%. Sensitivity values, reflecting the ability to correctly detect patients with disease, are similarly high, between 97.4% and 98%. The PSNR values, measuring the quality of the signal after processing, remain consistently high, suggesting good preservation of signal details. Low MSE values indicate that the models have minimal prediction errors. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the ECG-based methods in accurately identifying different types of cardiovascular diseases.

To establish the relevance of the present study within the framework of previous research, a detailed comparison was carried out with the techniques discussed in the literature review. The results clearly show that the proposed method outperforms all existing models, attaining an accuracy of 98.84%, which stands as the highest among the approaches evaluated.

## **435.20.5** Conclusion

Heart diseases are the foremost cause of death globally, with conditions such as arrhythmia, coronary artery disease, and aortic disease significantly contributing to mortality rates. Early and accurate diagnosis plays a vital role in lowering these rates by enabling timely medical intervention and treatment. This study introduces a deep learning framework based on CNN to classify heart diseases using ECG signals.

ECG data utilized in this research is obtained from the PhysioBank database, a widely recognized collection of physiological recordings. The method involves combining signals from multiple sources through data fusion to enhance the information available for analysis. For feature extraction, the Pan–Tompkins algorithm is applied to accurately detect QRS complexes, which are essential for understanding heart activity.

To optimize the model’s classification capabilities, the OOA is used to fine-tune parameters and improve feature selection. The effectiveness of the model is assessed by examining accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Accuracy indicates how well the model distinguishes between healthy and diseased cases; sensitivity measures its ability to detect true positive cases, and specificity reflects the model’s capacity to correctly identify healthy individuals.

The system aims to classify ECG signals reliably into normal or abnormal categories, enhancing diagnostic accuracy while reducing the manual effort required for interpretation. This approach has the potential to accelerate diagnosis, support clinical decisions, and ultimately contribute to lowering the risk of fatal outcomes by facilitating early detection.

Nevertheless, the approach has limitations. Its performance heavily relies on the diversity and quality of the training data, which may limit effectiveness when applied to new or rare cardiac conditions. Additionally, deep learning models often lack interpretability, making it challenging for healthcare providers to understand how 436.decisions are made. High computational demands may also restrict use in environments with limited resources.

Future research should focus on expanding the dataset to include more varied cardiac cases and patient demographics to increase the model’s generalizability. Efforts to integrate explainability features can improve trust and usability in clinical settings. Moreover, developing systems for real-time monitoring and mobile integration could provide continuous heart health assessment, improving accessibility and enabling earlier interventions.
