# 440.21Sentiments of SustainabilityExploring Ecological Narratives in the Mahabharata through Natural Language Processing

Aarushi Yadav, Santosh Kumar Yadav, Irfan Ahmad Pindoo, and Prakash Singh Tanwar

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-21](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-21)

## **21.1** Introduction

The Mahabharata is one of the two great epics of India, the other being the Ramayana ([Thapar, 2009](#ch29.xhtml#r692)). Traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa, the Mahabharata is a colossal work that is believed to have been composed over many centuries, with the final version emerging around 500 AD ([Jha, 1998](#ch29.xhtml#r669)). This epic narrates the story of the Kuru dynasty and the great war between the Pandavas and the Kauravas, two rival branches of the family, over the rightful claim to the kingdom ([Hooper, 2018](#ch29.xhtml#r667)). The Mahabharata delves into complex philosophical and spiritual teachings, exploring themes of morality, duty, and the eternal struggle between good and evil ([Hooper, 2018](#ch29.xhtml#r667)). The core theme of the Mahabharata is the exploration of rightful conduct or dharma, as highlighted in the Bhagavad Gita. The epic is structured across 18 major sections called parvas, each delving into various aspects of the grand narrative and its philosophical underpinnings ([Prasad, 2015](#ch29.xhtml#r683)). This battle for power serves as the backdrop for a broader exploration of moral dilemmas, human nature, duty (dharma), and the consequences of one’s actions ([Upadhyaya, 2024](#ch29.xhtml#r693)). One of the most remarkable aspects of the Mahabharata is its portrayal of the human relationship with nature ([Agri, 2012](#ch29.xhtml#r656)). Forests are not just the setting of war or exile, but also locations of spiritual growth and ecological harmony. Water, earth, and trees are all sacred, and their sacredness is emphasized throughout the epic ([Chapple, 2015](#ch29.xhtml#r671)). The sanctity of nature is intertwined with the moral teachings of the text, emphasizing the responsibility of human beings to preserve and protect the natural world ([Mahata, 2024](#ch29.xhtml#r669)). The Mahabharata educates us on lessons from nature. It tells us about the relationship of human beings with nature and how we must not harm nature, cut so many trees, and exploit resources ([Brodbeck, 2024](#ch29.xhtml#r660)).

441.In a world constantly fighting environmental issues such as climate change, deforestation, and lack of water, the ancient works like the Mahabharata have a wealth of information waiting to be explored and converted into modern sustainable actions. Such ancient works contain not just cultural and historical importance but also timeless ecological knowledge ([Renugadevi, 2012](#ch29.xhtml#r684)). There have been several studies across the world to establish the importance of religious texts in promoting eco-spirituality and sustainability ([Lal, 2015](#ch29.xhtml#r672); [Sivaramakrishnan, 2015](#ch29.xhtml#r689)). Several studies have demonstrated that Hinduism texts have an intricate relationship woven with nature, which is reflected in rituals, ideas, and practices ([Agoramoorthy, 2015](#ch29.xhtml#r655); *Environmental Ethics in the Hindu Vedas*, n.d.; [Horn, 2006](#ch29.xhtml#r668); [Radhakrishnan, 1922](#ch29.xhtml#r685)). However, the use of such works to inform modern global ecological issues using modern technologies has been hitherto ignored in conventional scholarship. An application of present computational techniques like natural language processing (NLP) offers a new avenue to re-reading such works afresh ([McDonald, 2014](#ch29.xhtml#r675)). NLP, an artificial intelligence domain, allows for the study of large collections of text by the extraction, interpretation, and generation of human language in an efficient and objective manner ([Galanis et al., 2021](#ch29.xhtml#r664)). NLP is a powerful tool of artificial intelligence that allows computers to interpret and process human language. One of the powerful NLP methods is Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT). The model transformed text processing by learning how the words relate to one another in a sentence. In contrast to earlier models that read words from left to right, BERT reads words from both sides, left and right. This improves the word meanings depending on the text context ([Caffagni et al., 2025](#ch29.xhtml#r686)). Another NLP technique is Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), which is applied in topic modeling. LDA assists in identifying significant topics in lengthy texts by examining how frequently words occur together ([Jiang, 2024](#ch29.xhtml#r666)). Applying the models to ancient texts such as the Mahabharata opens up new avenues for studying recurring ecological patterns and sustainability concerns. Fine-tuning BERT on certain ancient languages or texts assists in achieving more profound meanings, which assists in detecting themes more effectively that conventional methods might otherwise overlook ([Sommerschield et al., 2023](#ch29.xhtml#r690)). In this research, NLP techniques such as BERT and LDA assist in examining the ecological messages in the Mahabharata. This bridges ancient wisdom with contemporary environmental concerns ([Tutrone et al., 2025](#ch29.xhtml#r684)). Using methodologies such as sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and machine learning, NLP provides researchers with structured methods of monitoring repetitive ecological themes within ancient documents, providing minute-level insights that are hard to acquire from common reading ([Tutrone et al., 2025](#ch29.xhtml#r684)).

In this study, we apply NLP techniques to analyze environmental discourses in the Mahabharata. We implement algorithms using BERT, LDA, and others to detect specific patterns in the Epic related to sustainability, resource management, and ethics concerning nature. Sentiment analysis will assist us in capturing the emotional stance toward nature in the text, whether there is reverence or concern, or nature is treated with violence and disregard. With these methodologies, the Mahabharata can be more effectively examined for the ethical and moral dilemmas posed in its text regarding nature. Ecological approaches to literature were primarily developed in response to 442.the contemporary environmental crisis ([Sherma, 2021](#ch29.xhtml#r688)). Given the severity of climate change and ongoing biodiversity crises, there is a need to interact with the past in radically different ways. Employing NLP on ancient texts like the Mahabharata opens new possibilities for deriving ecological information that can influence modern approaches to sustainability practice. Using NLP for large-scale text analysis helps researchers accurately identify patterns and recurring themes that may be overlooked. This sheds light on issues pertaining to contemporary environmental crises and provides critical, actionable knowledge. Hence, the ecological narratives of the Mahabharata serve as guides toward more effective modern sustainable practices and the management of environmental resources.

The research deepens our comprehension of the Mahabharata while simultaneously reinforcing the ancient text’s significance to contemporary environmental discourse. In the context of an age characterized by global warming, natural resource degradation, and environmental pollution, the ancient teachings of the Mahabharata offer timeless lessons on ecologically sound living. Through the recovery of these stories in the context of contemporary technology, this study demonstrates how ancient wisdom can inform contemporary attempts at solving global environmental issues. In the light of contemporary technology, the ecological stories of the Mahabharata continue to be relevant, providing us with eternal and persuasive lessons in responding to the environmental issues of the time.

## **21.2** Literature Review

The following section discusses the literature survey on the present topic. It first reviews the studies conducted on the eco-awareness in the Mahabharata, and then it explores the usage of NLP in the context of ancient texts and extends it to the usage of NLP to study the Mahabharata from a distinct perspective.

### 21.2.1 Eco-Awareness in the Mahabharata

The investigation of environmental consciousness in ancient Indian literature, specifically the Mahabharata, provides essential information on humans living in harmony with nature. [Mahata (2024)](#ch29.xhtml#r669) points out the deep respect for nature shown in ancient Indian rituals and literary texts like the Rigveda, where nature is not just a commodity but sacred. [Patra et al. (2016)](#ch29.xhtml#r689) point out the immense respect ancient Indians had for natural elements like rivers, mountains, and trees, citing interdependence as the core of Indian civilization’s development. [Prasad (2015)](#ch29.xhtml#r683) emphasizes the interdependent relationship between humankind and nature, citing the significance of the five elements as the basis for the sustenance of life, as described by the Upanishads and Bhagavad Gita that remain relevant today in environmental discourse. In the Mahabharata, [Jhaveri (2006)](#ch29.xhtml#r665) discusses the destruction of Khandav Van by Arjun and Krishna, with a conflict between forest societies and urban forces living in harmony with nature and destroying it. It is a tale that represents today’s environmental loss. [Magar (2020)](#ch29.xhtml#r668) writes about the spirituality of the ecosystem in the 443.Mahabharata, advocating harmony between *prakrti* (nature) and *purusa* (spirit) to restore cosmic order (*Rta*) and restore the environment from harm. [Indriani et al. (2023)](#ch29.xhtml#r663) write about the Pandava brothers, Nakula and Sahadewa, whose commitment to the humane treatment of animals and restoring habitats says a lot about environmental stewardship in the Mahabharata. How the two brothers interact with nature, shown as using rivers to sustain themselves, is an expression of mutual relations with the environment. [Devi and Piraji (2023)](#ch29.xhtml#r690) employ ecocriticism to illustrate how nature is represented as kindly and wrathfully in the Mahabharata, trying to bring about concordance between the natural world and humankind.

### **21.2.2** NLP in Indian Texts

Use of NLP on ancient Indian texts has become more common in recent times. This synchronizes ancient religious and cultural texts with current computer approaches. Pare Guha and Patnaik’s (n.d.) paper illustrates an NLP method for taking mindfulness into account in the Bhagavad Gita. Their paper uses tokenization, removal of stop words, and lemmatization to categorize verses in terms of states of mindfulness like awareness, concentration, and calmness. Their study synchronizes ancient spiritual texts with modern mental health practice and AI and demonstrates gaps in data and cultural sensitivities in NLP models (Pare Guha & Patnaik, n.d.). [Tuhina and Vashist (2024)](#ch29.xhtml#r693) outline how NLP supports creative writing by allowing writers to solve story issues. Their study outlines ethical issues in AI-generated literature, for instance, authorship and bias, and states how NLP can enhance creativity, enhance text accessibility through translation, and offer new methods for literary criticism. They present AI and NLP as creative work collaborators, not tools ([Tuhina & Vashist, 2024](#ch29.xhtml#r693)). Geoffrey et al. (n.d.) present an NLP tool for text summarization and processing lengthy texts. Their tool utilizes extractive and abstractive summarization techniques, supporting scholars in studying historic texts, such as texts on pandemics. Employing an analysis of Aristotle’s texts on courage, their tool demonstrates its use to contemporary global problems, for instance, the COVID-19 pandemic. This study demonstrates how AI can support humanities research and states how certain NLP algorithms are required (Geoffrey et al., n.d.). [Nigam and Chandra (2024)](#ch29.xhtml#r678) suggest “Dharmaśāstric Informatics,” a project to enhance Dharmaśāstra texts through text mining, NLP-based tokenization, sentiment analysis, and concept tagging. Their system supports bilingual searching, real-time translation, and interpretation, which support research in various fields and facilitate greater access to Sanskrit literature globally. This paper mentions the incorporation of AI for making ancient Indian scholarship more useful and accessible for scholars today ([Nigam & Chandra, 2024](#ch29.xhtml#r678)). [Miyagawa et al. (2024)](#ch29.xhtml#r676) use computer techniques like Word2Vec and stylometric analysis to analyze the Vedic Sanskrit texts, *Maitrayani Samhita* and *Kathaka Samhita*. In this paper, they show patterns of semantic similarity and editing cooperation in these texts that show how ancient texts were standardized. This paper mentions how computer techniques can complement traditional textual studies, broadening our knowledge of Vedic literature ([Miyagawa et al., 2024](#ch29.xhtml#r676)).

### **444.21.2.3** NLP in the Mahabharata

The use of NLP in the Mahabharata has introduced novel ways of searching for the epic’s social relationships, character interaction, and emotional undertones. [Mathangi (2021)](#ch29.xhtml#r692) employs NLP techniques like Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) and a locally weighted K-nearest neighbors (KNN) graph algorithm to determine the networks of characters in the Mahabharata. The research is able to identify the major social groups, including the Pandavas and the Kauravas, without knowing the roles, to prove the superiority of word vector techniques over co-occurrence analysis in representing latent character relationships. [Srijeyarankesh et al. (2022)](#ch29.xhtml#r681) shatter the horizon of sentiment and semantic analysis with the utilization of sophisticated NLP tools like BERT and GPT-2. Their work charts emotional and narrative developments over the Mahabharata, offering a computationally augmented perspective on the epic’s intricate narrative and emotional gradations. [Paul and Das (2017)](#ch29.xhtml#r693) describe character recognition as an activity facilitated by semi-supervised learning tools such as Named Entity Recognition (NER) and syntactic parsing. Their research demonstrates how Neural Net classifiers and FP-Growth algorithms enhance character recognition accuracy while facilitating a high-level examination of the epic structure of literature. [Gultepe and Mathangi (2023)](#ch29.xhtml#r666) apply quantitative social network analysis to networks of characters in the Mahabharata. Through applications of NLP techniques such as LSA and KNN, they forecast character relationships and present the social dynamic between the Pandavas and Kauravas, while demonstrating how analytical techniques can uncover complex stories and social relationships in historical writings. From the literature review, some gaps in previous research on eco-awareness in the Mahabharata and the use of NLP for processing ancient texts have been recognized. Although previous works, such as those of [Mahata (2024)](#ch29.xhtml#r669), [Patra et al. (2016)](#ch29.xhtml#r689), and [Jhaveri (2006)](#ch29.xhtml#r665), examine ecological and spiritual wisdom in the Mahabharata, they are mostly philosophical interpretations or some tales, such as the destruction of Khandav Van and the worship of nature. However, these studies do not consider a computational data-driven analysis of the thematic and emotional richness of the work. Similarly, NLP application in the analysis of the Mahabharata has primarily been limited to character analysis, sentiment mapping, and social network structures ([Mathangi, 2021](#ch29.xhtml#r692); [Gadesha et al., 2022](#ch29.xhtml#r657)) with fewer attempts at more abstract thematic representations of sustainability values or the more concrete emotional landscape of environmental stories.

## **21.3** Methodology

This study integrates NLP techniques and machine learning techniques to analyze the ecological themes of the Mahabharata. Using sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and BERT-based classification, this study provides a computational perspective on how ancient literature engages with sustainability, conservation, and ecological equilibrium. The methodology is structured as follows:

1.  *Data Collection:* The Mahabharata text is taken from a digitized.docx file. A thematic category, such as water conservation, nature preservation, and eco-spirituality, is specified in an Excel sheet along with corresponding keywords and synonyms for detailed analysis.
2.  445. *Text Preprocessing:* Using Python’s python-docx and nltk.tokenize.regexp\_tokenize, sentences are extracted for preprocessing, and normalization ensures consistency, paving the way for effective NLP processing.
3.  *Keyword Mapping:* Thematic topics and keywords from an Excel file are applied in mapping. Sentences that include keywords are selected for study to provide focus on environmental subjects.
4.  *Topic Modeling:* LDA finds topics in accordance with sustainability, with clusters shown in conservation of forest, water sustainability, and environmental cost of war.
5.  *Sentiment Analysis:* The sentiment ratings (1–5 stars) from the nlptown/bert-base-multilingual-uncased-sentiment model are categorized under negative, neutral, and positive labels to analyze the emotional tone of ecological language.
6.  *Emotion Classification:* The cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-emotion model classifies emotions (joy, sadness, fear, anger) per sentence to measure the emotional affinity towards the environment.
7.  *Output Generation:* The results are compiled into a comprehensive table containing the following data: 
    *   Sentence from the text
    *   Matched keyword
    *   Thematic class (e.g., water, conservation)
    *   Sentiment label and score
    *   Dominant emotion label
    *   Raw emotion scores This table is saved to an Excel file, ensuring transparency and reproducibility of the analysis.
8.  *Visualization:* Various visualizations, such as Sentiment distribution, emotion distribution, and word cloud, are created to present the findings.
9.  *BERT-Based Classification:* A BERT model trained on environmental texts and the Mahabharata classifies verses under the conservation and water sustainability themes. Its context sensitivity enhances accuracy to provide a nuanced classification of environmental discourse in the Mahabharata.

By combining these advanced NLP techniques, this study offers a comprehensive, computational perspective on the ecological themes in the Mahabharata. The methodology bridges the gap between ancient wisdom and contemporary environmental discussions, providing insights into the sustainability concepts embedded within the epic and their relevance to modern-day ecological concerns.

## **21.4** Findings and Discussion

### **21.4.1** Sentiment Orientation in Mahabharata’s Ecological Discourse

The emotional undertone embedded in the environmental discourses of the Mahabharata is revealed through the detailed sentiment analysis that has been conducted on the environment-related verses that are depicted in [Figure 21.1](#ch29.xhtml#f209).

![Figure 21.1 Sentiment distribution in Mahabharata.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C021_001.jpg)

**Figure 21.1** Sentiment distribution in Mahabharata.[⏎](#ch29.xhtml#f209b)

#### **446.21.4.1.1** Positive Sentiment

The results indicate a strongly positive trend in the textual treatment of nature and sustainability issues, with major but contrasting occurrences of negative and neutral sentiments. As it is visible in the sentiment distribution chart, most verses with more than 27,000 occurrences carry positive sentiment. This avalanche of positivity indicates that the Mahabharata invariably describes nature with reverence, awe, and profound moral value. Forests are not only described as geographical locations but as penitentiaries and sites of spiritual attainment. Rivers are not just bodies of water but are also worshiped as sacred mothers and givers of life. Mountains, animals, trees, and stars are threaded with spiritual, moral, and emotional stories that raise the world of nature beyond material use into the sacred. This strong positive mood indicates that nature in the Mahabharata is seen to be necessary for spiritual upliftment and moral justice. Nature has been portrayed as a being that is to be worshiped, nurtured, and thanked for, and that symbiotic interaction between man and nature is cited as an optimal condition of existence. The relentless positive emotional placement instils an ecology of reverence and a culture of sustainability decades before such notions were officially formulated.

> Sauti then said, “Having bowed down to the primordial being Isana, to whom multitudes make offerings, and who is adored by the multitude; who is the true incorruptible one, Brahma, perceptible, imperceptible, eternal; who is both a non-existing and an existing-non-existing being; who is the universe and also distinct from the existing and non-existing universe; who is the creator of high and low; the ancient, exalted, inexhaustible one; who is Vishnu, beneficent and the beneficence itself, worthy of all preference, pure and immaculate; who is Hari, the ruler of the faculties, the guide of all things moveable and immoveable; I will declare the sacred thoughts of the illustrious sage Vyasa, of marvellous deeds and worshipped here by all.”

This statement is positive because it praises and reveres the divine qualities of Isana (a form of Shiva), describing him as incorruptible, eternal, pure, and beneficent. 447.The language used emphasizes his supreme, exalted nature and his role as the creator and ruler of all, highlighting his sacredness and importance in the cosmic order. The description reflects deep admiration, reverence, and spiritual awe, all of which contribute to the positive tone.

#### **21.4.1.2** Negative Sentiments

Conversely, around 12,000 verses were tagged with negative tones. These accounts point to situations where natural balance was disrupted, usually as the result of greed by humans, war, or ethical violations. Forest fires, rivers drying up, pollution of holy places, and accounts of famine and ecological catastrophes are included under this category. The negative sentiment proportion highlights the Mahabharata’s sharp consciousness of the vulnerability of environmental systems and acts as a story that cautions against environmental abuse. The emotional representation of ruin or abandonment of nature contains a hidden moral teaching: the violation of nature causes spiritual and social collapse.

> To frighten one that has sought protection, the slaying of a woman, the theft of what belongs to a Brahmana, and injuring a friend, each of these four, O Shakra, is I think equal to the abandonment of one that is devoted.

This is a negative statement because it depicts deeds that are ethically and morally incorrect, such as killing a woman, robbing a Brahmana, and wounding a friend. These acts are seen as highly harmful and unfair, showing a breach of social and moral standards. The alignment with leaving someone devoted further highlights the seriousness and negativity of such actions.

#### **21.4.1.3** Neutral Sentiments

Neutral feeling, in the sense of less than 5,000 lines, is modest relative to the negative and the positive. These lines are typically matter-of-fact descriptions or ritual allusions to nature with no apparent appeal on any emotional level. The neutral tone appears in lines describing the flora and fauna of some countries, the cycles of the seasons, or the scope of kingdoms’ geography. Although emotionally withdrawn, these lines contribute by creating a vivid environmental scene and thereby displaying the omnipresence as well as prominence of natural phenomena within the epic world.

> Not having been able to devise any other means, I entered myself for the purpose of preventing the water running out.

The sentence has neutral polarity as it only reports an action done without expressing any strong emotion or value judgment, concentrating on a utilitarian choice made in a circumstance.

Analyzing the polarity of sentiment in such a manner discovers that the ecological discourse of the Mahabharata is not one-dimensional but complex and dynamic, and that it can experience awe, reverence, caution, sorrow, and neutrality. The dominance of positive sentiment overwhelmingly points toward a pervasive philosophy of ecological reverence and harmony. Sentiment analysis indicates the ways in which the ecological narratives in the Mahabharata are not simply tales of 448.the environment but also place the environment emotionally at the heart of a moral lifestyle. By putting high positive and negative emotions in positions surrounding environmental dilemmas, the narrative produces a moral imagination by which sustainability, harmony, and harmony with nature are organic values. Thus, affective mapping described through sentiment orientation evokes an ancient but infinitely nuanced environmental sensitivity one which remains hugely pertinent to our contemporary ecological debates.

### **21.4.2** Thematic Representation of Sustainability Concepts

A thorough scrutiny of the responses of the Mahabharata on emphasizing environmental themes through classes of sustainability reveals the preference order of various environmental concerns. The way various ecological ideas were given preference by means of the complex network of narration in the epic is reflected by the spread of classes of sustainability, as depicted in [Figure 21.2](#ch29.xhtml#f210). The most predominant theme among all the categories is eco-spirituality, taking up a majority percentage of categorized verses.

![Figure 21.2 Distribution of sustainability classes in Mahabharata.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C021_002.jpg)

**Figure 21.2** Distribution of sustainability classes in Mahabharata.[⏎](#ch29.xhtml#f210b)

This ubiquitous presence informs us that the Mahabharata incessantly interlaces environmental elements with spirituality, morality, and cosmic responsibility. Nature in the book is often not a passive setting, but an energetic partner linked with the attainment of dharma (righteous duty). Forests are described as heavenly abodes of sages, rivers as goddesses, and creatures as heavenly friends. The pervasiveness of eco-spirituality shows that sustainability in ancient philosophy was inseparably intertwined with religious sensitivity, where environmental stewardship was a religious responsibility and not a material issue.

> I was formerly a Rishi by name Sahasrapat. And it is by the curse of a Brahmana that I have been transformed into a snake.
> 
> *Adi Parva*

449.This verse mentions the transformation of human into snake reflecting the interconnectedness between human beings and animals and how they get transformed into each other based on their deeds.

> At the command of Pashupati, that Lord of all creatures, I am ready to become a worm or a tree with many branches directed to things that are the result of the attributes of Sattwa, Rajas, and Tamas.
> 
> *Anushashana Parva*

Similarly, this verse reflects the concept of eco-spirituality, where the speaker expresses a willingness to merge with nature, transcending human identity to embody any life form within the cosmic order. It signifies the interconnectedness of all beings and the fluidity of existence, emphasizing the harmony between the soul and the natural world, governed by the three gunas (Sattwa, Rajas, and Tamas).

In the wake of eco-spirituality, the second overarching theme is Water Sustainability. The Mahabharata gives enormous importance to rivers, lakes, and holy water bodies, acknowledging their vital function in sustaining life, agriculture, and ritual purity. The salience of water motifs indicates an early recognition of water as a key ecological and spiritual resource. Narratives highlighting the holiness of rivers, cleansing through sacred dips, and punishment for contaminating water bodies as a whole show a story that encourages water conservation as a moral necessity.

> I am Ganga, the daughter of Jahnu. I am ever worshipped by the great sages; I have lived with thee so long for accomplishing the purposes of the celestials.
> 
> *Adi Parva*

In the context of water spirituality, this verse personifies the Ganga as a divine, sacred entity with a vital role in the cosmic order. Revered by sages and associated with celestial purposes, the Ganga symbolizes the purifying, life-sustaining, and spiritually elevating power of water, embodying its sacred nature and its deep connection to both earthly and spiritual realms.

> The divine and illustrious Ocean then that lord of male and female rivers, surrounded by aquatic animals, appeared unto Rama in a vision. And addressing Rama in sweet accents, the genius of the Ocean, surrounded by countless mines of gems, said…
> 
> *Vana Parva*

This verse highlights the ocean as a divine and revered entity, symbolizing the vast, life-giving, and mysterious nature of water. The ocean, personified as a powerful deity surrounded by aquatic creatures and treasures, speaks to Rama, embodying the sacred and essential role of water in sustaining life, wealth, and spiritual balance. The ocean’s presence emphasizes the interconnectedness between nature, spirituality, and human life.

“Then those foremost of car-warriors (Krishna and Arjuna), riding in their cars and placing themselves on opposite sides of that forest, began a great slaughter, on all sides, of the creatures dwelling in Khandava” (Sabha Parva). This verse symbolizes the violent disruption of nature, where Krishna and Arjuna’s act of slaughtering the 450.creatures in the Khandava forest represents the destructive consequences of human actions on the environment. The forest, often seen as a sacred space in Indian spiritual thought, is destroyed as part of a larger cosmic order, highlighting the tension between the preservation and destruction of natural resources, and the karmic repercussions of such acts.

> Sanjaya said, “When the weapon called Narayana was invoked, violent. winds began to blow with showers of rain, and peals of thunder were heard. although the sky was cloudless. The earth trembled, and the seas swelled up in agitation. The rivers began to run in a contrary course. The summits of mountains, O Bharata, began to split. Diverse animals began to pass by the left side of the Pandavas. Darkness set in; the sun became obscure. Diverse kinds of carnivorous creatures began to alight on the field in joy. The gods, the Danavas, and the Gandharvas, O monarch, all became inspired with fear. Beholding that tremendous agitation (in nature), all began to ask one another loudly about its …”
> 
> *Drona Parva*

This verse symbolizes the catastrophic effects of human actions driven by violence and war, as exemplified by the invocation of the Narayana weapon. The violent natural upheavals—such as the reversal of rivers, earthquakes, and the appearance of carnivorous creatures—represent the environmental disasters that arise when humans disrupt the natural balance.

> And they also saw hillocks teeming with various minerals, thronged with Vidyadharas, inhabited on all sides by monkeys and Kinnaras and Kimpurushas, and Gandharvas, and filled with peacocks, and chamaras, and apes, and rurus, and bears, and gavayas, and buffaloes, intersected with a network of rivulets, and inhabited by various birds and beasts, and beautified by elephants, and abounding in trees and enraptured birds. After having thus passed many countries, and the Uttarakurus, they saw that foremost of mountains, the Kailasa, containing many wonders. And by the side of it, they beheld the hermitage of Nara and Narayana, with celestial trees bearing flowers and fruits in all seasons.

This verse portrays an idyllic, vibrant ecosystem, teeming with diverse flora and fauna, where nature flourishes harmoniously. The forest, inhabited by various creatures and beautified by celestial trees, symbolizes an untouched, sacred space that nurtures life in balance. The presence of divine hermitages further emphasizes the sacred and spiritual significance of such natural environments in ancient thought. Finally, thematic mapping discloses a hierarchy of sustenance in the Mahabharata:

*   Eco-spirituality
*   Water
*   Disaster
*   Agriculture and forests

451.This thematic emphasis is a deep insight into ancient Indian ecological philosophy, suggesting that environmental awareness must be situated in religious and moral contexts, and not merely viewed as a problem of utility.

### **21.4.3** Lexical Patterns across Ecological Domains

[Figure 21.3](#ch29.xhtml#f211) depicts the lexical patterns analysis via visualization through a word cloud, which adds additional depth to examining the way Mahabharata expresses its ecological awareness. Identification of the highest frequency words tied to sustainability courses enables us to determine the critical environmental themes as well as emotive connotations prioritized throughout the epic. The word cloud of the classified environmental texts highlights words like “earth,” “river,” “forest,” “tree,” “fire,” “ocean,” “sacred,” and “destruction” prominently. The size and density of these words in the visualization are a measure of their high frequency and thematic relevance in the narratives of sustainability. The word “earth” occupies the center of this lexical field with its double connotation of the physical and spiritual sense of the earth. The Earth is repeatedly anthropomorphized as a mother in the Mahabharata, as it represents care, endurance, and strength. Its prevalence reinforces the strong ecological roots of the text, where ecological health is inextricably linked to human moral action. In the same vein, the word “river” is repeated, testifying to the exceptional focus on water bodies in the ecological vision. Rivers are always sanctified as life-givers, sites of ritual purification, and sources of spiritual sustenance. The repeated reference to rivers like the Ganga, Yamuna, and the Saraswati is a pointer to the fact that water sustainability was not an empirical requirement but a deep spiritual interest. The occurrence of words like “forest” and “tree” is an indicator of the centrality of terrestrial ecologies. Forests are defined as sacred grounds for learning, contemplation, and shelter. The repeated use of trees symbolically and functionally bears witness to an appreciation for biodiversity and its value in the sustenance of ecological balance. 452.Noticeably, the terms “destruction” and “fire” also repeat, particularly in the disaster sustainability class. These terms are most likely to point to catastrophic events, such as the burning of the Khandava forest to destruction or other stories of environmental destruction due to human activity. Their use bears witness to an ecological vocabulary that recognizes destruction as real and regrettable consequences of disrespect for natural order. The second omnipresent category includes terms such as “sacred,” “divine,” and “purity,” which still bear witness to the fact that ecological objects were described mainly in a spiritual and moral vocabulary. Nature was not only sensed; it was also respected, whose preservation was part of religious obligations and cosmic order. Finally, the lexical density provided in the word cloud provides a solid measure of the Mahabharata’s rich ecological vocabulary. It shows that concerns about sustainability were expressed not only through explicit vocabulary but also through a deep symbolic environmental vocabulary that always points to nature’s existential and spiritual value.

![Figure 21.3 Lexical patterns across ecological domains in Mahabharata.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C021_003.jpg)

**Figure 21.3** Lexical patterns across ecological domains in Mahabharata.[⏎](#ch29.xhtml#f211b)

The word cloud indicates the Mahabharata’s environmental imagination, with expansive vision, emotional tone, and intense engagement with its cosmological and moral systems.

### **21.4.4** Emotional Narratives across Sustainability Classes

The emotional distribution across various classes of sustainability in the Mahabharata shows a nuanced emotional involvement with nature. By mapping common emotions like optimism, anger, sadness, and happiness against major ecological themes, the study offers a richer insight into how emotions were tactically deployed to communicate ecological stories. [Figure 21.4](#ch29.xhtml#f212) shows the dominant emotion linked with each class of sustainability, indicating how the epic imbues various aspects of environmental discourse with emotional meaning.

![Figure 21.4 Dominant emotion per sustainability class in Mahabharata.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C021_004.jpg)

**Figure 21.4** Dominant emotion per sustainability class in Mahabharata.[⏎](#ch29.xhtml#f212b)

453.The eco-spirituality course is optimistic in nature. This association is based on the tacit assumption that nature’s harmony contributes to spiritual fulfillment and social welfare. Hymns honoring sacred forests, holy brooks, and the earth mother’s powers of life evoke a bright and optimistic vision in which ecological balance is possible and desirable. Eco-spirituality’s optimism would have us believe that the ancient mind perceived sustainability as an effortless and delightful responsibility harmonizing with cosmic structure. In sharp contrast, the Water Sustainability class is overwhelmingly marked with anger. Such an emotional response arises out of stories pertaining to the desecration, misuse, or pollution of bodies of water, which was a serious transgression. Rivers within the Mahabharata are not just life-giving but also spiritually cleansing, and desecration gives rise to divine anger or catastrophes. The affective association of water passages with the emotion of anger indicates a sharp moral awareness about environmental degradation, particularly about life-sustaining resources. The disaster class is associated with sadness. Natural disasters such as floods and droughts, as well as environmental disasters that follow wars, are described with an immense sense of sorrow and mourning. Sadness here denotes the human and environmental cost of unsustainable activities, the loss of nature as a loss to the moment as well as to the future. This emotional assignment compels us to realize that nature is overlooked at the expense of irreparable damage and collective sorrow.

The emotional mapping, therefore, shows that the ecological stories in the Mahabharata are both emotionally dense and strategically subtle. Hope, ire, grief, and joy are not randomly distributed but rather expertly paired with thematic concerns for the purpose of underscoring the moral and existential significance of environmental care. Moreover, the range of feelings underscores that ancient ecological thinking recognized both the reward and the hazard of human activity towards nature. Happiness and optimism reward respect and harmony; fury and grief sanction abuse and desertion. This affective system is a moral compass guiding behavior toward environmentally ethical ethics. So, the affective stories mapped over sustainability classes reveal that the Mahabharata’s green imagination was affectively intelligent, using affective storying to engender a deep, abiding sense of environmental consciousness. By emotion, the epic not merely informs us about nature but, in fact, engages human feeling in aid of sustainability.

### **21.4.5** The Mahabharata’s Environmental Legacy: Ecological Lessons for the Present and Future

The present analysis of the ecological tales in the Mahabharata yields several significant conclusions that are directly supported by present scholarly readings of the text. By sentiment orientation analysis, thematic representation, lexical patterns, and emotional profiling, the epic is found to be a valuable source of ecological knowledge. Correlation of the findings with present scholarly work enriches the comprehension of the environmental consciousness of the Mahabharata.

454.455.456.First, the dominance of a positive tone in the sustainability-linked stanzas reinforces the Mahabharata’s thoughtful attitude toward nature. This is corroborated by [Magar (2020)](#ch29.xhtml#r668), who elucidates those ancient Indian scriptures, such as the Mahabharata, consider nature holy, calling for a spiritual relationship with nature as opposed to an exploitative one ([Magar, 2020](#ch29.xhtml#r668)). [Correspondingly, Indriani et al. (2023)](#ch29.xhtml#r663) also contend that characters such as the Pandavas show a deep concern for nature, employing it respectfully for sustenance without exploiting it ([Indriani et al., 2023](#ch29.xhtml#r657)). The positive representation of forests, rivers, and the earth in the epic, therefore, supports the principle of spiritual ecology manifested throughout the scholarship.

Second, thematic analysis revealed eco-spirituality as the most prevalent sustainability class, followed by Water, Disaster, Forest, and Agriculture. This thematic spread is supported by [Brodbeck (2024)](#ch29.xhtml#r660), who explains how the Mahabharata depicts the Earth as a living, sentient being enmeshed with cosmic cycles ([Brodbeck, 2024](#ch29.xhtml#r660)). The complaints made by the Earth to Brahma about being burdened demonstrate the sacred treatment of terrestrial life. [Prasad (2015)](#ch29.xhtml#r683) stresses that ancient Indian philosophy considered Earth and water to be the quintessence of life, which incorporated ecological components into human bodily and spiritual existence. The eco-spirituality at the center of the Mahabharata thus concurs with such perceptions, confirming that sustainability was inextricably linked with ethical and spiritual responsibilities.

Third, lexical examination of nature tales with such words as “earth,” “river,” “forest,” and “sacred” shows that ecological respect was inscribed in the language. [Jhaveri (2006)](#ch29.xhtml#r665) explains how the Mahabharata uses vivid tales of environmental desecration, especially in such incidents as the burning of Khandava forest, to create strong emotional reactions against environmental degradation ([Jhaveri, 2006](#ch29.xhtml#r665)). This intentional use of language supports the emotional, ethical, and spiritual weight given to ecological events, which is consistent with the results of the word cloud analysis.

Additionally, the emotional mapping showed a strong emotional leaning toward various sustainability classes, with optimism prevailing in eco-spirituality, anger in water themes, sadness in disaster narratives, and joy in forest and agriculture themes. This observation is corroborated by [Indriani et al. (2023)](#ch29.xhtml#r663), who point out that the Pandavas’ relationship with nature was not transactional but emotional and spiritual in nature, encompassing respect, gratitude, and grief during ecological loss ([Indriani et al., 2023](#ch29.xhtml#r663)). Likewise, [Brodbeck (2024)](#ch29.xhtml#r660) reveals that the planet’s lamentations and the accounts of cosmic devastation during the end of yugas are recounted in a mixture of sorrow, urgency, and spiritual seriousness ([Brodbeck, 2024](#ch29.xhtml#r660)). The emotional richness of the Mahabharata’s ecological stories is therefore immediately reflected in academic accounts.

In an extension to modern contexts, the spiritual ecology within the Mahabharata differs significantly from the anthropocentric worldview decried by [Magar (2020)](#ch29.xhtml#r668), according to whom environmental crises in modern times are rooted in the forfeiture of spiritual respect for nature ([Magar, 2020](#ch29.xhtml#r668)). The interconnectedness of nature, humankind, and the universe argued by [Prasad (2015),](#ch29.xhtml#r683) also attests that there is no separation of ecological well-being and human moral action ([Prasad, 2015](#ch29.xhtml#r683)). The Mahabharata’s illustration of environmental degradation as morally significant 457.also further highlights the significance of ancient ecological thinking in responding to environmental issues today. Lastly, the research findings here: dominance of positive sentiment, eco-spirituality as a central theme, environmentally embedded reverence linguistically, and emotional richness in narratives are all reinforced by previous research. Taken together, they affirm that the Mahabharata offers an integral model of sustainability based on spirituality, emotionalism, and moral accountability to nature, containing useful lessons that remain relevant to the contemporary world.

## 21.6 CONCLUSION

To conclude, this research reveals four major findings on the ecological themes in the Mahabharata. First, the pervasive recurrence of a positive tone in sustainability-related verses strengthens the epic’s spiritual and respectful attitude towards nature. The Mahabharata portrays nature as sacred, focusing on a symbiotic relationship between nature and human beings and not one of exploitation. Second, thematic analysis reiterates that eco-spirituality is the most prominent sustainability class, followed by water, disaster, forest, and agriculture. One of the epic’s best representations of deep ecological consciousness is the depiction of the Earth as a conscious and living entity linked to cosmic cycles. The dignified treatment of the Earth, apart from the sanctification of natural forces such as water and forests, emphasizes the central importance of nature in moral and spiritual life. Third, the lexical analysis of ecological narratives demonstrates that the vocabulary used in the Mahabharata reflects profound respect for nature, hence the ethical and emotional responses to environmental degradation. The detailed description of the destruction of the environment, particularly the conflagration of the Khandava forest, evokes powerful emotional reactions and highlights the urgent need for the conservation of nature. Lastly, the affective cartography of environmental issues illustrates multi-colored emotional colors optimism in the scenario of eco-spirituality, anger in the scenario of water, grief in the scenario of disaster, and joy in the scenario of forest and agriculture. These emotional foundations show how the characters are spiritually and emotionally connected to their surroundings.

Together, these results suggest that the Mahabharata offers a spirituality-based methodology for considering environmental sustainability. It offers perceptive advice on sustainable moral and affective responses to nature. These results also offer the promise of additional research on how the Mahabharata’s environmental lessons can be applied to inform current environmental policy, especially in terms of planning for sustainable resources. Besides that, future research on how ancient documents can help address modern environmentalism can also contribute to insight into how ancient understanding can help confront modern ecological crises. A comparative study of other ancient cultural books with each other can also bring insight into how universal sustainability themes and eco-spirituality exist across all cultures. Finally, studies on how the ecological ideas of the Mahabharata can be compared to modern environmental literature and philosophy can prove to be of great help for environmental thought today.

# 461.22Artificial Intelligence-Powered Animal Intrusion Detection for Preventing Vehicle Collisions and Agricultural Damage

Shobha Rani B.R. and Hemanth L.

DOI: [10.1201/9781003634768-22](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003634768-22)

## **22.1** Introduction

Collisions between animals and vehicles near roads and forest reserves are causing increasing concerns, inflicting significant damage on both human and animal populations. These occurrences result in fatalities, injuries, and considerable property damage. Roads commonly intersect or border wildlife areas, leading to animals wandering into highways, particularly at night or during migration, hence heightening the danger of collisions. Traditional safety measures, like animal crossing signs, are ineffective, as they do not offer real-time notifications, leaving vehicles oblivious to impending dangers.

This research presents an automated method utilizing Internet of Things (IoT) for monitoring wildlife encroachment, facilitating real-time decision-making and precise outcomes through deep neural networks for immediate detection. The system utilizes interconnected equipment such as sensors and cameras to notify drivers and authorities upon detecting animals near roadways, thereby reducing the likelihood of collisions. The system comprises motion detectors that detect movement and cameras that record pictures, which are analyzed using machine learning models to verify the presence of animals.

A vital component of the system is the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, which serves as the control unit. To enhance safety, the system triggers both visual and audible alerts when an animal is detected. A loud buzzer warns nearby drivers, while an LED light offers a visual signal, particularly useful in low-visibility conditions such as fog or nighttime driving. These warnings give drivers enough time to slow down or stop, preventing a collision and safeguarding wildlife. By combining IoT and deep 462.learning, the system provides a scalable and cost-effective solution to a significant safety concern.

MobileNet Single Shot Multibox Detector (SSD) is essential for real-time animal detection due to its ability to deliver fast and accurate object detection. Optimized for mobile and embedded systems, it is a perfect match for the Raspberry Pi, as it operates efficiently on low-power devices. The model, pre-trained on large datasets, is further refined to detect both domestic and wild animals that are common in deployment areas. This allows the system to perform real-time analysis without requiring extensive computational power, making it suitable for continuous use in the field.

Use of a Raspberry Pi as the central device makes the system more versatile and affordable. Known for its energy efficiency and processing capabilities, the Raspberry Pi is well-suited for real-time deep learning tasks. Additionally, the Ethernet connectivity of the Raspberry Pi ensures stable network communication, which allows data transmission and remote monitoring. This feature could be integrated with cloud platforms to monitor multiple systems deployed across different regions, further extending the system’s usefulness.

## **22.2** Literature Review

The integration of IoT and deep learning in animal detection systems has advanced significantly in recent years, enabling real-time monitoring and decision-making across a variety of applications. Several researchers have contributed to this domain, focusing on both efficiency and accuracy.

This paper \[[1](#ch30.xhtml#r694)\] explores the integration of IoT with deep learning in animal detection systems, emphasizing real-time monitoring capabilities that enhance wildlife management and reduce human-wildlife conflict. The author \[[1](#ch30.xhtml#r694)–[3](#ch30.xhtml#r696)\] presented an IoT-based smart animal detection system that utilizes continuous data transmission to monitor animal movements in agricultural areas, allowing immediate alerts to prevent potential damage.

This paper \[[4](#ch30.xhtml#r697), [5](#ch30.xhtml#r698)\] explains the application of deep learning in real-time animal detection, focusing on a surveillance system that employs convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for accurate classification. Their approach effectively addresses challenges such as varying lighting conditions and occlusion, thus improving the reliability of animal detection in dynamic environments.

Deer-vehicle collision prevention system uses deep learning techniques \[[6](#ch30.xhtml#r699)\] for animal detection. Deep learning models, particularly CNN-based methods, can effectively detect deer and reduce accidents. Effective use of deep learning in preventing wildlife-vehicle collisions provides a real-time detection system.

Animal detection is done using a deep learning algorithm \[[7](#ch30.xhtml#r700)\] to identify animals in various environments. Animal detection using CNNs achieved high accuracy, with models like MobileNet being well-suited for mobile systems. Deep learning provides a scalable solution for animal detection with high accuracy for different species.

Deep learning object-detection methods \[[8](#ch30.xhtml#r701)\] apply deep learning to object detection in ecological camera trap data for ecological camera trap data. Models like YOLO 463.and Faster R-CNN outperform traditional methods for ecological object detection tasks. Deep learning enhances ecological monitoring by improving object detection from camera traps.

Challenges and opportunities in animal detection and tracking with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs): a comprehensive review \[[9](#ch30.xhtml#r702)\] studied UAV-based animal detection and tracking methods using deep learning. UAVs combined with deep learning show potential in real-time animal tracking, despite challenges like battery life. UAVs equipped with deep learning algorithms offer efficient animal detection and tracking solutions.

Real-time object detection for Raspberry Pi-based IoT applications uses a Tiny-YOLOv4 model \[[10](#ch30.xhtml#r703)\]. Tiny-YOLOv4 provides a lightweight, real-time object detection solution that is efficient on resource-limited devices. Tiny-YOLOv4 is highly effective for real-time object detection in IoT applications due to its low computational requirements.

Earlier studies \[[11](#ch30.xhtml#r704)–[14](#ch30.xhtml#r707)\] outline a novel framework for developing an animal intrusion detection system that leverages deep learning techniques. This work emphasizes the critical role of computer vision in enhancing detection accuracy, thereby addressing key security issues faced in wildlife monitoring and conservation. The proposed system aims to facilitate real-time detection and response, significantly improving the efficacy of existing methods.

Lastly, another study \[[15](#ch30.xhtml#r708)\] focused on creating a fine-grained dataset specifically for the re-identification of elephants. This dataset serves as a valuable resource for wildlife monitoring applications, supporting the development of more effective identification and tracking systems. By providing a robust foundation for training deep learning models, this research contributes to ongoing efforts in wildlife conservation and monitoring.

These studies collectively emphasize the significance of integrating IoT and deep learning to develop sophisticated animal detection systems. The literature reveals a growing trend toward implementing intelligent systems that enhance real-time detection capabilities, providing sustainable and efficient solutions applicable in various domains, including agriculture, forestry, and autonomous vehicle navigation.

## **22.3** Methodology

An artificial intelligence (AI)-based animal intrusion detection system works in three stages. Stage 1 works with IoT sensors to check the movement of the animals near the roads and in the farmlands and sends the data to the deep learning model for identification and classification. Stage 2 consists of receiving the data from the IoT sensor model and training the deep learning model for the classification and identification of animals. Next, stage 3 uses IoT sensors with Buzzers and LEDs, helping the drivers to avoid collisions on roads, sends the message to the forest authorities, and alarms the villagers with automated lighting to reduce crop destruction.

### **464.465.22.3.1** System Architecture

The block diagram of the animal intrusion-detection system shown in [Figure 22.1](#ch30.xhtml#f213) depicts the main components that interact within the device. It starts with inputs from passive infrared (PIR) sensors and cameras that continuously capture video or detect motion. The video feed is then sent to the processing unit, usually a Raspberry Pi, where the data undergoes preprocessing and analysis using the machine learning model, like MobileNet SSD, to identify animals. When an animal is detected, the system activates an alert mechanism, which may include a buzzer, LED, or digital notifications sent to drivers. The diagram visually illustrates the collaboration between hardware and software components to enable real-time detection and alerting.

![Figure 22.1 System architecture.⏎](html/images/9781041062943_C022_001.jpg)

**Figure 22.1** System architecture.[⏎](#ch30.xhtml#f213b)

The proposed animal intrusion detection system combines IoT components with deep learning technology to create a real-time, responsive system that detects animals near roadways and issues immediate alerts to drivers. The system starts with a PIR sensor that detects motion, particularly sensitive to the heat signatures of animals. When the sensor identifies movement, it signals a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to activate a Pi Camera, which captures images/videos of the surrounding area. The captured images are then analyzed using a deep learning-based object detection model, specifically MobileNet SSD, which is pre-trained to recognize various objects and fine-tuned to focus on identifying animals. If an animal is detected, the system triggers both a buzzer and an LED light, alerting drivers and authorities to the presence of an animal on or near the road.

### **22.3.2** SSD-MobileNet Architecture

A SSD framework detects the real-time animals efficiently in comparison with traditional detectors such as Faster R-CNN. The SSD architecture is a singular convolutional network that simultaneously predicts bounding box locations and classifies these sites in a single run. SSD model with MobileNet architecture is efficient with instant alerts in road safety alerts and automated response with rapid classification in animal detection.

466.A CNN with ResNet as its backbone is employed to extract significant characteristics from an input picture. The convolutional layers draw bounding boxes on the input image to recognize various animals of differing sizes, accompanied by class scores. An anchor box with a high confidence score helps to plot the bounding box around the animal effectively by suppressing anchor boxes drawn around other features.

### **22.3.3** Animal Detection Module

At the core of the animal intrusion detection system lies the animal detection module, which leverages state-of-the-art deep learning techniques for real-time animal identification. This module utilizes the MobileNet SSD model, which is pre-trained on the COCO dataset—a comprehensive dataset containing images of various objects, including animals. This enables the system to achieve high accuracy in detecting different animal species. The camera module plays a crucial role by capturing continuous video footage of the surroundings. As the video streams in, it is processed by the MobileNet SSD model, which analyzes each frame for the presence of animals. Upon successful detection, the system takes immediate action, such as saving the video clip for documentation and triggering alert mechanisms. The entire processing task is efficiently handled by the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, which acts as the central processing unit, ensuring smooth operation and prompt responses to detected intrusions.

### **22.3.4** Motion Detection System

Complementing the animal detection capabilities, the Motion Detection System utilizes a PIR sensor to monitor environmental movement. This sensor is designed to detect variations in infrared radiation, which occurs when objects move within its range. When the PIR sensor identifies movement, it sends a signal to the system, prompting it to activate the camera and initiate the video recording process. The data from the PIR sensor is continuously monitored by the Microcontroller, which ensures that the system responds quickly to any potential intrusions. In addition to video recording, an LED Indicator provides a visual cue to indicate that motion has been detected. Simultaneously, a Buzzer emits an audible alert, notifying nearby individuals of the detected activity, thereby enhancing awareness of potential animal presence in the vicinity.

### **22.3.5** Alert and Notification System

The Alert and Notification System serves a vital role in communicating detected animal intrusions to relevant stakeholders. Once the detection algorithm identifies an animal, the system can initiate an alert to ensure that appropriate actions are taken. This alert mechanism may involve sending real-time notifications to predefined contacts through various communication channels, such as SMS or email. The integration of a Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) module enables SMS 467.notifications to be sent directly to mobile phones, providing immediate updates on animal activity. Alternatively, cloud services can be utilized for email alerts, allowing for comprehensive documentation of the incident. To further enhance situational awareness, both the buzzer and a secondary LED indicator are activated when an animal is detected, alerting individuals nearby to the potential risk of animal intrusion.

### **22.3.6** Video Recording and Storage

The Video Recording and Storage module is designed to optimize storage efficiency by recording video footage only when animals are detected. This selective recording ensures that valuable storage space on the Raspberry Pi is not wasted on unnecessary footage. The recorded videos are saved in MP4 format, a widely accepted format that balances quality and file size. The storage location is specifically set to the /home/pi/Desktop directory on the Raspberry Pi, allowing for easy access and retrieval of recorded footage. By retaining videos only when significant events occur, the system not only conserves storage space but also facilitates future analysis and documentation of animal intrusions. This functionality is crucial for understanding patterns of animal behavior and for developing strategies to mitigate potential collisions.

This comprehensive methodology highlights the systematic approach taken in developing the animal intrusion detection system, emphasizing its various components and their integration to enhance safety and effectiveness in managing animal presence near roadways.

## **22.4** Implementation

For implementation, we need to consider software that needs to be integrated into our Raspberry Pi modules. As we know, Raspberry Pi is a mini computer, we need an operating system for the same. Raspbian Buster OS is an ideal operating system for our Raspberry Pi module. For ease, we can opt for installing it on an SD Card using Raspberry Pi Imager. In the proposed system, as we need to access just the command lines, we can download and install the lite version instead of the user interface.

### **22.4.1** Data Preparation

Developing an animal intrusion detection system depends critically on data preparation, which guarantees the model’s dependability and correctness. Model is trained on COCO dataset, which contains labelled images of various animals. To refine the model’s performance, annotations are checked and upgraded using Labeling, guaranteeing high-quality labeling of the existing data and enabling the insertion of more photos if needed. Data augmentation techniques, like as rotation and scaling, are utilized to boost dataset variety, enabling the model to adapt better to varied real-world settings. The dataset is subsequently separated into training, validation, and testing subsets, which promotes successful model training and assessment. Normalization and preparation techniques, like shrinking photos and scaling pixel values, normalize the input data for effective learning.

### **468.22.4.2** Developing the Animal Detector Model

Building the animal detector involves integrating various components and technologies to create a reliable and efficient system for identifying animals in real time. At the core of this process is the MobileNet SSD model, which is trained using the COCO dataset to recognize various animal species accurately. The system initiates by recording video footage via a camera module, which transmits the pictures to the MobileNet SSD model for processing. This model uses deep learning methodologies to examine the frames and identify animals according to established characteristics. To improve detection efficacy, the system employs methods like non-maximum suppression to remove redundant detections and guarantee that only the most pertinent data are preserved.

The depth-wise separate cost is given by Equation 22.1 where depth-wise convolution is applied to each filter and point-wise convolution is applied to output channels.

*C*[*f* ]\* *C*[*f*] \* *M* \* *C*[*k* ]\* *C*[*k*] + *C*[*f* ]\* *C*[*f*] \* *M* \* *N* (22.1) where *C*[*f* ] *C*[*f*] are feature maps,  *C*[*k* ]\* *C*[*k*] are 3 \* 3  kernel size *M* is number of input channels and *N* is number of output channels. 

MobileNet employs ReLU6 in place of conventional ReLU as given in Equation 22.2. By clipping activation values at 6, it offers non-linearity similar to regular ReLU, encourages computational efficiency in low-precision calculation, and uses value bounds to help avoid overfitting.

*f*(*x*) = min(max(0,*x*),6) (22.2) 

The processed output elicits suitable actions, like the activation of warning systems or the capturing of video footage upon the detection of animals. The animal detector efficiently tackles the issue of monitoring animal invasions and activates alert mechanisms or recording video clips by integrating advanced machine learning algorithms with real-time video processing, therefore enhancing safety in regions susceptible to animal–vehicle collisions.

By combining robust machine learning algorithms with real-time video processing, the animal detector effectively addresses the challenge of monitoring animal intrusions, ultimately contributing to improved safety in areas prone to animal–vehicle collisions.

### **22.4.3** Training Objective

The training objective of SSD is derived from the MultiBox objective \[[7](#ch30.xhtml#r700), [8](#ch30.xhtml#r701)\] but is extended to handle multiple object categories. Let *x*[*i**j* ]^(*p*) = {1, 0} be an indicator for matching the *i*th default box to the *j*th ground truth box of category *p*, *c*[*i*]^(*p*) is the predicted confidence (after softmax) for class *p* at position *I* and *c*[*i*]⁰  is the predicted confidence (after softmax) for the background class.

470.471.In the matching strategy above, we can have Pi *x*[*i**j* ]^(*p*) ≥ 1. The overall objective loss function given in Equation 22.3 is a weighted sum of the localization loss (loc) and the confidence loss (conf).

$L\\left( {x,c,l,g} \\right) = \\frac{1}{N}\\left( {L\_{conf}\\left( {x,c} \\right) + \\propto L\_{loc}\\left( {x,l,g} \\right)} \\right)$ (22.3) 

where *N* is the number of matched default boxes. If *N* = 0, we set the loss to 0. The localization loss is a Smooth L1 loss \[[6](#ch30.xhtml#r699)\] between the predicted box (*l*) and the ground truth box (*g*) parameters. Similar to Faster R-CNN \[[4](#ch30.xhtml#r697)\], we regress to offsets for the center (*cx*, *cy*) of the default bounding box (*d*) and for its width (*w*) and height (*h*).

The confidence loss in Equation 22.4 is the softmax loss over multiple classes’ confidences (*c*), and the weight term *α* is set to 1 by cross-validation.

$L\_{conf}\\left( {x,c} \\right) = - \\sum\\limits\_{i \\in Pos}^{N}x\_{ij}^{p}\\log\\left( c\_{i}^{p} \\right) - \\sum\\limits\_{i \\in Neg}\\log\\left( c\_{i}^{0} \\right)\\text{where~}c\_{i}^{p} = \\frac{\\text{exp}\\left( c\_{i}^{p} \\right)}{\\sum\_{p}\\text{exp}\\left( c\_{i}^{p} \\right)}$ (22.4)

The *Y*\-axis shows the confidence score, while the *X*\-axis reflects the number of detections, which ranges from 0 to 30. As 472.observed, most detections fall within the mid-range confidence levels, indicating that while the model reliably identifies objects with a higher accuracy of 0.94. This distribution highlights the model’s performance in real-world scenarios, balancing between precision and recall, where detections with moderate confidence are more frequent, allowing for practical use in the animal detection system.

## **475.22.5** Conclusion and Future Scope

The development and implementation of the animal detection system represent a significant advancement in safeguarding wildlife and preventing animal–vehicle collisions. By leveraging a combination of hardware and advanced deep learning techniques, this system provides a robust solution for real-time animal detection in critical areas such as highways and wildlife reserves.

The system’s architecture is meticulously designed to integrate a PIR sensor, a Pi camera, and a TensorFlow Lite model running on a Raspberry Pi. The PIR sensor is pivotal in detecting motion and triggering image capture, ensuring that the system responds promptly to any potential animal presence. The captured images are processed by the TensorFlow Lite model, which is specifically trained to detect and classify animals. This model, built on the MobileNet SSD architecture, balances accuracy and computational efficiency, making it suitable for deployment on the resource-constrained Raspberry Pi. By implementing bounding boxes around detected animals and classifying them, the model effectively distinguishes between various species and reduces the likelihood of false detections.

The animal data collected from IoT sensors is passed to the SSD model with MobileNet as backbone to provide automated analysis for animal detection in a timely manner. Another approach using YOLOv5 can also be employed to train and detect animals. However, when compared with SSD with MobileNet, SSD demonstrates more effective and accurate real-time detection than YOLOv5. The SSD model has achieved an accuracy of 93% in detecting and classifying animals. It sends the alarm to the nearby forest officer in case of wild animals and simultaneously shares the information with the villages being intruded upon by the wild animals to avoid damage.

Furthermore, automatic protective measures against animal interference are activated by animal intrusion detection systems through their integration with intelligent fences and deterrent systems. The system implementation decreases the chances of wildlife collisions and agricultural damage to create a sustainable balance between human operations and wildlife exploration.

The current system can be enhanced by integrating multi-model sensors with thermal imaging and acoustic sensors to improve the accuracy in real time. Further, drone surveillance systems across larger geographical areas, from wildlife corridors to farm lands, would improve the detection process in real time from sensors integrated with deep learning algorithms with fifth-generation (5G) edge computing tools.
